en: *Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Song.
Translated by Guṇabhadra and Bodhiyaśas. Chapter One: The Five Dharmas. Question:
What are the five?
Answer:
They are: form, mind, mental factors, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned.
What is form? It refers to the four great elements and the derived matter produced by the four great elements.
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What is derived matter?

That is to say: the eye faculty, the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, and body; a portion of the spheres of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects; and non-manifesting matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
These are called material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).
What is mind (*citta*)?
This refers to the mind and the six consciousnesses.
What are the six?
They are eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
These are called mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). What are mental factors?

They are those phenomena that are associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*), namely: feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), desire (*chanda*), liberation (*adhimokṣa*), attention (*manaskāra*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), negligence (*pramāda*), non-negligence (*apramāda*), the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), the roots of unwholesomeness (*akuśala-mūla*), the roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-mūla*), all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); as well as knowledge (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), and clear realization (*abhisamaya*). These, and whatever else arises in association with the mind, are called mental factors.
What are the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)?

They are those factors that are not associated with the mind, namely: the acquisitions (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*), the acquisition of spheres (*āyatanaprāpti*), the acquisition of things (*vastuprāpti*), the acquisition of entrances (*āyatanaprāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the group of names (*nāmakāya*), the group of phrases (*padakāya*), and the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*). These, as well as others that arise together with them and are dissociated from the mind, are called the formations dissociated from mind.
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to the three unconditioned phenomena:
space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation.
This is called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*)?
It is solidity.
What is the water element?
It is moisture.
What is the fire element?
It refers to warmth.
What is the wind element?
It refers to movement.
What is the eye faculty?
It is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
What is the ear faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that is the basis for auditory consciousness.
What is the nose faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that is the basis for olfactory consciousness.
What is the tongue faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness.
What is the body faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that serves as the basis for body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). What is this matter?

It refers to matter that is beautiful, ugly, or intermediate; it is cognized by two types of consciousness: first, visual consciousness, and subsequently, mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). This is what is called matter.
What is sound?

Sound is of two kinds: that which arises dependent on the four great elements that are appropriated (*upātta*), and that which arises dependent on the four great elements that are not appropriated (*anupātta*).
It is cognized by two types of consciousness: first by auditory consciousness, and subsequently by mental consciousness; this is what is called sound.
What is fragrance?

It refers to fragrance that is pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral; it is cognized by two types of consciousness: first by olfactory consciousness, and subsequently by mental consciousness. This is called fragrance.
What is taste?

Taste refers to that which is pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral; it is cognized by two types of consciousness: first by the tongue-consciousness and subsequently by the mental consciousness. This is called taste.
What is the limited portion of the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*)?

It refers to roughness, smoothness, lightness, heaviness, cold, hunger, and thirst. These are cognized by two types of consciousness: first by body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and subsequently by mental-consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is called the limited portion of the sense-base of tangibles.
What is non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?

It refers to matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), which is cognized by a single consciousness—namely, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is called non-informative matter.
What is eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*)?
That is to say, it functions with respect to visible forms based on the eye-faculty.
What is ear-consciousness?
It is that which functions with respect to sounds based on the ear-faculty.
What is nose-consciousness?
It is that which, depending on the faculty of the nose, operates upon odors.
What is tongue-consciousness?
That is to say, it functions with respect to tastes based on the tongue-faculty.
What is body-consciousness?
It is that which functions with respect to tangibles based on the body-faculty.
What is mental consciousness?
It refers to that which operates upon mental objects (dharmas) based on the faculty of mind (manas).
What is feeling (vedanā)?
There are three feelings, namely: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is perception?
There are three perceptions, namely: limited perception, vast perception, and immeasurable perception.
What is volition?
It is the mental formation that gives rise to three kinds of karma: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
What is contact?
This refers to the arising of three kinds of contact through the conjunction of the three factors: namely, painful contact, pleasant contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact.
What is mindfulness?
It refers to the arousal of awareness by the mind, of which there are three kinds:
[These are] those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
What is desire?
It refers to the mind’s intention to act.
What is liberation? It refers to the mind’s having been liberated, its being liberated, and its being about to be liberated.
What is mindfulness?
It means that the mind does not forget.
What is concentration?
It means one-pointedness of mind.
What is wisdom?
It is the definitive discernment regarding phenomena.
What is faith?
It refers to the purity of mind.
What is diligence?
It refers to the mind’s capacity for vigor and courage.
What is vitarka?
It is the coarseness of the mind.
What is vicāra?
It refers to the subtlety of the mind.
What is negligence?
It refers to the non-cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
What is non-negligence?
It is the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
What are the roots of goodness?
There are three roots of goodness, namely: non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
What are the unwholesome roots?
There are three unwholesome roots, namely: attachment, hatred, and delusion.
What are the indeterminate roots?
There are four indeterminate roots, namely: indeterminate craving, indeterminate views, indeterminate conceit, and indeterminate ignorance.
What are the fetters?

There are nine fetters, namely: the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
What is the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to craving (*rāga*) within the three realms.
What is the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
This refers to hostility toward sentient beings.
What is the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*)?

There are seven types of pride: namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
What is pride (*māna*)?

To consider oneself superior to those who are inferior, or to consider oneself equal to those who are superior; to give rise to a mind of contempt toward them, exalting and elevating oneself—this is called pride.
What is overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?

To consider oneself superior to those who are equal, or to consider oneself equal to those who are superior; to give rise to a mind of contempt toward them while exalting and elevating oneself—this is called overweening pride.
What is the pride of pride (*mānātimāna*)?
To consider oneself superior when one is actually superior, and thereby giving rise to a mind of contempt toward others while exalting and elevating oneself—this is called the pride of pride.
What is the pride of self (*asmimāna*)?

To conceive of a self or what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging, and on that basis to give rise to a mind of contempt for others, self-exaltation, and self-inflation—this is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
What is *adhimāna* (overweening pride)?

To claim one has attained what has not been attained, reached what has not been reached, touched what has not been touched, or realized what has not been realized; to give rise to a sense of superiority toward others and to exalt and elevate oneself—this is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
What is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*)?
To regard one who is vastly superior as being slightly inferior, thereby giving rise to a mind of contempt toward them while exalting and elevating oneself—this is called the pride of inferiority.
What is false pride (*mithyāmāna*)?
To claim virtues that one does not possess, thereby giving rise to a mind of contempt for others and exalting and elevating oneself—this is called false pride.
These seven types of pride are termed the fetter of pride (*mānasaṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of ignorance?
It refers to lack of knowledge regarding the three realms.
What is the fetter of views?
There are three views, namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
What is the view of a self-identity?

It refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); to see them as "I" or "mine," and to give rise to desire, acceptance, and views regarding them—this is called the view of a self-identity.
What is the view of extremes?

It refers to the five aggregates of clinging, which one views as either eternal or as subject to annihilation; to give rise to desire, acceptance, and views regarding them—this is called the view of extremes.
What is wrong view?
It refers to the denial of cause and effect; to give rise to desire, acceptance, and views regarding that [denial] is called wrong view.
These three types of views are termed the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of clinging to views?
There are two views, namely, clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
What is clinging to views?

That is to say, regarding the five aggregates of clinging as foremost, supreme, and most excellent, to give rise to desire for them, to give rise to acceptance of them, and to give rise to views regarding them—this is called the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
What is the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

That is to say, regarding the purification, liberation, and essential means of deliverance from the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha), to give rise to desire, to give rise to acceptance, and to give rise to views therein—this is called the attachment to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
These two types of views are termed the fetter of attachment to others' views (parāmarśasaṃyojana).
What is the fetter of doubt?
It refers to the lack of clear understanding regarding the Truths.
What is the fetter of envy?
This refers to the mind’s increase and expansion of hatred.
What is the fetter of stinginess?
It refers to the mind’s firm attachment.
These are called the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
What are the bonds (*bandhana*)?
It is said that the fetters themselves are the bonds.
Furthermore, there are three fetters, namely: the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ill will, and the fetter of ignorance.
What are the latent tendencies?

There are seven latent tendencies, namely: the latent tendency of sensual desire, the latent tendency of ill will, the latent tendency of craving for existence, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of views, and the latent tendency of doubt.
What is the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*)? It is of five kinds:

namely, sensual desire belonging to the realm of desire that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; sensual desire belonging to the realm of desire that is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, the cessation, and the path; and sensual desire belonging to the realm of desire that is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation. These five kinds are called the latent tendency of sensual desire.
What is the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*)? There are five kinds:

namely, aversion to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) bound to the desire realm; aversion to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path; and aversion to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). These five kinds are called the latent tendency of aversion.
What is the latent tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*)?
It is of ten kinds: namely, five kinds bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and five kinds bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What are the five kinds bound to the realm of form?

This refers to craving associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; and craving associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through the path of cultivation.
As there are five types associated with the form realm, so it is for those associated with the formless realm.
These ten types are called the latent tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*).
What is the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*)?
It consists of fifteen types: namely, five types bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), five types bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and five types bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What are the five types of conceit bound to the desire realm?

They are: conceit to be abandoned through the vision of suffering bound to the desire realm; and conceit to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through the path of cultivation, all bound to the desire realm.
Just as there are five types bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
These fifteen types are called the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*).
What is the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*)?

There are fifteen kinds, namely: five kinds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), five kinds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and five kinds bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What are the five kinds bound to the desire realm?

This refers to the ignorance associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; and the ignorance associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, cessation, and path, as well as through the path of cultivation.
As there are five types associated with the desire realm, so it is for those associated with the form and formless realms.
These fifteen types are called the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*).
What is the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*)?

It consists of thirty-six types: namely, twelve types bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), twelve types bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and twelve types bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What are the twelve types associated with the desire realm? They are:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—these being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) within the desire realm; false view and the esteeming of views abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*) within the desire realm; false view and the esteeming of views abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) within the desire realm; and false view, the esteeming of views, and the esteeming of precepts and observances abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga*) within the desire realm.
Just as there are twelve types bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
These thirty-six types are called the proclivities of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*).
What is the proclivity of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*)?
There are twelve kinds, namely: four kinds bound to the desire realm, four kinds bound to the form realm, and four kinds bound to the formless realm.
What are the four kinds bound to the desire realm?

This refers to doubt abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) bound to the desire realm, and doubt abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya), cessation (nirodha), and the path (mārga) bound to the desire realm.
As there are four such types bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form (rūpa) and formless (ārūpya) realms.
These twelve kinds are called the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
What are the afflictions that are superior afflictions?
It is said that the afflictions themselves are the superior afflictions.

Furthermore, there are higher-level afflictions that are not [primary] afflictions; these refer to the remaining defiled aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), excluding the primary afflictions themselves.
What are the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)?

There are eight envelopments: namely, torpor (*styāna*), drowsiness (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), avarice (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). Among the ten envelopments, anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are excluded.
What is knowledge?

There are ten knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of the origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?

It refers to the untainted knowledge that knows the suffering of formations bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge that knows the cause of formations bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge that knows the cessation of formations bound to the desire realm; and the untainted knowledge that knows the path leading to the abandonment of formations bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, dharma-knowledge also takes as its object the untainted knowledge of the stage of dharma-knowledge;
this is called dharma-knowledge.
What is subsequent knowledge?

That is to say: untainted knowledge that cognizes the suffering of formations associated with the realm of form and the formless realm; untainted knowledge that cognizes the cause of formations associated with the realm of form and the formless realm; untainted knowledge that cognizes the cessation of formations associated with the realm of form and the formless realm; and untainted knowledge that cognizes the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the realm of form and the formless realm.
Furthermore, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) also takes as its object the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) of the stage of subsequent knowledge;
this is called subsequent knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna)?

This refers to the knowledge that is the fruit of cultivation, attained through cultivation and not lost; it is the knowledge of the present minds and mental factors of other sentient beings in the desire realm and the form realm, as well as their untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors—this is called the knowledge of others' minds.
What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
It refers to outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*); this is called conventional knowledge.
What is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?

It refers to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) that contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna)?
That is to say, untainted wisdom that contemplates the cause of tainted phenomena as cause, origin, existence, and condition—this is called the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)?
It is untainted wisdom that contemplates cessation as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation—this is called the knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
It refers to untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that contemplates the path as the way, as suchness, as the track, and as the vehicle; this is called the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?

That is to say, "I have known suffering, I have abandoned its origin, I have realized its cessation, and I have cultivated the path"—to give rise to knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, wisdom, and suchness regarding this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of non-arising?
It means: "I have already known suffering; there is nothing further to be known.
I have already abandoned the origin [of suffering]; there is nothing further to be abandoned."
"I have already realized cessation and shall not realize it again;

I have already cultivated the path and shall not cultivate it again. To give rise therein to knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, and wisdom of such immediate realization—this is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, "my outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*) has been exhausted" is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*);
"it shall not arise again" is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
"My outflow of existence (*bhava-āsava*) and my outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsava*) have been exhausted" is called the knowledge of exhaustion.
That which will no longer arise is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is "vision" (*darśana*)?
It means that knowledge itself is vision.

There are some views that are not wisdom, namely the eight uninterrupted patiences (*anantarya-kṣānti*): the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*), the patience regarding the dharma of origin (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*), the subsequent patience regarding origin (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*), the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), the subsequent patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti*), the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), and the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*).
This is called "vision.
Whether it be wisdom or vision, it is precisely "immediate realization" (abhisamaya).
How is it attained?
This refers to the attainment of the state.
What is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?

It is when one who is free from desire for the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna-deva*) but not yet free from desire for the higher realms, having formed the thought of "escaping from conception" through prior preparatory effort, brings about the cessation of mind and mental factors; this is called the attainment of non-conception.
What is the attainment of cessation?

It refers to one who has become detached from the sphere of nothingness but is not yet detached from the higher stages; having first applied the preparatory means consisting of the perception of rest, there occurs the cessation of mind and mental factors—this is called the attainment of cessation.
What is the heaven of non-perception?
It refers to sentient beings born in the heaven of non-perception, wherein the mind and mental factors have ceased; this is called the heaven of non-perception.
What is the life-faculty?
This refers to the life-span of the three realms.
What is "category"?
It refers to the category of sentient beings.
What is acquisition by location?
It refers to the acquisition of a spatial location.
What is acquisition by entity?
This refers to the attainment of the aggregates (*skandha*). What is the attainment of the sense-bases (*āyatana*)?
It refers to the attainment of the internal and external sense-bases.
What is birth? It is the transformation of the aggregates.
What is aging?
It refers to the ripening of the aggregates (*skandha*). How does it abide?
It refers to the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*) that have not yet perished.
What is impermanence? It refers to the arising and destruction of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is called the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*)?
This refers to the "designation.
What is the collection of phrases (*padakāya*)?
It refers to the completion of syllables (*vyañjana*).
What is the body of flavor?
It is said that the body of syllables is the body of flavor. What is space?
That is to say, space is not full; it accommodates all forms and allows for coming and going without obstruction.
What is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
It is said that analytical cessation is liberation.
What is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? It refers to cessation that is not through analytical discernment and is not liberation.
Chapter 20: Analysis of Knowledge (*Jñāna-vibhāga*). What are the ten types of knowledge?

That is to say: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), knowledge of the origin (samudayajñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
What is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
It refers to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as objects, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*) objects.
What is the object-condition of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?

This refers to the object-condition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) being the formations (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpya-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*).
What is the object-condition of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)?
It refers to the knowledge of others' minds taking as its object the present minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) of others associated with the desire and form realms, as well as the untainted.
What is the object of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
It means that conventional knowledge takes all phenomena as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
That is to say, the knowledge of suffering has the five aggregates of clinging as its object.
What is the object of the knowledge of origination?
It is the conditioned causes and conditions that are with outflows.
What is the object-condition for the knowledge of cessation?
It refers to the analytical cessation as the object-condition for the knowledge of cessation.
What is the object-condition for the knowledge of the path?
That is to say, path-knowledge has as its objects the factors of training and the factors beyond training.
What is the object of the knowledge of exhaustion?
It is all conditioned phenomena and analytical cessation as the objects of the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as objects, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as an object.
Question:
For what reason is dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) conditioned by the objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and by the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer:

It is because dharma-knowledge knows the suffering of formations associated with the desire realm, knows the cause of formations associated with the desire realm, knows the cessation of formations associated with the desire realm, and knows the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the desire realm; therefore, it is said that dharma-knowledge is conditioned by the objects of the desire realm and by the untainted.
For what reason is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) conditioned by the formations associated with the form and formless realms, as well as by the untainted (anāsrava)?

It is because subsequent knowledge knows the suffering of the formations associated with the form and formless realms, knows the cause of the formations associated with the form and formless realms, knows the cessation of the formations associated with the form and formless realms, and knows the path for abandoning the formations associated with the form and formless realms; therefore, subsequent knowledge is conditioned by the formations associated with the form and formless realms, as well as by the untainted.

For what reason is it said that the knowledge of others' minds has as its objects the present minds and mental factors of others belonging to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as the untainted?

It is because the knowledge of others' minds knows the present minds and mental factors of others belonging to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as the untainted; therefore, the knowledge of others' minds has as its objects the present minds and mental factors of others belonging to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as the untainted.
For what reason does conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) take all phenomena as its object?
It is because conventional knowledge knows all phenomena as being skillful, unskillful, or neither skillful nor unskillful; therefore, conventional knowledge takes all phenomena as its object.
For what reason is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) conditioned by the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha)?

It is because the knowledge of suffering knows that the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; therefore, the knowledge of suffering is conditioned by the five aggregates of clinging.
For what reason is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) conditioned by outflows?
It is because the knowledge of origination knows the cause of outflows as cause, origination, existence, and condition; therefore, the knowledge of origination is conditioned by outflows.
For what reason is the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) conditioned by calculated cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)?

It is because the knowledge of cessation knows calculated cessation as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation; therefore, the knowledge of cessation is conditioned by calculated cessation.
For what reason does the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) take the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training as its object?

It is because the knowledge of the path knows the path as the way, as suchness, as the track, and as the vehicle; therefore, the knowledge of the path takes the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training as its object.
For what reason is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) the condition for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*)?

It is because the knowledge of exhaustion knows: "I have already known suffering, I have already abandoned the origin, I have already realized cessation, and I have already cultivated the path. Therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion is the condition for all conditioned phenomena and analytical cessation.

For what reason is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?

It is because the knowledge of non-arising knows: "I have already known suffering and shall not know it again; I have already abandoned the origin and shall not abandon it again; I have already realized cessation and shall not realize it again; I have already cultivated the path and shall not cultivate it again. For this reason, the knowledge of non-arising is the object-condition for all conditioned phenomena and analytical cessation.
Question:
How many knowledges (jñāna) is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), and how many are partial aspects of it?

Answer: The knowledge of phenomena is itself the knowledge of phenomena; it is also a partial aspect of seven knowledges, namely: the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Question:
Of how many knowledges is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) composed, and of how many knowledges is it a partial portion?
Answer:

Inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is itself inferential knowledge; it is also a portion of seven knowledges, namely: the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Question:
Of how many knowledges (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) composed, and of how many knowledges is it a partial portion?
Answer:

The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is itself the knowledge of others' minds; it is also a partial portion of four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Question:
Of how many knowledges is conventional knowledge a complete entity, and of how many knowledges is it a partial portion?
Answer:
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is itself conventional knowledge; it is also a portion of one other knowledge, namely, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Question:
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and how many are portions of knowledges?
Answer:

The knowledge of suffering is itself the knowledge of suffering; it is also portions of four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
As it is with the knowledge of suffering, so it is with the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of cessation.
Question:
How many knowledges is the knowledge of the path, and how many knowledges are its partial components?
Answer:

Path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna) is itself path-knowledge; it is also a partial portion of five knowledges, namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising.
Question:
Of how many knowledges is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) composed, and of how many knowledges is it a partial portion?
Answer:

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is itself the knowledge of exhaustion; it is also a portion of six knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
As with the knowledge of exhaustion, so it is with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) as such?

It means that the knowledge of phenomena knows the suffering of formations bound to the desire realm, knows the cause of formations bound to the desire realm, knows the cessation of formations bound to the desire realm, and knows the path leading to the abandonment of formations bound to the desire realm; therefore, the knowledge of phenomena is indeed the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of others' minds through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It means that the knowledge of phenomena knows the untainted minds and mental factors of others who are practicing the path to sever the fetters of the desire realm; therefore, the knowledge of phenomena is the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of phenomena that is the knowledge of suffering?

It means that the knowledge of phenomena knows the five aggregates of clinging bound to the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; therefore, the knowledge of phenomena is the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) regarding the origin [of suffering] (samudayajñāna)?

It means that the knowledge of phenomena knows the cause, the origin, the existence, and the condition of the formations (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm; therefore, it is the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin.
What is the knowledge of cessation within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It means that the knowledge of phenomena knows the cessation of formations bound to the desire realm as cessation, stillness, excellence, and renunciation; therefore, it is the knowledge of cessation within the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) that is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?

It refers to the knowledge of phenomena that knows the path, the way, the track, and the vehicle for abandoning that which is bound to the desire realm; therefore, it is the knowledge of phenomena that is the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) as the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna)?

It means that through the knowledge of phenomena, one knows: "I have already known the suffering of formations associated with the desire realm"; "I have already abandoned the origin of formations associated with the desire realm"; "I have already realized the cessation of formations associated with the desire realm"; and "I have already cultivated the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the desire realm. Therefore, the knowledge of phenomena is the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) as the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna)? It refers to the knowledge of phenomena wherein one knows:

"I have already known the suffering associated with the desire realm; there is nothing further to be known. "I have already abandoned the origin associated with the desire realm; there is nothing further to be abandoned. "I have already realized the cessation associated with the desire realm; there is nothing further to be realized. "I have already cultivated the path for abandoning that which is associated with the desire realm; there is nothing further to be cultivated. Therefore, this is the knowledge of phenomena as the knowledge of non-arising.
What is inferential knowledge that is itself inferential knowledge?

It refers to inferential knowledge that knows the suffering of formations associated with the form and formless realms, knows the cause of formations associated with the form and formless realms, knows the cessation of formations associated with the form and formless realms, and knows the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the form and formless realms; therefore, inferential knowledge is itself inferential knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds through subsequent knowledge?

It means that subsequent knowledge knows the untainted minds and mental factors of others as they practice the path to sever the fetters of the form and formless realms; therefore, it is called the knowledge of others' minds through subsequent knowledge.
What is the knowledge of suffering through subsequent knowledge?

It means that subsequent knowledge knows the five aggregates of clinging associated with the form and formless realms as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; therefore, it is the knowledge of suffering through subsequent knowledge.
What is the subsequent knowledge of origin?

It refers to the subsequent knowledge that knows the cause, the origin, the existence, and the condition of the formations associated with the form and formless realms; therefore, it is called the subsequent knowledge of origin.
What is the subsequent knowledge of cessation?

It means that subsequent knowledge knows the cessation of formations associated with the form and formless realms as cessation, stillness, excellence, and renunciation; therefore, it is called the subsequent knowledge of cessation.
What is subsequent knowledge as the knowledge of the path?

It refers to subsequent knowledge that knows the path, the way, the track, and the vehicle for the practice that leads to the abandonment of the fetters belonging to the form and formless realms; therefore, it is subsequent knowledge as the knowledge of the path.
What is subsequent knowledge as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)? It means that subsequent knowledge knows:

"I have already known the suffering of formations associated with the form and formless realms"; "I have already abandoned the origin of formations associated with the form and formless realms"; "I have already realized the cessation of formations associated with the form and formless realms"; and "I have already cultivated the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the form and formless realms. Therefore, subsequent knowledge is the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is subsequent knowledge of non-arising? It means that through subsequent knowledge one knows:

"I have already known the suffering associated with the form and formless realms; there is no more to be known. One knows: "I have already abandoned the origin associated with the form and formless realms; there is no more to be abandoned. One knows: "I have already realized the cessation associated with the form and formless realms; there is no more to be realized. One knows: "I have already cultivated the path for abandoning what is associated with the form and formless realms; there is no more to be cultivated. Therefore, this is subsequent knowledge of non-arising.
What is meant by "the knowledge of others' minds is itself the knowledge of others' minds"?

It means that the knowledge of others' minds knows the present minds and mental factors associated with the desire realm and the form realm, as well as untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors; therefore, the knowledge of others' minds is itself the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is dharma-knowledge?

It refers to the knowledge of others' minds knowing the untainted mind and mental factors of another’s path of practice for abandoning the fetters of the desire realm; therefore, it is the knowledge of others' minds that is dharma-knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is inferential knowledge?

It refers to the knowledge of others' minds knowing the untainted mind and mental factors of another’s path of cultivation that severs the fetters of the form and formless realms; therefore, the knowledge of others' minds is inferential knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds and so forth?
It refers to the knowledge of others' minds that knows the other's contaminated (*sāsrava*) states of mind and mental factors; therefore, it is called the knowledge of others' minds and so forth.
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is the knowledge of the path?
It refers to the knowledge of others' minds that knows the other's untainted (anāsrava) mind and mental factors; therefore, the knowledge of others' minds is the knowledge of the path.

What is meant by "conventional knowledge is itself conventional knowledge"? It means that conventional knowledge knows all phenomena as being skillful, unskillful, or neither skillful nor unskillful; therefore, conventional knowledge is itself conventional knowledge.
What is conventional knowledge as the knowledge of others' minds?
It means that conventional knowledge knows the tainted minds and mental factors of others; therefore, conventional knowledge is the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of suffering as the knowledge of suffering?

It means that through the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), one knows the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; therefore, the knowledge of suffering is itself the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of suffering that is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?

It means that the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) knows the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) bound to the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; therefore, the knowledge of suffering is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of suffering that is inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?

It means that the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) knows the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) bound to the realms of form and formlessness as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; therefore, the knowledge of suffering is inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of suffering that is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
It means that the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) knows, "I have already known suffering"; therefore, the knowledge of suffering is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of suffering as the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna)?
It means that the knowledge of suffering knows, "I have already known suffering and shall not need to know it again"; therefore, the knowledge of suffering is the knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of origination that is itself the knowledge of origination?

It is the knowledge of origination that knows the cause of the outflows as cause, origination, existence, and condition; therefore, the knowledge of origination is itself the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of origination that is also the knowledge of phenomena?

It refers to the knowledge of origination knowing that the causes of formations bound to the desire realm are their cause, origin, existence, and condition; therefore, it is the knowledge of origination that is the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*)?

It means that the knowledge of origination knows the cause, the origination, the existence, and the condition of the formations (*saṃskāra*) associated with the form and formless realms; therefore, it is the subsequent knowledge regarding the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) as the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
It means that the knowledge of origination knows: "I have already abandoned origination. For this reason, the knowledge of origination is the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of origination as the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna)?

This means that the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) knows: "I have already abandoned origination and shall not abandon it again. Therefore, the knowledge of origination is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) as the knowledge of cessation?
It means that the knowledge of cessation knows cessation as cessation, as stilling, as sublime, and as detachment. Therefore, the knowledge of cessation is the knowledge of cessation itself.
What is the knowledge of cessation that is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It refers to the knowledge of cessation that knows the cessation of formations bound to the desire realm as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation; therefore, it is the knowledge of cessation that is the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of cessation that is subsequent knowledge?

It refers to the knowledge of cessation that knows the cessation of formations associated with the form and formless realms as cessation, stilling, excellence, and renunciation; therefore, it is the knowledge of cessation that is subsequent knowledge.
What is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
It means that the knowledge of cessation knows: "I have realized cessation. For this reason, the knowledge of cessation is the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of cessation as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?

This means that through the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), one knows: "I have already realized cessation; it shall not be realized again. Therefore, the knowledge of cessation is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
How is it that the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) is itself the knowledge of the path?

It means that through the knowledge of the path, one knows the path as the path, as the method, as the track, and as the vehicle. Therefore, the knowledge of the path is itself the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of the path that is also the knowledge of phenomena?

It refers to the knowledge of the path that knows the path, the reality, the track, and the vehicle for practicing the way that leads to the abandonment of what is bound to the desire realm; therefore, it is the knowledge of the path that is the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) as subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?

It refers to the knowledge of the path that knows the path, the method, the track, and the vehicle for practicing the cultivation that severs the fetters belonging to the realms of form and formlessness; therefore, it is called the knowledge of the path as subsequent knowledge.
What is the knowledge of the path that is the knowledge of others' minds?
It means that the knowledge of the path knows the other's uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind and mental factors; therefore, the knowledge of the path is the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of the path that is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) knows: "I have already cultivated the path. Therefore, the knowledge of the path is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
What is the knowledge of the path that is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna)?
It is when the knowledge of the path knows: "I have already cultivated the path; it need not be cultivated again. Therefore, the knowledge of the path is the knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) as such?

It means that through the knowledge of exhaustion one knows: "I have already known suffering; I have already abandoned its origin; I have already realized its cessation; I have already cultivated the path. Therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion is indeed the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion that is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It refers to the knowledge of exhaustion that knows: "I have already known the suffering of formations associated with the desire realm; I have already abandoned the origin of formations associated with the desire realm; I have already realized the cessation of formations associated with the desire realm; I have already cultivated the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the desire realm. Therefore, it is the knowledge of exhaustion that is the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the subsequent knowledge of the knowledge of exhaustion? It refers to the knowledge of exhaustion that knows:

"I have already known the suffering of formations associated with the form and formless realms; I have already abandoned the origin of formations associated with the form and formless realms; I have already realized the cessation of formations associated with the form and formless realms; I have already cultivated the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the form and formless realms. Therefore, it is called the subsequent knowledge of the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion regarding the knowledge of suffering?
It means that through the knowledge of exhaustion, one knows: "I have already known suffering. Therefore, it is the knowledge of exhaustion regarding the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion regarding the knowledge of origin?
It means that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) knows, "I have already abandoned the origin [of suffering]"; therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion is the knowledge of the origin.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)?
It means that the knowledge of exhaustion knows, "I have already realized cessation"; therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion is the knowledge of cessation.

What is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) as the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)? It means that through the knowledge of exhaustion, one knows: "I have cultivated the path. Therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion is the knowledge of the path. What is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) as the knowledge of non-arising? It means that through the knowledge of non-arising, one knows: "I have already attained liberation; there is no further cultivation of the path to be done.
Therefore, the knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of non-arising.

That is to say, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) knows: "I have already known suffering; it need not be known again. I have already abandoned the origin; it need not be abandoned again. I have already realized cessation; it need not be realized again. I have already cultivated the path; it need not be cultivated again. For this reason, the knowledge of non-arising is indeed the knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of non-arising that is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? It refers to the knowledge of non-arising which knows:

"I have already known the suffering of the formations associated with the desire realm; it need not be known again. I have already abandoned the origin of the formations associated with the desire realm; it need not be abandoned again. I have already realized the cessation of the formations associated with the desire realm; it need not be realized again. I have already cultivated the path for the abandonment of the formations associated with the desire realm; it need not be cultivated again. For this reason, it is the knowledge of non-arising that is the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the subsequent knowledge of the knowledge of non-arising? It means that the knowledge of non-arising knows:

"I have already known the suffering of formations associated with the form and formless realms; there is nothing further to be known. I have already abandoned the origin of formations associated with the form and formless realms; there is nothing further to be abandoned. I have already realized the cessation of formations associated with the form and formless realms; there is nothing further to be realized. I have already cultivated the path leading to the abandonment of formations associated with the form and formless realms; there is nothing further to be cultivated. Therefore, this is the subsequent knowledge of the knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of non-arising regarding the knowledge of suffering?
It means that the knowledge of non-arising knows: "I have already known suffering; it need not be known again. Therefore, the knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) regarding the origin of suffering (samudaya-jñāna)?
It means that the knowledge of non-arising knows: "I have already abandoned the origin; it need not be abandoned again. Therefore, the knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of the origin.
What is the knowledge of non-arising and the knowledge of cessation?
It means that the knowledge of non-arising knows: "I have already realized cessation; it shall not be realized again. Therefore, this is the knowledge of non-arising and the knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of non-arising as the knowledge of the path?
It means that the knowledge of non-arising knows: "I have already cultivated the path and shall not cultivate it again. Therefore, the knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of the path.
Question:
Of these ten knowledges, how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer:
One is with outflows (*sāsrava*), eight are without outflows (*anāsrava*), and one is to be analyzed.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is either with outflows or without outflows.
What is with outflows?
This means that the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the other's contaminated (sāsrava) mind and mental factors.
What is uncontaminated (anāsrava)?
It means that the knowledge of others' minds cognizes the other's uncontaminated mind and mental factors.
Question:
Of these ten knowledges, how many have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana) and how many have non-outflowing objects (anāsrava-ālambana)?
Answer:
Two have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana), namely the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna);
two have outflow-free objects (anāsrava-ālambana), namely the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna);
six are to be distinguished.
Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) has either contaminated objects (sāsravālambana) or uncontaminated objects (anāsravālambana).
What are its contaminated objects?
They are the objects of suffering (duḥkha) and origination (samudaya) within dharma-knowledge.
What is the object of the untainted (anāsrava)?
It refers to the cessation-object and path-object of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
As it is with the knowledge of phenomena, so it is with subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
The knowledge of others' minds has either impure objects or pure objects.
What is meant by having impure objects?
It refers to the knowledge of others' minds that knows the impure minds and mental factors of others.
What is that which has the untainted as its object?
It refers to the knowledge of others' minds that knows the untainted minds and mental factors of others.
As for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), it may have either the tainted or the untainted as its object.
What is that which has outflows as its object?
It refers to conventional knowledge having suffering or origination as its object.
What is that which is without outflows as its object?
That is to say, conventional knowledge has as its objects cessation, the path, space, and analytical cessation.
Question:
Of these ten knowledges, how many are conditioned and how many are unconditioned?
Answer:
It is said that all ten knowledges are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); none are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Question:
Among these ten knowledges, how many have conditioned objects and how many have unconditioned objects?
Answer:
Four have conditioned objects, namely: the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path.
One has unconditioned objects as its condition, namely, the knowledge of cessation;
five are to be analyzed.
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) may have conditioned objects as its condition or unconditioned objects as its condition.
What is the conditioned object-condition?
It refers to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) having suffering as its object-condition, origination as its object-condition, and the path as its object-condition.
What is the unconditioned object-condition?
This refers to the dharma-knowledge that takes cessation as its object.
As it is with dharma-knowledge, so it is with subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) may take conditioned phenomena as its object or unconditioned phenomena as its object.
What is the conditioned object-condition?
It refers to conventional knowledge having suffering as its object-condition, origination as its object-condition, and the path as its object-condition.
What is the unconditioned object-condition?
That is to say, the two kinds of cessation-conditions and the space-condition for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.
Chapter Three: Analysis of the Bases (Āyatana-vibhaṅga) As the Blessed One said to the Brahmin Śāṭhīśūluna: "Brahmin, you should know that 'all' refers to the twelve bases."
What are the twelve?

They are the eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, the tangible-base, the mind-base, and the mental-object-base.
Question:
Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are material (rūpa) and how many are non-material (arūpa)?
Answer:
Ten are form; one is non-form; [the remainder] are to be analyzed.
As for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is sometimes form and sometimes non-form. What is form?
That is to say, bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are form; the remainder are non-form.
Among these twelve spheres (*āyatana*), how many are visible and how many are invisible?
One is visible; eleven are invisible.
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
It is said that ten are with resistance and two are without resistance.
Of these twelve bases, how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
That is to say, ten are with-outflows (sāsrava), and two are to be analyzed.
As for the mind-base (manāyatana), it is either with-outflows or without-outflows (anāsrava).
What is with-outflows?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) associated with tainted mental formations.
What is untainted?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with untainted mental formations.
The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What is with outflows?

It refers to the outflowing bodily and vocal actions included within the sphere of mental objects, as well as the outflowing aggregates of feeling (vedanā-skandha), perception (saṃjñā-skandha), and formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?

It refers to untainted bodily and vocal karma, the untainted aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Among these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and how many are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
That is to say, eleven [bases] are conditioned;
one portion of the *dharmāyatana* is either conditioned or unconditioned.
What is conditioned?
This refers to bodily and vocal karma included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to space, cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha), and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha).
Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are with conflict (saraṇa) and how many are without conflict (araṇa)?
It is said that ten are with conflict; two are to be distinguished: if they are with outflows (sāsrava), they are with conflict; if they are without outflows (anāsrava), they are without conflict.
As it is with the contentious and the non-contentious, so it is with the mundane and the supramundane;

the faulty and the faultless; the household life and the renunciation of the household; the proclivities and that which is not a proclivity; the acquisitions and that which is not an acquisition; and the fetters and that which is not a fetter—all are likewise.
Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are determinate (vyākṛta) and how many are indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
Eight are indeterminate; four are to be analyzed.
The base of form (rūpāyatana) is sometimes determinate and sometimes indeterminate.
What is determinate?
It refers to the wholesome and unwholesome spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*).
What is indeterminate?
This refers to all remaining bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), excluding wholesome and unwholesome bases of form.
As it is with the base of form, so it is with the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), the base of mind (*manāyatana*), and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are obscured (*nivṛta*) and how many are unobscured (*anivṛta*)?
It is said that eight are unobscured and four are to be analyzed.
As for the base of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is either obscured or unobscured.
What is "concealed"?
It refers to that which is defiled.
What is "unconcealed"?
That is to say, they are undefiled.
As it is with the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), so it is with the sense-bases of sound (*śabdāyatana*), mind (*manāyatana*), and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Among these twelve sense-bases, how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and how many are not to be cultivated?
That is to say, eight [bases] should not be cultivated, while four are to be analyzed.
As for the base of form (*rūpāyatana*), it may either be cultivated or not be cultivated.
How is it that it should be cultivated?
This refers to the wholesome sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the unwholesome and indeterminate spheres of form.
As it is with the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), so it is with the sense-spheres of sound (*śabdāyatana*) and mind (*manāyatana*).
As for the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it is either to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) or not to be cultivated. What is to be cultivated?
This refers to the entry into wholesome conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the entry into unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena (*dharma*), as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and how many are undefiled (*akliṣṭa*)?
Eight are undefiled; four are to be distinguished.
The base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is either defiled or undefiled.
What is defiled?
It refers to that which is obscured. What is undefiled?
That is to say, they are non-obscured.
As it is with the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana), so it is with the sense-bases of sound (śabdāyatana), mind (manāyatana), and mental phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Among these twelve sense-bases, how many are faulty (sāvadya) and how many are faultless (anavadya)?
That is to say, eight are without fault (*anavadya*), and four are to be analyzed.
As for the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), it may be with fault (*sāvadya*) or without fault. What is with fault?
This refers to unwholesome forms and obscured-neutral forms.
What is blameless?
This refers to wholesome forms and non-obscured-neutral forms.
As it is with the sense-base of form, so it is with the sense-bases of sound, mind, and mental phenomena.
Of these twelve sense-bases, how many have retribution and how many are without retribution?
It is said that eight are without retribution, while four are to be analyzed.
The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is either with retribution (savipāka) or without retribution (avipāka).
What is with retribution?
It refers to wholesome and unwholesome sense-bases of form.
What is that which has no retribution?
It refers to the indeterminate sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
As it is with the sphere of form, so it is with the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
The mind-base (manāyatana) is either retributive (savipāka) or non-retributive (avipāka).
What is retributive?
It refers to the unwholesome and wholesome-with-outflows (sāsrava) mind-bases.
What is that which has no retribution?
It refers to the indeterminate and untainted mind-base (*manāyatana*).
As with the mind-base, so it is with the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are seeing (*darśana*) and how many are non-seeing?
One is seeing; ten are non-seeing; and one is to be analyzed.
As for the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it is sometimes seeing and sometimes non-seeing.
What is "view"?

It is said that eight types of views are called "views," namely: the five false views, mundane right view, the view of one in training (śaikṣa), and the view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa); all others are not views.
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are internal and how many are external?
They are six internal and six external.
Of these twelve bases, how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
That is to say, three are non-appropriated (*anupātta*), and nine are differentiated.
The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What is appropriated?
This refers to feeling by its own nature.
What is non-feeling?
It refers to that which is not feeling by its own nature.
As it is with the eye-base, so it is with the form-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, and the tangible-base.
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are mind (*citta*) and how many are not mind?
One is mind; eleven are not mind.
Of these twelve bases, how many are with an object (*sālambana*) and how many are without an object (*anālambana*)?
That is to say: one [of the twelve bases] has an object, ten have no object, and one is to be analyzed.
As for the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it either has an object or has no object. What has an object?
That is to say, mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
What is "without an object" (*anālambana*)?
That is to say, non-mental factors.
Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are mental factors (citta-dharma) and how many are non-mental factors?
Eleven are non-mental factors; one part of the base of phenomena (dharma-āyatana) is either a mental factor or a non-mental factor.
What are mental factors?
They are those that possess an object.
What are non-mental factors?
That is to say, they are without an object.
Among these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are karma and how many are not karma?
It is said that nine are not karma, while three are to be analyzed.
The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is either karma or non-karma. What is karma?
It refers to bodily action; the remainder is non-karma.
The sense-base of sound is either karma or non-karma.
What is karma?
It refers to that which is produced by the mouth; the rest is non-karma.
The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is either karma or non-karma. What is karma?
That which is comprised within the sphere of mental objects—namely, bodily and vocal karma as well as volition (cetanā)—is karma; the remainder is non-karma.
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
It is said that eight are indeterminate and four are to be analyzed.
The base of form (*rūpāyatana*) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to wholesome bodily action.
What is unwholesome?
This refers to unwholesome bodily action.
What is neutral?
It refers to all other bodily action-forms, excluding wholesome and unwholesome bodily action-forms.
The sense-base of sound may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to vocal sounds that are wholesome.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to unwholesome vocal sounds.
What is indeterminate?
This refers to all vocal sounds other than those that are wholesome or unwholesome.
As for the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with wholesome mental attention.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with unwholesome mental attention.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) associated with indeterminate mental volition (manasikāra).
As for the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana), it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?

It refers to wholesome bodily and vocal actions included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), as well as the wholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha).
What is unwholesome?
This refers to unwholesome bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), as well as the unwholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is indeterminate?
It refers to the indeterminate aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations subsumed under the sphere of mental objects, as well as space and analytical cessation.
Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are abandoned by vision (darśana-prahātavya), how many are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), and how many are not to be abandoned (aprahātavya)?
It is said: ten are abandoned by cultivation; two are to be distinguished.
As for the mind base (manāyatana), it is either abandoned by vision, or abandoned by cultivation, or not to be abandoned.
What is abandoned through vision?

It is that which is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) within the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*).
How is it abandoned?
This refers to the mind-base (manāyatana) associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by seeing.
What is abandoned by cultivation?
It is the mind-base of one in training (śaikṣa) who has seen the path and abandons it through cultivation.
How is it abandoned?

It refers to the mental sense-sphere (*manāyatana*) associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the untainted (*akliṣṭa*) impure (*sāsrava*) mental sense-sphere.
How is it not abandoned?
This refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind-base (*manāyatana*) and phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).
These are either to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
What is to be abandoned by seeing?

If the *dharmāyatana* is abandoned by the *anantarya-kṣānti* (uninterrupted patience) and so forth of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), how is it abandoned?

It refers to the eighty-eight *anuśayas* (proclivities) to be abandoned through seeing, the *dharmāyatana* associated with them, and the non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them.
What is abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to those factors included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are abandoned through cultivation by one who has entered the path of seeing and attained the track of the trainee (*śaikṣa*). How are they abandoned?

This refers to the entry into the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, the mental states associated with them, the bodily and vocal actions they give rise to, the formations dissociated from mind that they produce, and the non-defiled impure (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
What is "not to be abandoned"?
It refers to the untainted (anāsrava) dharma-entrances (dharmāyatana).
Among these twelve entrances (āyatanas), how many are associated with training (śaikṣa), how many are beyond training (aśaikṣa), and how many are neither associated with training nor beyond training?
That is to say, ten [bases] are neither-learner-nor-non-learner; two are to be analyzed.
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it is either learner, or non-learner, or neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is learner?
This refers to the sense-base of mind associated with the mental attention of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with the mental attention of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) associated with outflowing mental attention (sāsrava-manasikāra).
As for the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana), it may be trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
What is training (*śaikṣa*)?
It refers to the training in bodily and vocal actions, and the training in the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
That is to say: the bodily and vocal karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations of one beyond training.
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? That is to say:
