the contaminated bodily and vocal karma included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), the contaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).

Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
It is said: two are bound to the desire realm; ten are to be analyzed.
The eye-base is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the eye-base produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the realm of form.
As it is with the sense-base of the eye, so it is with the sense-bases of visible form, the ear, sound, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
The sense-base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) is either bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) or bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the sense-base of tangibles produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
It refers to the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form.
The sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the realm of form, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*) bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) associated with mental attention (manasikāra) bound to the form realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with mental attention bound to the formless realm.
What is non-bound?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
As for the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it may be bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or non-bound.
What is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

It refers to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is bound to the desire realm and is comprised therein: namely, the bodily and vocal karma comprised therein, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations comprised therein.
What is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

This refers to the dharmāyatana associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), which includes the bodily and vocal karma subsumed therein, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations subsumed therein.
What is associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

That is to say, the *dharmāyatana* bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of the aggregates (*skandha*) of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*) included therein. What is not bound?

It refers to bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) included in the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as the untainted aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are past, how many are future, and how many are present?
It is said that eleven are either past, future, or present; this is the analysis.
As for the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), if it is conditioned, it is either past, future, or present;
if it is unconditioned, it is neither past, nor future, nor present.

Of these twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), how many under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), how many under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), how many under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), and how many are not subsumed under any Truth?
That is to say, ten [bases] are subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin; two are distinguished.
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin;
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is subsumed under the truth of the path.
As for the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana): if it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin;
if it is without outflows (anāsrava), it is subsumed under the truth of the path if it is conditioned, or under the truth of cessation if it is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Space and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are not included within the [Four] Truths.

Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), how many are abandoned by the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), how many are abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya), how many are abandoned by the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), how many are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), and how many are not to be abandoned (aprahātavya)?
That is to say, ten [bases] are abandoned through cultivation, while two are to be analyzed.

As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it is either abandoned through the vision of suffering, or abandoned through the vision of origin, or abandoned through the vision of cessation, or abandoned through the vision of the path, or abandoned through cultivation, or not abandoned at all.
What is meant by "abandoned through the vision of suffering"?

It refers to that which is abandoned by the patience regarding the non-arising of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and so forth, belonging to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) within the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*).
How is it abandoned?
This refers to the mind-base (*manāyatana*) associated with the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?

It is the mind-base that is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption regarding origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and so forth, for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned through the vision of the origin?
It refers to the mental sense-base associated with nineteen proclivities abandoned through the vision of the origin.
How are they abandoned through the vision of cessation?

If the mind-base (*manāyatana*) of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) is abandoned through the patience that arises immediately after cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), how is it abandoned?
It refers to the mind-base associated with the nineteen proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).
What is abandoned by the path of seeing?

It is that which is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth on the path of cultivation for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How is it abandoned?
This refers to the mind-base (manāyatana) associated with the twenty-two proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It is the mind-base of one in training (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks [of the path] and abandons it through cultivation.
How are they abandoned?

It refers to the mental sense-base (*manāyatana*) associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the untainted (*akliṣṭa*) out-flowing (*sāsrava*) mental sense-base.
How are they not abandoned?
This refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind-base (*manāyatana*) and phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*),

which are either abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
What is abandonment through the vision of suffering?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are abandoned by the patience of non-interval regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) and so forth, belonging to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?

This refers to the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), the sense-sphere bases (*āyatana*) associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising therefrom.
What is abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?

It refers to those factors within the sense-sphere bases that are abandoned by the patience of non-interruption regarding origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

How are they abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)? It refers to the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin, the sense-sphere (*dharmāyatana*) associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them.
How are they abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*)?

If the *dharmāyatana* is abandoned by the *nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* (patience following the knowledge of cessation) of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*),
how is it abandoned?

It refers to the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*darśana-heya*), the *dharmāyatana* associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them.
What is abandoned by the path of seeing?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantaryakṣānti*) and so forth on the path of the person who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the person who follows by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?

This refers to the twenty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) arising from them.

What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)? It refers to those factors within the mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are abandoned through cultivation by one who has entered the state of training (*śaikṣa*) and seen the tracks [of the noble path].
How are they abandoned?

It refers to the cultivation-abandonment of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the entry into the factors associated with them, the bodily and vocal actions produced by them, the formations dissociated from mind produced by them, and the untainted yet impure (*sāsrava*) entries into phenomena.
What is non-abandonment?
It refers to the entry into untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Question:
Regarding the five aggregates (skandhas) and the twelve bases (āyatanas): do the five aggregates subsume the twelve bases, or do the twelve bases subsume the five aggregates?
Answer:
The twelve bases subsume the five aggregates; it is not that the five aggregates subsume the twelve bases.
What is not included?
It refers to the unconditioned dharma-entrance (*asaṃskṛta-dharmāyatana*).
Question:
Regarding the five aggregates (skandhas) and the eighteen elements (dhātus): do the five aggregates subsume the eighteen elements, or do the eighteen elements subsume the five aggregates?
Answer:
The eighteen elements subsume the five aggregates; it is not that the five aggregates subsume the eighteen elements.
What is not included?
It refers to the unconditioned dharma-realm (asaṃskṛta-dharmadhātu).
Question:

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśati-indriya*): do the five aggregates subsume the twenty-two faculties, or do the twenty-two faculties subsume the five aggregates?
Answer:
Two aggregates and a portion of two aggregates subsume the twenty-two faculties; the twenty-two faculties likewise subsume two aggregates and a portion of two aggregates.
What is not included?
It refers to one aggregate (skandha) and a portion of two aggregates.
Question:

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the ninety-eight proclivities (*aśīty-anuśaya*): do the five aggregates encompass the ninety-eight proclivities, or do the ninety-eight proclivities encompass the five aggregates?
Answer:
A small portion of one aggregate encompasses the ninety-eight proclivities, and the ninety-eight proclivities also encompass a small portion of one aggregate.
What is not included?
It refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) and a portion of one aggregate.
Question:
Regarding the twelve bases (āyatana) and the eighteen elements (dhātu): do the twelve bases subsume the eighteen elements, or do the eighteen elements subsume the twelve bases?
Answer:
They subsume one another reciprocally, as appropriate.
Question:
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), do the twelve bases subsume the twenty-two faculties, or do the twenty-two faculties subsume the twelve bases?
Answer:

The six internal bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one external base encompass the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*); the twenty-two faculties also encompass the six internal bases and a portion of one external base.
What is not included?
It refers to the five external bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one external base.

Question: Regarding the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) and the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), do the twelve bases include the ninety-eight proclivities, or do the ninety-eight proclivities include the twelve bases?
Answer:
A portion of one external base (bāhyāyatana) subsumes ninety-eight proclivities (anuśaya), and the ninety-eight proclivities also subsume a portion of one external base.
What is not so subsumed?
That is to say, the eleven bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one external base.
Question:

Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), do the eighteen elements subsume the twenty-two faculties, or do the twenty-two faculties subsume the eighteen elements?
Answer:

The twelve internal elements (*āyatana*) and a portion of one external element subsume the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*); likewise, the twenty-two faculties also subsume the twelve internal elements and a portion of one external element.
What is not included?
It refers to the five external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) and a portion of one external base.
Question:

Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): do the eighteen elements subsume the ninety-eight proclivities, or do the ninety-eight proclivities subsume the eighteen elements?
Answer:
A small portion of one external element subsumes the ninety-eight proclivities, and the ninety-eight proclivities also subsume a small portion of one external element.
What is not included?
It refers to seventeen elements (*dhātu*) and a portion of one external element.
Question:

Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) and the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): do the twenty-two faculties subsume the ninety-eight proclivities, or do the ninety-eight proclivities subsume the twenty-two faculties?
Answer:
They do not mutually include one another. Chapter 48:

Classification of the Seven Matters, from the *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*. The seven matters are: the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), the six elements (*dhātu*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten minor defiled universal mental factors (*parīttakleśabhūmika-dharma*), the five defilements (*kleśa*), the five contacts (*sparśa*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five factors (*dharma*), the six groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*), the six groups of contact (*sparśakāya*), the six groups of feeling (*vedanākāya*), the six groups of perception (*saṃjñākāya*), the six groups of volition (*cetanākāya*), and the six groups of craving (*tṛṣṇākāya*).

What are the eighteen elements? They are: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible-object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
What are the twelve bases (*āyatana*)?

They are the eye-base and the form-base; the ear-base and the sound-base; the nose-base and the odor-base; the tongue-base and the taste-base; the body-base and the tangible-base; and the mind-base and the mental-object-base.
What are the five aggregates?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
What are the five aggregates of clinging?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
What are the six elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
What are the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma)?

They are: sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), mindfulness (smṛti), desire (chanda), resolve (adhimokṣa), attention (manaskāra), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).
What are the ten universal factors of affliction (kleśamahābhūmika-dharma)?
They are: lack of faith, indolence, forgetfulness, distraction, ignorance, wrong wisdom, wrong mindfulness, wrong liberation, restlessness, and negligence.
What are the ten minor universal defilements? They are:
anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, guile, arrogance, and harmfulness.
What are the five afflictions?
They are sensual desire, desire for form, desire for the formless, ill will, and delusion.
What are the five contacts?
They are: contact through opposition, contact through predominant speech, contact with clarity, contact with ignorance, and contact that is neither with clarity nor with ignorance.
What are the five views? They are:
the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, false view, the view of clinging to views, and the view of clinging to precepts and observances.
What are the five faculties?
They are the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
What are the five factors?
They are vitarka, vicāra, vijñāna, āhrīkya, and anapatrāpya.
What is the group of six consciousnesses?
They are eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
What are the six groups of contact?
They are: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
What are the six groups of feeling?
That is to say: feelings born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What are the six groups of perception?
They are: perceptions born of eye-contact, and perceptions born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What are the six groups of volition?
They are volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
What are the six groups of craving?
This refers to craving born of eye-contact, and craving born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What is the eye-element?
It is that which, with respect to forms, has seen, now sees, or will see; it possesses a portion corresponding to each of those instances.
What is the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*)?
It is that form which has been seen, is being seen, or will be seen by the eye, according to its respective portion.
What is the element of visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*)?

If the eye sees forms and gives rise to eye-consciousness, or if one sees forms with the eye as the predominant condition; whether it be the eye-consciousness regarding forms or the consciousness that discriminates and knows forms—this is called the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
What is the ear-element (*śrotradhātu*)?
It is that which has heard, is hearing, or will hear sounds; it consists of each respective part thereof.
What is the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*)?
If sound has been heard, is being heard, or will be heard by the ear, it exists in accordance with its respective portion.
What is the ear-consciousness element (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*)?

When the ear hears a sound and ear-consciousness arises—the hearing of sound with the ear as its predominant condition—or when ear-consciousness [perceives] the sound, or when consciousness discriminates and knows the sound: this is called the ear-consciousness element.
What is the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*)?
It is that which, regarding odors, has been cognized, is being cognized, or will be cognized by the nose; it consists of each respective constituent part thereof.
What is the odor element (*gandhadhātu*)?
If an odor has been smelled, is being smelled, or will be smelled by the nose, it exists in accordance with its respective portion.
What is the element of nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*)?

If the nose perceives an odor and nose-consciousness arises, or if there is the perception of an odor through the predominance of the nose, or if the nose-consciousness [is directed] toward an odor, or if consciousness discerns and knows the odor—this is called the element of nose-consciousness.
What is the tongue element (*jihvā-dhātu*)?
It is when the tongue has tasted, is tasting, or will taste an object; it possesses a portion corresponding to each of those instances.
What is the flavor element (*rasa-dhātu*)?
If a taste has been tasted, is being tasted, or will be tasted by the tongue, it exists according to its respective portion.
What is the tongue-consciousness element (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*)?

When the tongue tastes a flavor and tongue-consciousness arises, or when there is tasting of flavor with the tongue as the dominant condition, or when tongue-consciousness [perceives] the flavor, or when consciousness discriminates and knows the flavor—this is called the tongue-consciousness element.
What is the body element (*kāyadhātu*)?
It is that which, regarding tangibles, has been felt, is being felt, or will be felt by the body; it possesses a portion corresponding to each of those [tangibles].
What is the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*)?
If there is contact with the body that has been felt, is being felt, or will be felt, it exists in accordance with its respective portion.
What is the element of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñānadhātu*)?

When the body feels contact and body-consciousness arises, or when there is the predominance of the body in feeling contact—whether it be the body-consciousness regarding contact, or the consciousness that discriminates and knows contact—this is called the element of body-consciousness.
What is the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
It is that which has cognized, is cognizing, or will cognize mental objects (*dharma*), according to each respective part [of its function].
What is the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon has been cognized by the mind, is being cognized, or will be cognized, one possesses a portion thereof.
What is the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?

When the mind takes phenomena as its object and gives rise to mental consciousness—wherein the mind is the predominant condition for the phenomena—or when mental consciousness relates to phenomena, or when consciousness discerns and knows phenomena, this is called the mental consciousness element.
The same detailed explanation applies to the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
It refers to the ten types of form-bases (*rūpāyatana*) and the form included within the sense-base of mental objects.
What is the aggregate of feeling?
It refers to the six groups of feeling.
What are the six?
That is to say: feelings born of eye-contact, up to and including feelings born of mind-contact.
What is the aggregate of perception?
It refers to the six groups of perception.
What are the six?
They are the perceptions born of eye-contact, up to and including the perceptions born of mind-contact.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha)?
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is of two kinds: those associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and those dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
What is the aggregate of formations associated with the mind?

It refers to volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), desire (*chanda*), liberation (*vimukti*), attention (*manasikāra*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), negligence (*pramāda*), non-negligence (*apramāda*), the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), the roots of unwholesomeness (*akuśalamūla*), the roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛtamūla*), all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); all forms of knowledge (*jñāna*), all views (*dṛṣṭi*), and all types of immediate realization (*abhisamaya*). Such categories of mental factors associated with the mind are called the aggregate of formations associated with the mind.
What is the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*)?

It refers to all acquisitions (*prāpti*), the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the generic similarity of body (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the acquisition of bases (*āyatana-prāpti*), the acquisition of things (*vastu-prāpti*), the acquisition of entrances (*dhātu-prāpti*), arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*anityatā*); as well as the group of names (*nāma-kāya*), the group of phrases (*pada-kāya*), and the group of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). Such factors dissociated from mind as these are called the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind.
Those two factors together constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
What is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.
What are the six?
They are the group of visual consciousnesses, up to and including the group of mental consciousnesses.
What is the aggregate of the predominance of form?

If form is characterized by outflows and intense grasping—meaning that regarding this form, whether past, future, or present, desire has arisen, does arise, or will arise, or greed, hatred, or delusion [arise]—and each of those mental factors of affliction has arisen or will arise, this is called the "aggregative mass of form characterized by intensity" (rūpa-oghāyatana).
The aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations are also like this.
What is the aggregate of consciousness?

If consciousness is associated with outflows and is a state of intense grasping—meaning that regarding this consciousness, whether in the past, future, or present, desire has arisen, is arising, or will arise; or greed, hatred, or delusion [has arisen, is arising, or will arise]; and each of those mental factors of affliction has arisen, is arising, or will arise—this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the earth element?
It is characterized by solidity, and so on, up to the wind element, as explained in the *Pañcadharmaka-varga*.
What is the space element?
This refers to form that has space as its limit.
What is the element of consciousness?
It refers to the five groups of consciousness and the group of consciousness associated with outflows (āsrava).
What is feeling (*vedanā*)?
It refers to the experience, perception, and cognition of the three types of objective spheres—suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither—which arise as such.
What is perception (*saṃjñā*)?
That is to say, perception (*saṃjñā*), conceptualization (*saṃjñāna*), and predominant perception operate with respect to images and appearances.
What is volition (*cetanā*)?
It refers to volition, conceptual volition, and predominant volition; it is volition that initiates mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) toward karma.
What is contact (*sparśa*)?
It refers to contact, equal contact, and predominant contact; it functions through the conjunction of the mind with its conditions and objects.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
This refers to the mind’s awakening, recollecting, and reflecting upon the objects of mental activity.
What is desire?
It is the longing for an object, maintaining it firmly, becoming deeply attached to it, and taking pleasure in its production.
What is liberation?
It refers to the liberation of the mind and the release of the intellect from its objects.
What is mindfulness?
This means mindfulness and constant recollection do not abandon the object of focus, nor do they allow for negligence, distraction, or forgetfulness.
What is concentration?
It means the mind abides evenly, remaining unmoved and not shifting from its object; it is neither scattered nor distracted, but is gathered and unified in stillness.
What is wisdom?
It refers to the mind’s engagement with phenomena through the characteristic of discernment, involving decisive judgment, cognitive awareness, clear illumination, and investigation.
What is lack of faith?

That is to say: the mind does not have faith and acceptance, lacks correct reflection, does not cultivate the roots of virtue, does not plant seeds of wholesome conduct, does not perform superior deeds, and the intention is not pure.
What is indolence?
It refers to a mind that is inferior, lacking diligence and vigor, and not swift in its mental activity.
What is forgetfulness?
This refers to mindfulness of the false and outwardly directed erroneous explanations.
What is distraction?
It refers to the mind being agitated, scattered, drifting, racing, and moving, such that its objects of focus do not remain on a single point.
What is ignorance? It refers to the delusion regarding the three realms, being dark and lacking knowledge.
What is wrong wisdom?
This refers to the resolution of wrong understanding that does not accord with right mindfulness.
What is wrong recollection?
It is the defiled mental activity of crookedly perceiving objects through improper reflection.
What is false liberation?
It refers to the liberation of defiled mental formations from their objects.
What is agitation?
It refers to the mind being restless and not relying on tranquility.
What is negligence?
It refers to abandoning correct application, performing what should not be done, and failing to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas.
What is anger (*krodha*)?
It refers to the arising of a mind of resentment toward harmful matters or toward the continuity of hatred.
What is resentment (*upanāha*)?
This refers to the arising of a mind of resentment when encountering circumstances that do not accord with one's desires.
What is concealment (*mrakṣa*)?
It refers to the hiding of one's own transgressions.
What is resentment (*pradāsa*)?
It refers to when the mind is heated and scorched.
What is envy (*īrṣyā*)?
This refers to the arising of a mind of envy and jealousy toward someone one dislikes, wishing them no benefit.
What is stinginess?
It refers to the mind’s firm attachment to what it has received, refusing to let go.
What is deception? It is the act of cheating or deceiving others.
What is flattery?
This refers to the arising of mental crookedness and conduct.
What is *mada*?
It refers to the mind being intoxicated, uplifted, and deluded.
What is ill will (*vyāpāda*)?
It refers to the arousal of a mind that oppresses and torments sentient beings.
What is sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)?
If there is desire-greed and so forth, a gathering of greed, a chamber of greed, and firm attachment with craving and delight—
what is greed for forms? If there is greed for forms and so forth, a gathering of greed, a chamber of greed, and firm attachment with craving and delight.
What is lust for the formless?
It is the lust for the formless, the pervasive lust, the fetter, the accumulation, the lustful dwelling, and the firm attachment and delight therein.
What is ill will?
That is to say, toward those sentient beings,
one gives rise to a mind of harm,
slanders them, and oppresses them with harshness.
What is doubt? It refers to confusion regarding the truths and a lack of clear understanding.
What is contact through opposition?
This refers to contact associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness.
What is predominant verbal contact?
It refers to contact associated with the group of mental consciousness.
What is contact associated with clarity?
It refers to untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*).
What is contact associated with ignorance?
That is to say, defiled contact.
What is contact that is neither clarity nor ignorance?
That is to say, non-defiled, out-flowing contact.
What is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
It refers to the arising of views regarding a self or what belongs to a self with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*), and to endure, delight in, and adhere to them.
What is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
This refers to the endurance of and attachment to views of annihilationism or eternalism regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
What is wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*)?
It refers to the denial of cause and effect, the disparagement of what ought to be done, and the endurance of and attachment to such [views].
What is the clinging to views?

It refers to giving rise to the view that the five aggregates of clinging are the foremost, the highest, and the most excellent, and then accepting them with endurance, delighting in, and adhering to them.
What is the clinging to precepts and observances?

This refers to giving rise to views regarding the five aggregates of clinging as being purity, liberation, and the essential way out, and then becoming patient with, delighting in, and attached to them.
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
It is when one is touched by a contact that is pleasant, and there arises bodily or mental pleasure, as well as the perception of awareness.
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?
It is when one is touched by a contact that is painful, and there arises bodily pain and so forth, as well as the perception of being aware of it.
What is the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*)?
If one is touched by a pleasant feeling-contact, and there arises in the mind a perception of joy and the experience of feeling born thereof—this is the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*).
What is the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*)?
If one is touched by an unpleasant feeling-contact, and there arises in the mind a perception of suffering and the experience of feeling born thereof—this is the faculty of grief.
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
When one is touched by a contact that is neither painful nor pleasant, there arises in the body and mind a feeling that is neither a perception nor a non-perception.
What is perception (*saṃjñā*)?

If the mind is characterized by initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), and if the perception of form increases the perception of form, then the coarse mind proceeds through the mental activity of perceiving, enumerating, and discerning.
How does it observe?
If the mind moves with little movement and follows subtle movement, it proceeds in accordance with the subtle mind.
What is consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
What is lack of shame?

If the mind lacks a sense of shame, it does not feel aversion toward faults, nor does it feel intense renunciation; it is neither reverent nor supple, neither self-terrified nor self-abashed, and thus acts according to its own whims with total autonomy.
What is lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*)?

It is being without shame before others; having no dread of wrongdoing, no fear of wrongdoing, and no perception of wrongdoing; and not feeling bashfulness before others regarding various faults and evils.
What is eye-consciousness?

It refers to the arising of eye-consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms; with the eye as the predominant condition for visible forms, the eye-consciousness cognizes or discriminates those visible forms—this is called eye-consciousness.
This applies likewise up to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
What is eye-contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsparśa*)?
It refers to the arising of eye-consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms; from the conjunction of these three, contact is produced.

When the eye, as the predominant condition, [encounters] forms, and the eye-consciousness [arises] with respect to those forms, if there is contact or the like of contact, this is called "eye-contact.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
What is "mind-contact"?
That is to say: when the mind takes dharmas as its object, mental consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact is produced.
When the mind is the predominant condition for dharmas and mental consciousness [arises] with respect to those dharmas, whether it be contact or equal contact, this is called "mental contact."
What is feeling born of eye-contact? It is as follows:
with the eye as condition and forms as object, eye-consciousness arises; the coming together of these three gives rise to contact; and with contact as condition, feeling arises.

With the eye as the predominant condition for forms, there is eye-contact as cause, eye-contact as origin, eye-contact as birth, and eye-contact as existence. Associated with the mental attention of eye-contact, regarding forms through eye-consciousness, whatever experience of feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that occurs, this is called feeling born of eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
What is the feeling born of mental contact?
It refers to the arising of mental consciousness with mental phenomena as its object; from the conjunction of these three arises contact, and with contact as condition, feeling arises.

With the mind as the predominant condition, there are phenomena that are the cause of mind-contact, the accumulation of mind-contact, the arising of mind-contact, and the existence of mind-contact; associated with the mental volition of mind-contact, when the mental consciousness experiences objects and undergoes various feelings such as sensation, this is called feeling born of mind-contact.
What is the perception born of eye-contact?
It is said that when the eye conditions visible forms, visual consciousness arises; from the coming together of these three, contact is produced, and contact conditions perception.

With the eye as the predominant condition for visible forms, there is eye-contact as cause, eye-contact as origin, eye-contact as arising, and eye-contact as existence. Associated with the mental attention of eye-contact, whatever perception, equal perception, predominant perception, or differentiated perception there is regarding visible forms by means of visual consciousness—this is called the perception born of eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
What is the perception born of mental contact?
It is said that when the mind takes dharmas as its object, mental consciousness arises; the coming together of these three produces contact, and contact conditions perception.

With the mind as the predominant condition, there are phenomena that are the cause of mind-contact, the accumulation of mind-contact, the arising of mind-contact, and the existence of mind-contact; associated with the volition of mind-contact, when consciousness engages with phenomena, whatever perception, equal perception, predominant perception, or differentiated perception arises—this is called "perception born of mind-contact."

What is volition born of eye-contact? It refers to the arising of eye-consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms; from the conjunction of these three arises contact, and contact conditions volition.

With the eye as the dominant condition and visible forms as the object, there is the cause of eye-contact, the accumulation of eye-contact, the production of eye-contact, and the existence of eye-contact. This is associated with the mental attention of eye-contact and pertains to eye-consciousness regarding visible forms. Whether it be volition, equal volition, or predominant volition, this volition turns the mind toward action; this is called volition born of eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
What is volition born of mind-contact?
It refers to the arising of mental consciousness conditioned by mental phenomena; from the conjunction of these three arises contact, and contact conditions volition.

With the mind as the predominant condition for phenomena, there is the cause of mind-contact, the accumulation of mind-contact, the arising of mind-contact, and the existence of mind-contact; it is associated with the mental application of mind-contact. When consciousness engages with phenomena, whether through volition, equal volition, or predominant volition, the volition turns the mind toward action; this is called "volition born of mind-contact."
What is craving born of eye-contact? It is as follows:
with the eye as condition and forms as object, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three gives rise to contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving.

When, with the eye as the predominant condition, one feels desire, attachment, and infatuation toward forms through eye-consciousness—clinging firmly with fondness and delight—this is called craving born of eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
How does craving arise from mental contact?

It is said that when the mind takes dharmas as its object, mental consciousness arises; the coming together of these three gives rise to contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; and conditioned by feeling is craving.

When the mental consciousness, with the mind as its predominant condition, encounters phenomena and becomes greedy, accumulates greed, and dwells in greed toward those phenomena—firmly clinging to them with craving and delight—this is called "craving born of mental contact.
Question:
By how many elements (dhātu), how many bases (āyatana), and how many aggregates (skandha) is the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) subsumed?
Regarding the phenomena subsumed under the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), how many elements, how many bases (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) do they comprise?
Regarding the phenomena not subsumed under the eye-element, how many elements, how many bases, and how many aggregates do they comprise?

Regarding the phenomena included in the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and those not included: how many elements (*dhātu*), how many bases (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) do they comprise?
Regarding the phenomena other than those included in the eye-element: how many elements, how many bases, and how many aggregates do they comprise?
Excluding those phenomena not included within the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), how many elements, how many bases (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) include the remaining phenomena?
Excluding those phenomena both included and not included within the eye-element, how many elements, how many bases, and how many aggregates include the remaining phenomena?
As it is with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so it is for everything up to the craving born of mental contact (*manasparśajātā tṛṣṇā*).
Answer:
The eye-element is subsumed under one element, one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it does not subsume seventeen elements, eleven bases, or five aggregates.
As with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so it is with the phenomena subsumed under the eye-element.
Phenomena not subsumed under the eye-element are subsumed by seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are not subsumed by one element, one base, or one aggregate.

Regarding the phenomena included and not included within the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*): they are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).

Excluding the phenomena included within the eye-element, the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are not subsumed within one element, one base, and one aggregate.

Excluding the factors not included within the eye-element, all remaining factors are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are not subsumed under seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates.
Excluding those phenomena subsumed under the eye-element, other phenomena are like those not subsumed under the eye-element.
Excluding those phenomena not subsumed under the eye-element, other phenomena are like the eye-element.
Excluding both phenomena subsumed and not subsumed under the eye-element, if one asks about other phenomena—such as space—there is no basis for discussion.
As with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so it is for the nine form-elements (*rūpadhātu*) and the ten form-bases (*rūpāyatana*).
The eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate (*skandha*); it does not subsume seventeen elements, twelve bases, or five aggregates.

As with the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), so it is with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements; the six groups of consciousness (*ṣadvijñānakāya*) are likewise.
The mind element (*manodhātu*) is subsumed under seven elements, one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it does not subsume eleven elements, eleven bases, or four aggregates.
As with the mind-element (*manodhātu*), so it is for the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*).
The dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is comprised by one element, one base, and four aggregates; it does not comprise seventeen elements, eleven bases, or two aggregates.
As it is with the dharma-dhātu, so it is with the dharma-āyatana.
The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and one aggregate; it does not subsume eight elements, two bases, or four aggregates.

The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate; it does not subsume the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, or the four aggregates.

As with the aggregate of feeling, so it is for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the universal mental factor of feeling (*vedanā-mahābhūmika*), and the universal mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā-mahābhūmika*).

The aggregate of the predominance of form (*rūpādhipati-skandha*) is subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate; it does not subsume eight elements, two bases, or five aggregates.

The aggregate of the predominance of sensation (*vedanādhipati-skandha*) is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; it does not subsume eighteen elements, twelve bases, or five aggregates.

As with the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), so it is with the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the five elements (*dhātu*), the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten universal factors of affliction (*kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten minor universal factors of affliction (*parītta-kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*), the five afflictions, the five contacts (*sparśa*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the four factors of the five faculties; the same applies to the five and the six as well.

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is subsumed under seven elements (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate; it does not subsume thirteen elements, twelve bases, or five aggregates.
As with the aggregate of consciousness, so it is with the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu).
The eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) consists of one element, one base, and is associated with three aggregates;
as for those that are not associated, they consist of eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.

As it is with the eye-consciousness element, so it is with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), the consciousness element, and the six groups of consciousness (ṣadvijñānakāya).
The mind-element (manodhātu) is associated with one element, one base, and three aggregates;
as for those that are dissociated, they consist of eighteen elements, twelve bases, and three aggregates.
As it is with the mind-element, so it is with the mind-base (manāyatana), the consciousness aggregate (vijñānaskandha), and the consciousness-factor (vijñānadharma).
The dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is associated with eight elements (dhātus), two bases (āyatanas), and four aggregates (skandhas).
Those that are dissociated are eleven elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates.
As it is with the dharma-element, so it is with the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), and the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma).
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is associated with eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and three aggregates;
as for those that are dissociated, it is dissociated from eleven elements, eleven bases, and three aggregates.

As with the aggregate of feeling, the same applies to the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), the universal mental factors of feeling (vedanā-mahābhūmika), and the universal mental factors of perception (saṃjñā-mahābhūmika).
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is associated with eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates;
as for those that are dissociated, it consists of thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
As it is with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is associated with eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates;
as for those that are dissociated, they consist of thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
As it is with the aggregate of formations, so it is with the factors of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Non-faith (*āśraddhya*) is associated with eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*);
it is dissociated from eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.

As with non-faith, so it is with the other universal afflictive mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*): sensual greed (*kāmarāga*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). These are likewise [associated with eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates, and dissociated from eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates].
Anger (*krodha*) is associated with three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*).
As for its dissociated factors, it is dissociated from eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.

As with anger, the same applies to the other minor defilements (*upakleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-rāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), contact of clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the six groups of feeling (*vedanā-kāya*).
Attachment to form (*rūparāga*) is associated with six elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*);
as for its dissociation, it is dissociated from eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Contact through opposition (*pratighasaṃsparśa*) is associated with seven elements, two bases, and four aggregates.
Regarding those that are dissociated: they consist of thirteen elements (dhātus), twelve bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas).
As for the contact associated with the faculty of speech (vāg-vijñapti-saṃsparśa): it is associated with three elements, two bases, and four aggregates;
those that are dissociated from it consist of seventeen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
As with the contact of predominant speech, so it is with the six groups of contact and the six groups of volition.
The faculty of pleasure is associated with eight elements, two bases, and three aggregates;
those with which it is not associated are eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
As with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), so it is with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is associated with seven elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*);
those with which it is not associated consist of the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
The faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) is associated with three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*).
Those not associated with it consist of the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
As with the faculty of joy, so it is with the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*).
The feeling produced by eye-contact is associated with three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*).
Those that are dissociated consist of seventeen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
As it is with the feeling produced by eye-contact, so it is for the feelings produced by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact, as well as for the six groups of perception (*saṃjñā-kāya*).
The *Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Two;
The *Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.
Chapter Five: The Analysis of the Latent Tendencies (Anuśaya). Question:
Of the ninety-eight latent tendencies, how many are bound to which realms?
Answer:
Bound to the three realms, namely the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Question:

Of these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer:
Thirty-six are bound to the desire realm, thirty-one are bound to the form realm, and thirty-one are bound to the formless realm.
Question:
Of these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer:
Eighty-eight are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), and ten are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Question:
Of these thirty-six proclivities (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm, how many are abandoned by insight and how many are abandoned by cultivation?
Answer:
Thirty-two are abandoned through vision; four are abandoned through cultivation.
Question:

Regarding these thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), how many are abandoned by vision (darśana-prahātavya) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya)?
Answer:
Twenty-eight are abandoned by vision; three are abandoned by cultivation.
As it is with those bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), so it is with those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question:

Of these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), how many through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and how many are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

Answer: Twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of suffering; nineteen are abandoned through the vision of origin; nineteen are abandoned through the vision of cessation; twenty-two are abandoned through the vision of the path; and ten are abandoned through cultivation.
Question:

Of these thirty-six proclivities (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm, how many are abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), how many by the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), how many by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya), how many by the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), and how many are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya)?
Answer:

Ten are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), seven are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), seven are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), eight are abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and four are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Question:

Of these thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the realm of form (rūpadhātu), how many are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), how many through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), how many through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya), how many through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), and how many are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya)?
Answer:
Nine are abandoned through the vision of suffering, six through the vision of the origin, six through the vision of cessation, seven through the vision of the path, and three through cultivation.
As it is for those bound to the realm of form, so it is for those bound to the formless realm.
Question:
What is the meaning of "outflow" (āsrava)?
Answer:

Subtlety is the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*); being a proclivity is the meaning of "proclivity"; following and entering is the meaning of "proclivity"; pursuing and tracking is the meaning of "proclivity"—that is to say, those proclivities are neither severed nor known.
Two types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
those that function as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) and those that function through association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*); these belong to their own realm and not to other realms.
Twelve latent dispositions:

The latent tendency of greed, the latent tendency of hatred, the latent tendency of greed for the realm of form, the latent tendency of greed for the formless realm, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity, the latent tendency of the view of extremes, the latent tendency of false views, the latent tendency of the esteeming of views, the latent tendency of the esteeming of precepts and observances, and the latent tendency of doubt.
What is the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*)?
It refers to craving, attachment, and clinging, characterized by delighting in and finding pleasure in what is agreeable.
What is the latent tendency of ill will (*pratighānuśaya*)?
That is to say: it is not loved, not delighted in, not remembered, not rejoiced in, and is disagreeable.
How does the latent tendency of lust for form (rūparāgānuśaya) function?
It is that which is loved, delighted in, pure, agreeable, and pleasing to the mind.
What is the latent tendency of desire for the formless (ārūpyarāgānuśaya)?
It refers to craving for and delighting in what is agreeable.
What is the latent tendency of pride (mānānuśaya)?
It refers to arrogance and self-exaltation.
What is the latent tendency of ignorance?
It refers to the lack of illumination, darkness, and folly.
What is the proclivity of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi-anuśaya)?
It refers to reckoning "I" and "mine.
What is the proclivity of the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi-anuśaya)?
That is to say, one speculates on either annihilation or permanence.
How does the underlying tendency of wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya) exert its influence?
It refers to the arising of views that involve denial, such as claiming there is no action and nothing to be attained.
What is the driving force of the underlying tendency toward views of grasping (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-anuśaya)?
It is [the view that] "this is supreme, excellent, and foremost.
What is the driving force of the underlying tendency toward grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa-anuśaya)?
This refers to the view that arises from the necessity of purification, liberation, emergence, and transcendence.
What is the latent tendency of doubt?

It is the failure to understand the Truths, which gives rise to the latent tendency of sensual desire in three respects. This latent tendency of sensual desire is neither abandoned nor understood; one is bound by the fetters of sensual desire, delighting in sense objects and engaging in unwholesome mental reflections.
In this way, up to three points, one gives rise to the underlying tendency of doubt.

This underlying tendency of doubt does not sever or understand the phenomena entangled by the fetter of doubt; it delights in and clings to sense objects, and proceeds through the mental activity of unwholesome reflection.
Question:
Regarding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the twelve underlying tendencies, do the seven encompass the twelve, or do the twelve encompass the seven?
Answer:
They are mutually inclusive according to their respective natures.
How are they included according to their respective natures?
The latent tendency of sensual desire is included within the latent tendency of sensual desire.
The latent tendency of aversion is subsumed under the latent tendency of aversion.
The latent tendency of sensual desire is subsumed under two latent tendencies.
The latent tendency of pride is subsumed under the latent tendency of pride.
The latent tendency of ignorance is subsumed under the latent tendency of ignorance.
The latent tendencies of views are subsumed under the five latent tendencies of views.
The latent tendency of doubt is subsumed under the latent tendency of doubt.

These seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subsume the twelve underlying tendencies, and the twelve underlying tendencies likewise subsume the seven; therefore, it is said that they mutually subsume one another according to their respective natures.
Question: Regarding the seven underlying tendencies and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies, do the seven subsume the ninety-eight, or do the ninety-eight subsume the seven?
Answer:
They mutually encompass one another according to their respective functions.
What does "according to their respective functions" mean?

The latent tendency of sensual desire comprises five; the latent tendency of ill will comprises five; the latent tendency of attachment to existence comprises ten; the latent tendency of pride comprises fifteen; the latent tendency of ignorance comprises fifteen; the latent tendency of views comprises thirty-six; and the latent tendency of doubt comprises twelve.

These seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) encompass the ninety-eight underlying tendencies, and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies also encompass the seven; therefore, it is said that they mutually encompass one another according to their respective categories.
Question: Regarding the twelve underlying tendencies and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies, do the twelve encompass the ninety-eight, or do the ninety-eight encompass the twelve?
Answer:
They mutually encompass one another according to their respective cases.
What does "according to their respective cases" mean?

The latent tendency of sensual desire comprises five; the latent tendency of ill will comprises five; the latent tendency of desire for the realm of form comprises five; the latent tendency of desire for the formless realm comprises five; the latent tendency of pride comprises fifteen; the latent tendency of ignorance comprises fifteen; the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity comprises three; the latent tendency of extreme views comprises three; the latent tendency of false views comprises twelve; the latent tendency of clinging to views comprises twelve; the latent tendency of clinging to precepts and observances comprises six; and the latent tendency of doubt comprises twelve.

These twelve underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subsume the ninety-eight underlying tendencies, and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies likewise subsume the twelve; therefore, it is said that they mutually subsume one another according to their respective natures.
Question:
Of these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and how many are not universal?
Answer:
Twenty-seven are universal (sarvatraga), sixty-five are not universal, and six are to be distinguished.
The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin is either universal or not universal.
What is the universal?
It refers to the ignorance that is dissociated from the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin, but are not universal.
What is the non-universal?
This refers to the ignorance associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
Question:
Among these thirty-six proclivities bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many are universal and how many are non-universal?
Answer:
Nine are universal (sarvatraga), twenty-five are non-universal, and two are to be distinguished.

Regarding the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) associated with the desire realm that is abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of its origin: it is either universal or non-universal.
What is the universal?
It refers to the ignorance dissociated from the proclivities that are not universal, which are bound to the desire realm and abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination.
What is the non-universal?
This refers to the ignorance associated with the non-universal proclivities (*asarvatraga-anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the desire realm.
Question:
Among these thirty-one proclivities bound to the form realm, how many are universal and how many are non-universal?
Answer:
Nine are universal (sarvatraga); twenty are not universal; two are to be distinguished.
The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu) and abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin is either universal or not universal.
What is the universal?
It refers to the ignorance dissociated from the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are not universal, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the realm of form.
What is the non-universal?

This refers to the ignorance associated with the universal-out-of-scope (asarvatraga) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
As it is for the realm of form, so it is for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question:

Of these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many are not universal and are not abandoned through cultivation?
Answer:
Thirty-seven [factors] are abandoned through cultivation and are universal; fifty-five are not universal and are not abandoned through cultivation; six are to be distinguished.
The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin is either universal or not universal.
What is the universal?
It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) that is dissociated from [the mind] and abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin.
What is the non-universal?
This refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with [the afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
Question:

Among these thirty-six latent tendencies bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are universal and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many are non-universal and not abandoned through cultivation?
Answer:
Thirteen are universal and abandoned through cultivation; twenty-one are not universal and are not abandoned through cultivation; two are to be distinguished.

Among the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin, some are universal and some are not universal.
What is the universal?

It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance that is not associated with the latent tendencies which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin within the desire realm, and which are not universal.
What is the non-universal?

This refers to the ignorance-tendency (avidyā-anuśaya) associated with the non-universal tendencies (asarvatraga-anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the desire realm.
Question:
Of these thirty-one tendencies bound to the form realm, how many are universal and abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and how many are non-universal and not abandoned through cultivation?
Answer:
Twelve [factors] are universal and abandoned through cultivation; seventeen are not universal and are not abandoned through cultivation; two are to be distinguished.
The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin is either universal or not universal.
What is the universal (sarvatraga)?

It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) that is associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya), and is not a non-universal [latent tendency].
What is the non-universal?

This refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) associated with the fetters of the form realm (rūpadhātu) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, but which are not all-pervasive (asarvatraga).
As it is for the fetters of the form realm, so it is for those of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Question:
Of these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) and how many have non-outflowing objects (*anāsravālambana*)?
Answer:
Eighty [latent dispositions] have impure objects; twelve have pure objects; and six are to be distinguished.
The latent dispositions of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path may have either impure objects or pure objects.
What is that which has outflows as its object (*sāsravālambana*)?

It refers to the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) associated with the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*), which have outflows as their objects.
What is that which has outflows-free as its object (*anāsravālambana*)?

This refers to the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of ignorance (avidyā) that are dissociated from [the other defilements] and take the outflow-tainted objects (sāsrava-ālambana) as their focus, which are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya) and the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-heya).
Question:
Among these thirty-six latent tendencies bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), how many have outflow-tainted objects and how many have outflow-free objects (anāsrava-ālambana)?
Answer:
Thirty [latent dispositions] have impure objects; four have pure objects; two are to be distinguished.

The latent dispositions of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm, which are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, may have either impure objects or pure objects.
What is that which has outflows as its object?

It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance associated with the latent tendencies that have outflows as their objects and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, which are bound to the desire realm.
What is that which has the outflow-free as its object?

This refers to the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of ignorance (avidyā) that are associated with the desire realm, abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, and which take contaminated objects as their conditions.
Question:
Of these thirty-one latent tendencies associated with the form realm, how many have contaminated objects as their conditions, and how many have uncontaminated objects as their conditions?
Answer:
Twenty-five are with-outflow objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), four are without-outflow objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), and two are to be distinguished.

The latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) are either with-outflow objects or without-outflow objects.
What is that which has outflows as its object (*sāsravālambana*)?

It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) associated with the latent tendencies that have outflows as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*), which are bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is that which has the outflow-free as its object (*anāsravālambana*)?

This refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) that is associated with the form realm, is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, and is not conjoined with the outflow-tending (sāsrava) objects.
As it is for the form realm, so it is for the formless realm as well.
Question:
Of these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many have conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*) and how many have unconditioned objects (*asaṃskṛta-ālambana*)?
Answer:
Eighty-nine [factors] have conditioned objects; six have unconditioned objects; three are to be analyzed.
The latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through the vision of cessation has either a conditioned object or an unconditioned object.
What is the condition of the conditioned?
It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance associated with the latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation that have the conditioned as their object.
What is the condition of the unconditioned?

This refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) that is dissociated [from the mind] and takes conditioned phenomena as its object, which is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Question:

Among these thirty-six latent tendencies bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many take conditioned phenomena as their object and how many take unconditioned phenomena as their object?
Answer:
Thirty-three are conditioned-object (saṃskṛta-ālambana) and two are unconditioned-object (asaṃskṛta-ālambana), with one being distinguished.

The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) is either conditioned-object or unconditioned-object.
What is the condition of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*)?

It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with the latent tendencies that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and which have the conditioned as their object within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-saṃprayukta*).
What is the condition of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya*)?
This refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) that is associated with the desire realm, abandoned through the vision of cessation, and takes conditioned phenomena as its object.
Question:
Of these thirty-one latent tendencies associated with the form realm, how many take conditioned phenomena as their object and how many take unconditioned phenomena as their object?
Answer:
Twenty-eight are conditioned-object (saṃskṛta-ālambana), two are unconditioned-object (asaṃskṛta-ālambana), and one is to be analyzed.

The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya) within the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) is either conditioned-object or unconditioned-object.
What is the condition of conditioned factors (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*)?
