It refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with the latent tendencies that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and which have conditioned factors of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) as their object.
What is the condition of unconditioned factors (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya*)?

This refers to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) that is associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya), and dissociated from conditioned objects (saṃskṛtālambana).
As it is for the form realm, so it is for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Question:

Among these ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are proclivities by way of object (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but not proclivities by way of association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*); how many are proclivities by way of association but not proclivities by way of object; how many are proclivities by way of both object and association; and how many are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association?
Answer:

There are none that are objects of the proclivities (anuśaya) but not associated with them; there are none that are associated with the proclivities but not objects of them—namely, those proclivities whose objects are untainted (anāsrava); there are those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them—namely, those proclivities whose objects are tainted (sāsrava); and there are none that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them.
Question:

Among these thirty-six proclivities (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm, how many are proclivities by way of object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) but not proclivities by way of association (samprayoga)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions:

there are none that are latent dispositions by way of object-condition but not associated; those that are latent dispositions by way of association but not by way of object-condition are the latent dispositions bound to the desire realm that take the outflow-free as their object; those that are both latent dispositions by way of object-condition and associated are the latent dispositions bound to the desire realm that take the outflow-possessing as their object; and there are none that are neither latent dispositions by way of object-condition nor associated.

Regarding these thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how many are underlying tendencies by way of object (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but not by way of association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*)?

This is analyzed in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). 1. Those that are underlying tendencies by way of object but not by way of association: none exist. 2. Those that are underlying tendencies by way of association but not by way of object: the underlying tendencies bound to the form realm that have the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object. 3. Those that are underlying tendencies both by way of object and by way of association: the underlying tendencies bound to the form realm that have the outflowing (*sāsrava*) as their object. 4. Those that are neither underlying tendencies by way of object nor by way of association: none exist.
As it is with those bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), so it is with those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

Regarding the twenty factors—the factors abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), the factors abandoned by seeing origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), the factors abandoned by seeing cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), the factors abandoned by seeing the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), and the factors abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—as they are not fixed for those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), so it is likewise for those bound to the realms of form and the formless.
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie those dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering?
Answer:
All [defilements] are abandoned through the vision of suffering; all pervasive [defilements] are abandoned through the vision of origin.
Question:
By how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are those factors abandoned through the vision of origin driven?
Answer:
All [factors] abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) and all pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
Question:
Regarding those dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them?
Answer:
All [underlying tendencies] abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive ones (*sarvatraga*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie those dharmas abandoned by the path of vision (darśanamārga)?
Answer:
[The defilements] abandoned by the path of seeing [comprise] all [defilements] and all pervasive [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie those dharmas abandoned by cultivation?
Answer:
They are abandoned through cultivation, as well as all pervasive [defilements].
Just as it is for those bound to the desire realm that are not fixed, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:

Among those dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), how many are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that function as objects (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as associated latent dispositions (*samprayuktānuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.

Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are conditions but not associated are all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated but not conditions.
Those that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanaparyavasthāna*) and associated-pervasive (*samprayogaparyavasthāna*) are all abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive include all those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) except for the non-universal ones, as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Question:

Regarding those phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated underlying tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.
Those that are pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), which are conditions but not associated, exist.
Those that are associated latent dispositions but not conditions do not exist.
Those that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanaparyavasthāna*) and associated-pervasive (*samprayogaparyavasthāna*) are all abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are: those abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Question:

Regarding those phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated underlying tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.
Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are pervasive conditions (*sarvatraga-pratyaya*) but not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are all-pervasive.

Those latent dispositions that are associated but not pervasive conditions are the latent dispositions with respect to the outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).

Those which are both object-conditioned proclivities (*ālambanapraheyānuśaya*) and associated proclivities (*samprayuktānuśaya*) are the proclivities with outflows (*sāsrava*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Those which are neither object-conditioned proclivities nor associated proclivities are all those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkhasamudayadarśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Question:

Among those dharmas abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), how many are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that function as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not function as associated latent dispositions (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.
Those latent tendencies (anuśaya) that are objects of condition but not associated are the universal ones.
Those latent tendencies that are associated but not objects of condition are those abandoned through the path of vision (darśana-mārga) which have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object.

Those latent tendencies (anuśaya) that are both object-conditions (*ālambana*) and associated (*samprayukta*) are the latent tendencies of the outflows (*sāsrava*) abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Those that are neither object-conditions nor associated are all those abandoned by the path of seeing suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned by the path of seeing cessation and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Question:

Among those dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how many are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that function as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not function as associated latent dispositions (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.
Those that are pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) by way of object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) but not by way of association (saṃprayoga) are all pervasive ones.
There are none that are associated latent dispositions but not by way of object-condition.
Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that function through both object-conditioning (*ālambana*) and association (*samprayoga*) are abandoned entirely by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those that function neither through object-conditioning nor through association are: those not all-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and origin (*samudaya*), as well as all those abandoned by seeing cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the path (*mārga-darśana*).
Just as it is for those not fixed to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.

These twenty dharmas—namely, these dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering, these abandoned through the vision of the origin, these abandoned through the vision of cessation, these abandoned through the vision of the path, and these abandoned through cultivation—are, as with those not fixed to the desire realm, likewise so for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:
Of these very dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as their drivers?
Answer:
That is to say, these are abandoned through the vision of suffering and are not universal.
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie those dharmas abandoned through the vision of origin?
Answer:
It is precisely this [view] abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) that is not all-pervasive (asarvatraga).
Question:
Regarding these very phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them?
Answer:
All [underlying tendencies] abandoned through the vision of cessation [underlie them].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie these very dharmas abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga)?
Answer:
This very [path] abandons everything through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie those dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
Answer:
All of these are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Just as it is for those not fixed [in the formless realm] that are bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:

Regarding these very dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated underlying tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: It is explained by means of four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are conditions but not associated;
there are none that are associated but not conditions.
Those that are both conditions and associated are those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), excluding the universal ones (*asarvatraga*).
There are none that are neither latent proclivities by way of object nor latent proclivities by way of association.
Question:

Among these very dharmas abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), how many are latent proclivities by way of object but not latent proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are none that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them.
There are none that are associated with the proclivities but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are the non-universal [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them.
Question:

Among these very dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but are not associated (*asaṃprayukta-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.
There are none that are conditions but not associated.
Those that are associated but not conditions are the [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object.
Those that are both object-pervasions (*ālambanānuśaya*) and associated-pervasions (*saṃprayuktānuśaya*) are the outflows to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are neither object-pervasions nor associated-pervasions.
Question:

Regarding these very dharmas abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) function as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but not as associated tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: Four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are to be made.
There are no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are objects of condition (*ālambana*) but not associated (*saṃprayukta*).

Those that are associated but not objects of condition are the [latent dispositions] abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) which have the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Those that are both objects of condition and associated are the [latent dispositions] abandoned by the path of seeing which have the outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*) as their object.
There are none that are neither object-condition proclivities nor associated proclivities.
Question:
Among these very dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how many are object-condition proclivities but not associated proclivities?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are none that are objects of the proclivities (anuśaya) but are not associated with them.
There are none that are associated with the proclivities but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are all those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
There are none that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them.
Just as it is for those that are indeterminate and bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.

Regarding the twenty types of mind—those abandoned by seeing suffering, those abandoned by seeing origination, those abandoned by seeing cessation, those abandoned by seeing the path, and those abandoned by cultivation—just as it is for those that are indeterminate and bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are associated with a mind that is abandoned through the vision of suffering?
Answer:
All [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering, and all pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of origin;
the factors associated with them are also all abandoned through the vision of suffering and all pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of origin.

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) and all-pervading [defilements] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the mind abandoned through the vision of origin?
Answer:
All [factors] abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) and all pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya-sarvatraga).
Their associated factors (saṃprayukta-dharma) are likewise all abandoned through the vision of the origin and all pervasive factors abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) and all-pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the mind abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*)?
Answer:
All [factors] abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive [factors],
and their associated factors, are abandoned by the vision of cessation and are pervasive.

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodhālambana-sāsrava*) and those that are universal (*sarvatraga*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the mind abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*)?
Answer:
All [factors] abandoned by the path of seeing and all pervasive [factors],
as well as the factors associated with them, are abandoned by the path of seeing and are pervasive.

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), and the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the mind to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer:
All [factors] abandoned by cultivation and all pervasive [factors],
as well as the factors associated with them, are abandoned by cultivation and are pervasive.
The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), including all those that are universal (*sarvatraga*).

Just as it is for those not fixed [in the higher realms] but bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Question:

Regarding the mind abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya-citta*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated underlying tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.
Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are conditions but not associated are all those universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated but not conditions.
Those that are both object-pervasive (*ālambana-anuśaya*) and associated-pervasive (*samprayoga-anuśaya*) are entirely abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive include all those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) except for the universal ones (*sarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The four propositions regarding those associated dharmas are as explained for the mind.
As for the formations dissociated from mind that arise from them, they are all abandoned through the vision of suffering and all pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of the origin.

These proclivities (anuśaya) are proclivities by way of object (ālambanānuśaya), not proclivities by way of association (samprayogānuśaya); the remainder are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:
Regarding the mind abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudayadarśana-prahātavya), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object, but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those that are conditions (*ālambana*) but not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are all the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are all those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither objects of latent dispositions nor associated with them are all those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal, as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The four propositions regarding those associated dharmas are as explained for the mind.

The formations dissociated from mind that arise from them are entirely abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and entirely abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

These proclivities (anuśaya) are proclivities by way of object (ālambanānuśaya), not proclivities by way of association (samprayuktānuśaya); the remainder are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:
Regarding the mind abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya-citta), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object, but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those that function as conditions (*ālambana-prayojaka*) but are not associated (*na saṃprayukta*) are the universal factors (*sarvatraga*).

Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are associated but not object-conditions are those abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) that have the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Those that are both object-conditions and associated are those abandoned by the vision of cessation that have the outflowing (*sāsrava*) as their object.

Those that are neither object-conditions nor associated are: all [tendencies] abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and origination (*samudaya-darśana*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all [tendencies] abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The four propositions regarding those associated phenomena are as explained for the mind itself.
The formations dissociated from mind that arise from them are those with outflows conditioned by the cessation of views, as well as the universal [factors].
These proclivities are proclivities by way of object, not proclivities by way of association; the remainder are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
As it is for those abandoned through the vision of cessation, so it is for those abandoned through the vision of the path.
Question:

Regarding the mind to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are those that take it as an object (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but are not associated with it (*asaṃprayukta-anuśaya*)?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are objects of condition (*ālambana*) but not associated (*samprayukta*) are all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).
Those that are associated but not objects of condition do not exist.
Those that are both objects of condition and associated are all those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those that are neither pervasive through objects (*ālambana-pravṛtti*) nor pervasive through association (*samprayoga-pravṛtti*) are: those abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.
Regarding the fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*) of their associated dharmas, it is exactly as explained for the mind.
The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as are all pervasive [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects of entanglement (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not act through association (*na saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remainder neither act as objects of entanglement nor act through association.
Just as it is for those [states] bound to the desire realm that are indeterminate, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.

Regarding the forty-eight types of consciousness: there is the consciousness associated with false view abandoned through the vision of cessation; the consciousness associated with doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation; the consciousness associated with both false view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation; the consciousness dissociated from false view abandoned through the vision of cessation; the consciousness dissociated from doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation; and the consciousness dissociated from both false view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation.
As it is with those abandoned by the vision of cessation, so it is with those abandoned by the vision of the path.
As it is with those not fixed as bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:
Regarding the mind associated with wrong view to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) bind it?
Answer:

The ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as those [tendencies] that have outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [tendencies].

The associated dharmas are: the ignorance associated with the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation, the outflow-tainted objects abandoned through the vision of cessation, and all pervasive [factors].
The non-associated formations arising from them are: the outflow-tainted objects abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [factors].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie the mind associated with doubt that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation?
Answer:
The ignorance associated with doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as the outflow-tainted objects and the universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation;

and the factors associated with them—the ignorance associated with doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as the outflow-tainted objects and the universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodha-ālambana-sāsrava*) and the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the mind associated with false view and doubt that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*)?
Answer:

The ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as those [factors] conditioned by outflows abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [defilements].

The factors associated with them are the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as those [factors] conditioned by outflows abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [defilements].

The formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodha-dṛṣṭi-heya-sāsrava-ālambana*) and the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie the mind dissociated from false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation?
Answer:

With the exception of the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and its associated ignorance (*avidyā*), all other factors abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive factors (*sarvatraga*), [are included].

Regarding their associated factors, with the exception of the ignorance associated with the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation, all other factors abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive factors, [are included].
The formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodha-ālambana-sāsrava*) and the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the mind dissociated from doubt (*vicikitsā-viprayukta-citta*) that is abandoned through the vision of cessation?
Answer:

With the exception of the ignorance associated with doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, all other [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [factors] [are included].

As for the factors associated with those, with the exception of the ignorance associated with doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, all other [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [factors] [are included].

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*) having cessation as their object (*nirodhālambana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*), as well as the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie the mind that is dissociated from wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation?
Answer:

With the exception of the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), all other [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [factors] (*sarvatraga*) are included.

As for their associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), with the exception of the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, all other [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [factors] are included.

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those conditioned by the outflows (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the universal [defilements].
Just as it is for those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, so it is for those to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
Just as it is for those [defilements] not fixed to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:

Regarding the mind associated with false view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) and how many act as non-associated [underlying tendencies] (*na-samprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that take objects (*ālambana*) but are not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are: those with outflow-objects (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), and all pervasive [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not objects (*ālambana*) are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are both objects and associated with the proclivities.

Those that are neither objects nor associated with the proclivities include, with the exception of the ignorance associated with the false view abandoned by the vision of cessation, all other [proclivities] abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object (*anāsrava-ālambana*), those abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), and all those abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The four propositions regarding those associated phenomena are as explained for the mind.
Those formations dissociated from the mind that arise from them are abandoned through the vision of cessation, are with outflows, have outflows as their object, and are universal.

These proclivities (anuśaya) are proclivities by way of object (ālambanānuśaya), not proclivities by way of association (samprayogānuśaya); the others are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the mind associated with doubt (vicikitsā) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them are: those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the universal [proclivities].

Those that are associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) but are not objects of them are the ignorance associated with doubt that is abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are both objects of the underlying tendencies and associated with them.

Those that are neither objects of the underlying tendencies nor associated with them include: all other [factors] abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object; those abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [factors] abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The four propositions regarding those associated dharmas are as explained for the mind.

The dissociated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising from them are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya), are with outflows (sāsrava), have the outflows as their object (sāsrava-ālambana), and are universal (sarvatraga).

These latent dispositions (anuśaya) are latent dispositions by way of object (ālambana-anuśaya), not latent dispositions by way of association (samprayoga-anuśaya); the others are neither latent dispositions by way of object nor latent dispositions by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the mind associated with false view and doubt to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya), how many latent dispositions are latent dispositions by way of object, and how many are not latent dispositions by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that take as their object (*ālambana*) but are not associated (*saṃprayukta*) with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) are: those [proclivities] associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), and the universal [proclivities] (*sarvatraga*).

Those which are associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them are: the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view and doubt that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are both objects of the underlying tendencies and associated with them.

Those that are neither objects of the underlying tendencies nor associated with them are: with the exception of the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, all other [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object (*anāsrava-ālambana*), those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), and all those abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The four propositions regarding those associated dharmas are as explained for the mind.

The non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising from them are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya), have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana), and are universal (sarvatraga).

These latent dispositions (anuśaya) are latent dispositions by way of object (ālambanānuśaya), not latent dispositions by way of association (samprayogānuśaya); the remainder are neither latent dispositions by way of object nor latent dispositions by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the mind dissociated from false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya), how many latent dispositions are latent dispositions by way of object, but not latent dispositions by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them are the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but are not objects of them are: with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the remaining [ignorance] abandoned through the vision of cessation that takes uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are: those abandoned through the vision of cessation that take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*).

Those that are neither object-conditions nor associated conditions are: the ignorance associated with the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation; those not-all-pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin; and all [factors] abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation.
The four propositions regarding those associated phenomena are as explained for the mind itself.
The non-associated formations arising from them are abandoned by the vision of cessation, are with outflows, have outflows as their object, and are universal.

These proclivities (anuśaya) are proclivities by way of object (ālambanānuśaya), not proclivities by way of association (samprayogānuśaya); the remaining ones are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the mind dissociated from doubt to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).

Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are associated but not object-conditions (*ālambana*) are: with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the remaining [ignorance] abandoned through the vision of cessation that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Those that are both object-conditions and associated are: those abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object.

Those that are neither object-pervasive (ālambana-anuśaya) nor associated-pervasive (saṃprayoga-anuśaya) are: the ignorance associated with doubt abandoned by the vision of cessation; those not universally pervasive abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin; and all [factors] abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation.
The four propositions regarding those associated phenomena are as explained for the mind itself.

The non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising from them consist of those with outflows (sāsrava) that have cessation as their object and are abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as the universal [defilements].

These proclivities (anuśaya) are proclivities by way of object (ālambana-anuśaya), not proclivities by way of association (samprayoga-anuśaya); the remaining ones are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the mind dissociated from false view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them are the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but are not objects of them are: with the exception of the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), the remaining [ignorance] abandoned through the vision of cessation which takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are those abandoned through the vision of cessation which take the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object.

Those that are neither object-conditions nor associated conditions are: the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation; those not-all-pervasive [ignorances] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin; and all [ignorances] abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation.
The four propositions regarding those associated phenomena are as explained for the mind itself.

The non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising from them are abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya), are with outflows (sāsrava), have cessation as their object (nirodhālambana), and are universal (sarvatraga).
These proclivities are proclivities by way of object, not proclivities by way of association; the others are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
As it is for those abandoned through the vision of cessation, so it is for those abandoned through the vision of the path.
Just as it is for those [fetters] bound to the desire realm that are indeterminate, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:

Regarding these thirty-six proclivities (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm—ten are abandoned through the vision of suffering, seven through the vision of origin, seven through the vision of cessation, eight through the vision of the path, and four are abandoned through cultivation.
What are the ten proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering?
Answer:

They are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), adherence to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), greed (rāga), hatred (pratigha), pride (māna), and ignorance (avidyā). These are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
What are the seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin?
They are: wrong view, adherence to views, doubt, greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance abandoned through the vision of the origin.
What are the seven underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation?
These are the false view, adherence to views, doubt, greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
What are the eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*)?
They are the false view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and observances, doubt, greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance abandoned through the vision of the path.
What are the four underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation?
They are the underlying tendencies of greed, hostility, pride, and ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation.
Question:
Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do they drive?

Answer: All [tendencies] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and all pervasive [tendencies] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
As for the factors associated with it (*tat-saṃprayukta-dharma*), they are all abandoned through the vision of suffering, and all pervasive [tendencies] abandoned through the vision of origin.

The mental formations dissociated from mind that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and all pervasive [factors] are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Just as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are abandoned through the vision of suffering, so too are false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) drive the false view that is abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya)?
Answer:

All [factors] abandoned through the vision of the origin are abandoned through the vision of the origin; all pervasive [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
As for those associated factors, all are abandoned through the vision of the origin, and all pervasive ones are abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and all are universal (*sarvatraga*) factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Just as with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of the origin, so it is for the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie the false view that is abandoned through the vision of cessation?
Answer:

The ignorance associated with the false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as that which has out-flowing objects and is universal—all these are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

The factors associated with them—the ignorance associated with the false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as that which has out-flowing objects and is universal—are likewise to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
The mental formations dissociated from mind that arise therein consist of those with outflows conditioned by the cessation of suffering (*nirodha*), as well as the universal [defilements].
Just as with the false view abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering, so it is with doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation?
Answer:

The ignorance associated with the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), as well as the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

The factors associated with those are the ignorance associated with the view of grasping at views to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as the outflow-tainted objects to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive [defilements].

The mental formations dissociated from mind that arise therein are those conditioned by the outflows (*āsrava*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), as well as the universal [defilements].
This is the same as for the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation; greed, hatred, and pride are also like this.
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) drive the ignorance that is abandoned through the vision of cessation?
Answer:

Regarding ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*): excluding that which has the untainted as its object (*anāsrava-ālambana*), it consists of all other factors abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive factors (*sarvatraga*).
As for the associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), they consist of all [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive factors.

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein consist of those with outflows conditioned by the cessation [of suffering] (*nirodha-ālambana-sāsrava*) which are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*darśana-heya*), as well as the universal [factors].
As it is for those abandoned through the vision of cessation, so it is for those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga*).
Question:
When cultivating the abandonment of greed (*rāga*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as its drivers?
Answer:
One cultivates the abandonment of all [defilements] and all pervasive [defilements].
Their associated dharmas are explained in the same manner as greed.
The non-associated formations (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) arising from them are also explained in the same way.
As it is with greed, so it is with hatred, conceit, and ignorance.
Question:

Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated underlying tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them include: all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); and all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Those that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them include all [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana*), those not universal (*asarvatraga*), and all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana*), the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Regarding those associated dharmas that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them: excluding the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they comprise all [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as all pervasive [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated latent tendencies (*saṃprayukta-anuśaya*) but not object latent tendencies (*ālambana-anuśaya*).
Those that are both object latent tendencies and associated latent tendencies are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

Those that are neither object latent tendencies nor associated latent tendencies are all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), and all pervasive [factors] are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are latent tendencies by way of object (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not latent tendencies by way of association (*samprayogānuśaya*); the remaining ones are neither latent tendencies by way of object nor latent tendencies by way of association.

Just as the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes are abandoned through the vision of suffering, so too are false views, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and rituals, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are underlying tendencies by way of object (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not underlying tendencies by way of association (*samprayogānuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.

Those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are conditions but not associated are: the ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering, and all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the origin.
There are none that are associated but not conditions.

Those that are both object-pervasive (ālambana-anuśaya) and associated-pervasive (saṃprayoga-anuśaya) are all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), with the exception of ignorance (avidyā).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are all those abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) that are not universal (asarvatraga), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya), the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), and through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).

Regarding those associated dharmas, those that are latent tendencies (anuśaya) by way of object-condition (*ālambana*) but not by way of association (*samprayoga*) are all the pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Those that are latent tendencies by way of association but not by way of object-condition do not exist.

Those that are both latent tendencies by way of object-condition and latent tendencies by way of association are all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them include: all [proclivities] abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal; all [proclivities] abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*), the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from these include all [proclivities] abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and all universal [proclivities] abandoned by the vision of the origin.

These proclivities are proclivities by way of object (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but not proclivities by way of association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*); the remaining ones are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the false view abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them consist of: all [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view; and all pervasive [proclivities] (*sarvatraga*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.

Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*).

Those that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them are all [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*), the vision of the path (*mārga*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Regarding those associated dharmas, those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them consist of: all [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of the origin; as well as all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.

Those that are both objects of the underlying tendencies and associated with them are the ignorance associated with the false view abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither objects of the underlying tendencies nor associated with them are all [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal, as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*), the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) function as object-conditions (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not function as associated conditions (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remainder neither function as object-conditions nor as associated conditions.

As it is with the false view abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*).
Question:

Regarding the ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of the origin, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them are: the ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are associated with the proclivities but not objects of them.

Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are all [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering, with the exception of the ignorance abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering.

Those that are neither latent by way of object nor latent by way of association are: all those abandoned through the vision of suffering that are not universal; and all those abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation.
Regarding their associated dharmas: those that are latent by way of object but not latent by way of association are all those abandoned through the vision of suffering that are universal.
There are none that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are all those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither objects of latent dispositions nor associated with them are all those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) except for the universal ones, as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*), the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are all abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as those universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

These latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are latent dispositions by way of object (*ālambanānuśaya*) and not latent dispositions by way of association (*samprayogānuśaya*); the remainder are neither latent dispositions by way of object nor latent dispositions by way of association.

Question: Regarding the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: Four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*) should be made.

Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are objects of condition (*ālambana*) but not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), as well as the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).
Those latent tendencies that are associated but not objects of condition are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
There are none that are both object-conditioning (ālambanapra-yoga) and associated-conditioning (saṃprayogaprayoga).

Those that are neither object-conditioning nor associated-conditioning include: with the exception of the ignorance associated with wrong view abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya), all other [afflictions] abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object; those abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana) and origin (samudayadarśana) that are not universal (asarvatraga); and all [afflictions] abandoned by the vision of the path (mārgadarśana) and through cultivation (bhāvanā).

Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are: the outflowing factors (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) which take [cessation] as their object, and the universal [proclivities] (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with the proclivities but do not take them as objects are: the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
There are none that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanānuśaya*) and associated-pervasive (*samprayuktānuśaya*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive include: all [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) that take the untainted as their object, excluding the ignorance associated with false view abandoned through the vision of cessation; all [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) and origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [factors] abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The formations dissociated from mind that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodha*), as well as the universal [defilements].

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects of entanglement (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not act as associated entanglements (*saṃprayuktānuśaya*). As for the remaining [defilements], they neither act as objects of entanglement nor as associated entanglements.
As it is with the abandonment of wrong view through the vision of cessation, so it is with doubt.
Question:

Regarding the adherence to views abandoned through the vision of cessation, how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) act as objects (ālambana-anuśaya) but do not act as associated tendencies (saṃprayoga-anuśaya)?
Answer: This is explained by four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them: excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) which is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), it includes all other outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive [proclivities].
There are none that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.

Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither objects of latent dispositions nor associated with them are: those abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding those associated dharmas that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them: excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) which is abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), they consist of the remaining outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive [proclivities].
There are none that are associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.

Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them are: those [proclivities] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that have the untainted as their object (*anāsravālambana*); those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*) and the origin (*samudayadarśana*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all those to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana*) and by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) that arise therein are those associated with the outflows (sāsrava) having cessation as their object (nirodhālambana), which are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-heya), as well as the universal [defilements].

These latent tendencies (anuśaya) function as objects of entanglement (ālambanānuśaya) but do not function as associated entanglements (saṃprayogānuśaya). As for the remaining [defilements], they neither function as objects of entanglement nor as associated entanglements.

As it is with the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*).
Question:

Regarding the ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated tendencies (*samprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them are: the outflow-tainted ignorance (*sāsravāvidyā*) associated with the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), as well as all pervasive [proclivities].

Those that are associated with latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them are: excluding the outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the remaining outflow-free objects abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Those that are both objects of latent tendencies and associated with them are: excluding the outflow-possessing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation, the remaining outflow-possessing objects abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Those that are neither object-conditioned nor associated with the proclivities are: the outflow-free object-universal ignorance abandoned by the vision of cessation; the non-universal [ignorance] abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin; and all [ignorance] abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation.
Regarding those associated dharmas, those that are pervasive (sarvatraga) function as proclivities by way of being objects (ālambana) but not by way of association (saṃprayoga).

Those that are proclivities by way of association but not by way of being objects are those abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya) which have the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.

Those that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanānuśaya*) and associated-pervasive (*saṃprayuktānuśaya*) are the outflows (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are all those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*) and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), as well as the universal [defilements].

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects of entanglement (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not act as associated entanglements (*samprayuktānuśaya*); the remaining ones neither act as objects of entanglement nor as associated entanglements.
As it is with those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
Question:

Regarding greed abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-rāga*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but do not act as associated underlying tendencies (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them consist of all other factors abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) factors, excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with greed abandoned through cultivation.
There are none that are associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with craving (*rāga*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those that are neither objects of the proclivities nor associated with them are all those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-heya*).

Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them consist of: all [proclivities] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with craving to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga*).
There are none that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but are not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with craving (*rāga*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those that are neither objects of latent dispositions nor associated with them are all those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-heya*).
The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as all pervasive [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) function as objects of entanglement (*ālambanānuśaya*) but are not associated entanglements (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remainder are neither objects of entanglement nor associated entanglements.
As it is with greed, so it is with anger and pride.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as object-tendencies (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as associated tendencies (*samprayuktānuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of cultivation (*ālambana*) but not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are the ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and all pervasive [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).
There are none that are associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) but not objects of them.
Those that are both objects of latent dispositions and associated with them are all [latent dispositions] abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), excluding the ignorance abandoned by cultivation.

Those that are neither objects of latent dispositions nor associated with them are those that are not universal (*asarvatraga*) and are abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), as well as all those abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*).
Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).
Those that are associated with the proclivities but not their objects do not exist.
Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are all those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those that are neither objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) nor associated with them are: all those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), as well as all those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path;
and the dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them, which include all those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) as well as the universal ones.
These latent dispositions (anuśaya) are those that function through objects (ālambanānuśaya) but are not associated with the mind (na saṃprayuktānuśaya);

the remainder are neither those that function through objects nor those that are associated.
