Regarding the forty-eight types of ignorance (avidyā): there is the ignorance associated with the false view abandoned by the vision of cessation; the ignorance associated with doubt abandoned by the vision of cessation; the ignorance associated with both the false view and doubt abandoned by the vision of cessation; the ignorance dissociated from the false view abandoned by the vision of cessation; the ignorance dissociated from doubt abandoned by the vision of cessation; and the ignorance dissociated from both the false view and doubt abandoned by the vision of cessation.
As it is with those abandoned by the vision of cessation, so it is with those abandoned by the vision of the path.
As it is with those not fixed as bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:
Regarding the ignorance associated with false views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as its drivers?
Answer:
The false views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, the [afflictions] with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodhālambana-sāsrava*), and all pervasive [afflictions] (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding those associated phenomena: the ignorance associated with false views abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as the outflow-tainted objects and the universal [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation;
and the non-associated formations arising from them, which are the outflow-tainted objects and the universal [factors] abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Question:
How many latent dispositions (anuśaya) drive the ignorance associated with doubt that is abandoned by the vision of cessation?
Answer:
Doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as the outflow-bound objects and all-pervasive factors abandoned through the vision of cessation;

and their associated phenomena: the ignorance associated with doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as the outflow-bound objects and all-pervasive factors abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodhālambana-sāsrava*) and the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view and doubt that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-heya*)?

Answer: The false views and doubts abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as those [factors] with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*) abandoned through the vision of cessation;

and their associated factors, namely the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false views and doubts abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as those with outflow-objects and the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation.

The formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) whose objects are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), as well as the universal [defilements].
Question:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie the ignorance (*avidyā*) dissociated from wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation?
Answer:

Doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation, and all pervasive factors (*sarvatraga*).

As for their associated factors (*samprayukta-dharma*): with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view abandoned through the vision of cessation, it includes all other factors abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive factors.
The formations dissociated from mind that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the universal [defilements].
Question: How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) drive the ignorance (*avidyā*) dissociated from doubt (*vicikitsā*) that is abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering?
Answer:

The false views abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as those with outflow that take cessation as their object (*nirodhālambana-sāsrava*) and all pervasive factors (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding their associated dharmas: with the exception of the ignorance associated with doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation, they include all other factors abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive factors.

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), as well as the universal [defilements].

Question: How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie the ignorance (*avidyā*) dissociated from wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation?
Answer:
Those with outflows conditioned by the cessation [of suffering] (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and all pervasive [factors] (*sarvatraga*),

as well as their associated factors— excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation— all other factors abandoned through the vision of cessation and all pervasive factors.

The formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that arise therein consist of those with outflows conditioned by the cessation [of suffering] (nirodha-ālambana) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as the universal [factors].
As it is for those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, so it is for those to be abandoned by the vision of the path (mārga).
Just as it is for those [defilements] bound to the desire realm that are indeterminate, so it is for those bound to the form and formless realms.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance associated with false view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as object-tendencies (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as association-tendencies (*saṃprayogānuśaya*)?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that take objects (*ālambana*) but are not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) and all pervasive [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) but do not take them as objects are the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).
There are none that are both objects of the underlying tendencies and associated with them.

Those that are neither objects of the underlying tendencies nor associated with them include, with the exception of the false views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, all other [factors] abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; those abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and origin (*samudaya-darśana*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [factors] abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*): those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are the outflowing factors (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the universal [proclivities].
Those that are associated with the proclivities but not their objects are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view of cessation (*nirodha-mithyādṛṣṭi*).
There are no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are both object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and associated (*saṃprayukta*).

Those that are neither object-conditions nor associated are: with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), all other [ignorance] abandoned through the vision of cessation that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object; all [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The mental formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that arise therein are those associated with the cessation of views (*dṛṣṭi-nirodha-prahātavya*), those conditioned by outflows (*sāsrava-ālambana*), and the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) function as object-tendencies (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as association-tendencies (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remaining ones are neither object-tendencies nor association-tendencies.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance associated with doubt that is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*) rather than acting as associated tendencies (*samprayoga-anuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.

Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are conditions but not associated are: those with outflow-conditions (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).
Those latent dispositions that are associated but not conditions are: doubt (*vicikitsā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation.
There are no [defilements] that are both object-conditioned (*ālambana-prayoga*) and associated (*saṃprayukta-prayoga*).

Those that are neither object-conditioned nor associated are: with the exception of doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), the remaining [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), those that are objects of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are: the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and all pervasive [latent tendencies] (*sarvatraga*).
Those that are associated but not objects are: the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt (*vicikitsā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation.
There are no [defilements] that are both object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and associated conditions (*samprayoga-pratyaya*).

Those that are neither object-conditions nor associated conditions include: (1) all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) except for the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt (*vicikitsā*); (2) those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and (3) all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodhālambana-sāsrava*) and the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) function as object-conditions (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not function as associated conditions (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remaining ones neither function as object-conditions nor as associated conditions.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance associated with wrong view and doubt that is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as object-tendencies (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as association-tendencies (*samprayuktānuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.

Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are objects (*ālambana*) but not associated (*saṃprayukta*) are those with outflow-objects (*sāsravālambana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), as well as the universal ones (*sarvatraga*).
Those latent tendencies that are associated but not objects are wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
There are none that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanaparyavasthāna*) and associated-pervasive (*samprayogaparyavasthāna*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive include: with the exception of wrong view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), all other [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object; those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding those associated dharmas, those that are driven by objects (*ālambana*) but not by association (*saṃprayoga*) are the outflowing (*sāsrava*) objects abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) and all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) [defilements].
Those that are driven by association but not by objects are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation.
There are no [defilements] that are both object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and associated conditions (*samprayoga-pratyaya*).

As for those that are neither object-conditions nor associated conditions: excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are the remaining [ignorances] abandoned through the vision of cessation that take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), as well as all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*), and all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodhālambana-sāsrava*) and the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects-conditioning latent tendencies (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as association-conditioning latent tendencies (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remaining ones are neither object-conditioning nor association-conditioning latent tendencies.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance that is dissociated from the false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as object-tendencies (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not as association-tendencies (*samprayuktānuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.

Those latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are conditions but not associated are the outflow-conditions (*sāsrava-ālambana*) ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as all pervasive [proclivities].
Those latent proclivities that are associated but not conditions are the doubt (*vicikitsā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

Those that are both object-pervasive (ālambanānuśaya) and associated-pervasive (saṃprayuktānuśaya) are: with the exception of the outflow-tainted ignorance (sāsravāvidyā) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya), all other outflow-tainted [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are: with the exception of doubt (vicikitsā) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, all other factors to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that have untainted objects (anāsravālambana), those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin that are not universal (asarvatraga), and all those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*): those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with the proclivities but not their objects are: with the exception of the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the remaining [ignorance] abandoned through the vision of cessation that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.

Those that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanānuśaya*) and associated-pervasive (*saṃprayuktānuśaya*) are the outflows with objects to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya-sāsrava*).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; those not-all-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*); and all [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga*) and by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those with outflows conditioned by cessation (*nirodha-ālambana-sāsrava*) and the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects of entanglement (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not act as associated entanglements (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remaining ones neither act as objects of entanglement nor as associated entanglements.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance that is dissociated from doubt and is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are latent as objects (*ālambanānuśaya*) but not latent through association (*samprayogānuśaya*)?
Answer:
This forms four propositions.

Those latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not associated (*samprayukta*) are the outflow-tainted ignorance (*sāsrava-avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and all pervasive [proclivities].
Those latent proclivities that are associated but not object-conditions are the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Those that are both object-pervasive (*ālambanānuśaya*) and associated-pervasive (*samprayuktānuśaya*) are: with the exception of the outflow-tainted ignorance (*sāsravāvidyā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) which has [other] outflow-tainted states as its object, all other outflow-tainted states to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that have [other] outflow-tainted states as their objects.

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are: with the exception of the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, all other [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that have untainted states (*anāsrava*) as their objects; those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*) and origination (*samudayadarśana*) that are not universal (*asarvatraga*); and all [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding those associated dharmas: those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with the proclivities but not their objects consist of the remaining [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) that take the untainted as their object, excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Those that are both object-pervasions (*ālambanānuśaya*) and associated-pervasions (*samprayuktānuśaya*) are the outflows with objects to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya-sāsrava*).
Those that are neither object-pervasions nor associated-pervasions are doubt (*vicikitsā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

The ignorance associated with that [ignorance] is not universal (*asarvatraga*) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); it is also all [ignorance] abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from that [ignorance] are those conditioned by the outflows (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and all universal [factors].

These proclivities are proclivities by way of object (*ālambana-anuśaya*) but not proclivities by way of association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*); the remainder are neither proclivities by way of object nor proclivities by way of association.
Question:

Regarding the ignorance (*avidyā*) dissociated from false view and doubt that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many proclivities are proclivities by way of object but not proclivities by way of association?
Answer: This is explained by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but are not associated with them are: the outflow-tainted ignorance (*sāsravāvidyā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), as well as all pervasive [proclivities].
There are none that are associated with the proclivities but not objects of them.

Those that are both objects of the proclivities and associated with them are: with the exception of the outflow-tainted ignorance abandoned by the vision of cessation that has outflow-tainted objects, all other outflow-tainted [ignorance] abandoned by the vision of cessation.

Those that are neither object-conditioned nor associated with the proclivities are: those abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the outflow-free as their object; those abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin that are not universal; and all those abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation.
Regarding those associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), those that are objects of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) but not associated with them are all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Those that are associated with the proclivities but not their objects are the remaining [proclivities] abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) which take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with false view and doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Those that are both object-pervasive (ālambanānuśaya) and associated-pervasive (saṃprayuktānuśaya) are the outflows with objects to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya-sāsrava).

Those that are neither object-pervasive nor associated-pervasive are the ignorance (avidyā) associated with wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi) and doubt (vicikitsā) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; those not universal (asarvatraga) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha) and origin (samudaya); and all [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the path (mārga) and by cultivation (bhāvanā).

The formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise therein are those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), those with outflows conditioned by [the Truths] (*sāsrava-ālambana*), and the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*).

These latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as objects of entanglement (*ālambanānuśaya*) but do not act as associated entanglements (*saṃprayogānuśaya*); the remaining ones are neither objects of entanglement nor associated entanglements.
As it is with those abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with those abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
As it is with those not fixed as bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), so it is with those bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Question:
If there is an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that has out-flowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana), is it an underlying tendency associated with those objects?
If it is an underlying tendency associated with those objects, does it have out-flowing objects?
Answer:

There are. If it is a latent tendency that conditions another latent tendency and is associated with it, then that is either a latent tendency conditioned by outflows (*sāsrava*), or a latent tendency that has outflows as its object; however, it is not a latent tendency that conditions it while being associated with it.
What is "existence"?

It refers to those universal [defilements] belonging to other realms; that is, the proclivities (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm that take as their object the form realm, those bound to the desire realm that take as their object the formless realm, those bound to the form realm that take as their object the formless realm, and those bound to the desire realm that take as their object both the form and formless realms.
Question:
If it is an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that has the untainted (anāsrava) as its object, is it an underlying tendency that is associated (saṃprayukta)?
If it is an underlying tendency that is associated, does it have the untainted as its object?
Answer: There are.

If it is an underlying tendency associated with an underlying tendency, it is either an underlying tendency that has the outflow-free as its object, or it is an underlying tendency associated with an underlying tendency that does not have the outflow-free as its object.
What is "existence"?

It refers to the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of other realms; that is, proclivities bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) taking as their object those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), those bound to the desire realm taking as their object those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), those bound to the form realm taking as their object those bound to the formless realm, and those bound to the desire realm taking as their object those bound to both the form and formless realms. This concludes the fifth chapter, "The Classification of Proclivities."
*Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Three;
*Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.

Chapter Six: The Chapter on the Analysis of Inclusion (Vibhaṅga-saṃgraha-varga). First: the dharma of initial application (*vitarka*), the dharma of discernment (*vicāra*), the dharma of both initial application and discernment, the dharma of object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the dharma of predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), material (*rūpa*) dharmas, non-material (*arūpa*) dharmas, visible (*sanidarśana*) dharmas, invisible (*anidarśana*) dharmas, resistant (*sapratigha*) dharmas, non-resistant (*apratigha*) dharmas, and outflowing (*sāsrava*) dharmas.

Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), phenomena associated with conflict (*saraṇa-dharma*) and phenomena free from conflict (*araṇa-dharma*),

mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) and supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*), phenomena that enter [into the cycle] and phenomena that do not enter, defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) and undefiled phenomena (*akliṣṭa-dharma*),
phenomena based on the household life and phenomena based on the essential departure [from it], and mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) and non-mental phenomena (*acitta-dharma*).
Mental phenomena and non-mental phenomena; phenomena associated with the mind and phenomena dissociated from the mind;
phenomena coexistent with the mind and phenomena not coexistent with the mind; phenomena that follow the mind and phenomena that do not follow the mind;
phenomena caused by the mind and phenomena not caused by the mind; phenomena that succeed the mind and phenomena that do not succeed the mind.
The first category consists of: mental factors and non-mental factors; factors predominant over the mind and factors not predominant over the mind;
factors that are results of the mind and factors that are not results of the mind; factors that are retribution of the mind and factors that are not retribution of the mind;
karmic factors and non-karmic factors; factors associated with karma and factors not associated with karma; and karma...
Dharmas shared with karma and dharmas not shared with karma; dharmas that follow after karma and dharmas that do not follow after karma;

dharmas that have karma as their cause and dharmas that do not have karma as their cause; dharmas that are the immediate succession of karma and dharmas that are not the immediate succession of karma;
dharmas conditioned by karma and dharmas not conditioned by karma; dharmas that have karma as their predominance and dharmas that do not have karma as their predominance.
Dharmas that are results of karma and dharmas that are not results of karma; dharmas that are retributions of karma and dharmas that are not retributions of karma;
existent dharmas and non-existent dharmas; dharmas associated with existence and dharmas not associated with existence;
dharmas co-existent with existence and dharmas not co-existent with existence; dharmas that follow and have causes and dharmas that do not follow and do not have causes... [and so forth].
There are dharmas that have causes, dharmas that follow a sequence and dharmas that do not follow a sequence;
dharmas that are conditioned and dharmas that are unconditioned; dharmas that possess predominance and dharmas that do not possess predominance;
dharmas that are fruits and dharmas that are not fruits; dharmas that are retributions and dharmas that are not retributions; dharmas to be abandoned through knowledge, and dharmas known by wisdom.

Dharmas that are objects of knowledge and dharmas that are not objects of knowledge by wisdom; dharmas to be abandoned by full comprehension and dharmas that are not to be abandoned by full comprehension;
dharmas to be cultivated and dharmas that are not to be cultivated; dharmas to be realized and dharmas that are not to be realized; dharmas to be practiced and dharmas that are not to be practiced;
blameworthy dharmas and blameless dharmas; dark dharmas and bright dharmas; dharmas subject to regression and [dharmas not subject to regression]...
The dharma of falling back; the dharma of being obscured and the dharma of not being obscured; the dharma of being determinate and the dharma of being indeterminate;
the dharma that has already arisen and the dharma that has not yet arisen; the dharma arising now and the dharma not arising now;

the dharma that has already ceased and the dharma that has not yet ceased; the dharma ceasing now and the dharma not ceasing now; and the dharma of dependent origination and the dharma that is not dependently originated.
Arising phenomena; dependently originated phenomena and non-dependently originated phenomena;
causal phenomena and non-causal phenomena; phenomena with causes and phenomena without causes; phenomena arising from causes and phenomena not arising from causes;
phenomena associated with causes and phenomena not associated with causes; fettering phenomena and non-fettering phenomena; phenomena that produce fetters and [phenomena that do not].

Dharmas that give rise to fetters, dharmas that are grasped and dharmas that are not grasped, dharmas that are felt and dharmas that are not felt, dharmas that produce grasping and dharmas that do not produce grasping,
dharmas that are afflictions and dharmas that are not afflictions, dharmas that are defiled and dharmas that are not defiled,
dharmas that possess defilement and dharmas that do not possess defilement, and dharmas that are entanglements and [dharmas that are not entanglements].
The phenomena of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*): phenomena that are fetters, phenomena that are not fetters; phenomena produced by fetters, phenomena not produced by fetters;
phenomena with an object, phenomena without an object; phenomena with applied thought (*vitarka*), phenomena without applied thought;
phenomena with sustained thought (*vicāra*), phenomena without sustained thought; phenomena that are delightful, phenomena that are not delightful; phenomena that are experienced...
Non-appropriated phenomena; phenomena with a basis and with an object, and phenomena without a basis and without an object; surpassable phenomena and unsurpassable phenomena;
remote phenomena and proximate phenomena; limited phenomena and immeasurable phenomena; phenomena that are views and phenomena that are not views;
phenomena that are bases for views and phenomena that are not bases for views; and phenomena associated with views.
Dharmas not associated with views; dharmas of ordinary persons and dharmas not of ordinary persons; dharmas common to ordinary persons and dharmas not common to ordinary persons;
determinate dharmas and indeterminate dharmas; afflictive dharmas and non-afflictive dharmas; root dharmas and non-root dharmas;
dharmas subsumed under the Noble Truths and dharmas not subsumed under the Noble Truths; and those that are shared.
Dharmas and non-common dharmas; associated dharmas and non-associated dharmas;

resultant dharmas and non-resultant dharmas; dharmas with results and dharmas without results; retributive dharmas and non-retributive dharmas; dharmas with retribution and dharmas without retribution;
dharmas that are causal conditions and dharmas that are not causal conditions; dharmas possessing causal conditions...
Dharmas that have causes and conditions and dharmas that do not; emerging dharmas and non-emerging dharmas;
dharmas with emergence and dharmas without emergence; continuous dharmas and non-continuous dharmas;
dharmas with continuity and dharmas without continuity—these two categories comprise two hundred and sixteen types in total.
Wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena;
phenomena of those in training, phenomena of those beyond training, and phenomena of neither training nor beyond training;
phenomena to be abandoned by vision, phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, and phenomena not to be abandoned.
Factors whose cause is to be abandoned by vision, factors whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation, and factors whose cause is not to be abandoned;
visible and resistant factors, invisible and resistant factors, and invisible and non-resistant factors.
Dharmas that are results, dharmas that are not results, and dharmas that are neither results nor non-results;
inferior dharmas, middling dharmas, and superior dharmas;
minor dharmas, great dharmas, and immeasurable dharmas.
Dharmas associated with the mental faculty, dharmas not associated with the mental faculty, and dharmas neither associated nor dissociated from the mental faculty;
dharmas accompanied by pleasure, dharmas accompanied by suffering, and dharmas accompanied by neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Dharmas that arise together, abide together, and cease together;
dharmas that do not arise together, do not abide together, and do not cease together;
dharmas that arise together with the mind, abide together with the mind, and cease together with the mind.
They are not dharmas that arise together with the mind, not dharmas that abide together with the mind, and not dharmas that cease together with the mind.
The three realms:
the realm of desire, the realm of hatred, and the realm of harm.
Furthermore, there are three realms:
the realm of renunciation, the realm of non-ill will, and the realm of non-harming.
Furthermore, there are three realms:
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are three realms:
the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation.
The three realms of existence (bhava):
the realm of desire (kāmadhātu-bhava), the realm of form (rūpadhātu-bhava), and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-bhava).
The three outflows (āsrava):
The outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*),
and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
The three periods of time: the past, the future, and the present.
The three ways of explaining phenomena:
Matters spoken of in the past, matters spoken of in the future, and matters spoken of in the present.
The three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned formations.
Three dharmas:
dharmas with vitarka and vicāra, dharmas without vitarka but with vicāra, and dharmas without vitarka or vicāra.
Three stages:
The stage with directed thought and sustained thought, the stage without directed thought but with sustained thought, and the stage without directed thought and without sustained thought.
The three types of action:
bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma:
wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and indeterminate karma.
Again, there are three types of karma:
There are the karmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the karmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the karmas of neither training nor beyond training.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma:
karma to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and karma not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
Furthermore, there are three types of karma:
karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced upon rebirth, and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma:
The three types of karma—karma resulting in pleasant feeling, karma resulting in painful feeling, and karma resulting in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—comprise ninety-three varieties in total.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna): namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.

The four right endeavors (samyakpradhāna) are: the right endeavor that consists of the application of skillful means to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen; the right endeavor that consists of the application of skillful means to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising; the right endeavor that consists of the application of skillful means to bring about wholesome states that have not yet arisen; and the right endeavor that consists of the application of skillful means to cultivate, maintain, prevent the loss of, fulfill the practice of, and further increase those wholesome states that have already arisen, thereby realizing wisdom.

The four bases of power (ṛddhipāda) are: the base of power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the desire for purification; the base of power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the exertion of purification; the base of power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the mind of purification; and the base of power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the investigation of purification.
The four dhyānas refer to the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

The four noble truths refer to the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
The four immeasurables are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The four formless attainments are the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are: the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains by begging; the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains by begging; the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding and seating one obtains; and the noble lineage of delighting in solitude and delighting in cultivation.

The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are: the fruit of śrāmaṇya of the srotāpanna, the fruit of śrāmaṇya of the sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of śrāmaṇya of the anāgāmin, and the unsurpassed fruit of śrāmaṇya of the arhat.

There are four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

Furthermore, there are four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are: the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

The four conditions (*pratyaya*) are: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The four nutriments (āhāra) are: edible food consisting of mouthfuls (kabaḷīkārāhāra), nutriment of contact (phassāhāra), nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra), and nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra).
The four floods (ogha) are: the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha), the flood of existence (bhavogha), the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), and the flood of ignorance (avijjogha).
The four yokes (yoga) are: the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
The four graspings (upādāna) are: grasping at sensual desire, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and observances, and grasping at a self-theory.
There are four categories of phenomena: namely, past phenomena, future phenomena, present phenomena, and phenomena that are neither past, future, nor present.

Furthermore, there are another four categories of phenomena: namely, phenomena bound to the desire realm, phenomena bound to the form realm, phenomena bound to the formless realm, and unbound phenomena.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas: namely, dharmas that are causes of the wholesome, dharmas that are causes of the unwholesome, dharmas that are causes of the indeterminate, and dharmas that are neither causes of the wholesome, nor causes of the unwholesome, nor causes of the indeterminate.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas: namely, dharmas with an object-condition (sālambana), dharmas without an object-condition (anālambana), dharmas both with and without an object-condition, and dharmas neither with nor without an object-condition. These four categories comprise eighty-four types in total.
The five aggregates (skandhas) are: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
The five aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandhas) are: the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The five destinies (gati) are: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of gods, and the destiny of humans.

The five groups of afflictions (kleśa-kāya) are: the group of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing suffering, the group of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing the origin, the group of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing cessation, the group of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing the path, and the group of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation.

There are five categories of phenomena: namely, material phenomena (rūpadharma), mental phenomena (cittadharma), mental concomitants (caitasikadharma), conditioned phenomena dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāradharma), and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma). These five categories comprise twenty-five types in total.
The six elements (*dhātu*) are: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

The six phenomena (*dharma*) are: phenomena to be abandoned by seeing suffering, phenomena to be abandoned by seeing the origin, phenomena to be abandoned by seeing cessation, phenomena to be abandoned by seeing the path, phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, and phenomena not to be abandoned. This concludes the twelve types of phenomena.

The seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are: the latent tendency of sensual desire, the latent tendency of ill-will, the latent tendency of craving for existence, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of views, and the latent tendency of doubt.

The seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are as follows: there are sentient beings with form who have diverse bodies and diverse perceptions—namely, humans and certain devas; this is called the first station of consciousness.
There are beings with form who have diverse bodies but a single perception, namely those who were the first to be born in the Brahma-world; this is called the second station of consciousness.
There are beings with form who have a single type of body but diverse perceptions; these are the Ābhāsvara devas, and this is called the third station of consciousness.
There are beings with form who have a single type of body and a single type of perception; these are the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and this is called the fourth station of consciousness.

As for formless beings, having already abandoned all perceptions of form, perceptions of resistance, and perceptions of diversity, they contemplate the sphere of infinite space and enter the base of infinite space; these are the gods of the base of infinite space, which is called the fifth station of consciousness.

As for formless beings who have already transcended the sphere of infinite space and, possessing immeasurable consciousness, enter the sphere of infinite consciousness—namely, the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness—this is called the sixth abode of consciousness.

As for formless beings, having already transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, they dwell in nothingness, entering the sphere of nothingness; these are the gods of the sphere of nothingness, which is called the seventh station of consciousness.

The seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) refer to the seven dharmas consisting of the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; this concludes the twenty-one types.
The eight bases of liberation: perceiving forms internally while observing forms externally is called the first base of liberation;
not perceiving forms internally while observing forms externally is called the second base of liberation.
Purifying the body and realizing the sphere of liberation is called the third sphere of liberation.

Having already abandoned all perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance, and having completely transcended perceptions of diversity, one contemplates the sphere of infinite space and enters the base of infinite space; this is called the fourth sphere of liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness; this is called the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the seventh stage of liberation.

Having already transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells having realized the cessation of perception and feeling through bodily witness; this is called the eighth liberation.

Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): first, there is the internal perception of form, while externally perceiving limited forms—whether beautiful or ugly—one generates the contemplative perception of those forms as being mastered; this is called the first base of mastery.

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms—whether beautiful or ugly—as many; by generating the contemplative perception of those forms as the sphere of mastery, this is called the second sphere of mastery.

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms—whether limited, beautiful, or ugly—and by generating the contemplative perception of those forms as the sphere of mastery, this is called the third sphere of mastery.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms—be they many, beautiful, or ugly—and thus generates the contemplative perception of those forms as the sphere of mastery; this is called the entry into the fourth sphere of mastery.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as blue—blue in color, blue in appearance, and emitting blue light—just like the color of a *kumuda* flower, or like a well-dyed blue Benares cloth, blue in color, blue in appearance, and emitting blue light.

In this way, a bhikṣu, having no perception of internal forms, perceives external forms as blue—blue in color, blue in appearance, and emitting blue light; he generates a contemplative perception regarding those forms as a sphere of mastery. This is called the entry into the fifth sphere of mastery.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as yellow—yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster. Just like the color of a *kariṇa* flower, or the yellow of a well-dyed Benares cloth—yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster;

so too, a bhikṣu, having no perception of internal forms, perceives external forms as yellow—yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster. Thus, he generates the perception of mastery over those forms; this is called the entry into the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Internally perceiving no form, one views external forms as red—red in color, with a red appearance, and emitting red light. Just as the color of the pāṇḍu-sivaka flower, or like the accomplished saffron robe of Vārāṇasī, which is red in color, has a red appearance, and emits red light;

so too does this bhikṣu, internally perceiving no form, view external forms as red—red in color, with a red appearance, and red in color. This refers to the arising of the contemplative perception regarding that superior base of form; this is called the entry into the seventh base of mastery.

With no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as white—white in color, with a white appearance, and emitting white light—just like the color of an *uśīra* flower, or like a well-wrought Benares cloth that is white in color, with a white appearance, and emitting white light.

In this way, a bhikṣu, with no perception of internal forms, perceives external forms as white—white in color, with a white appearance, and emitting white light—and by generating the meditative perception of those forms as a sphere of mastery, it is called the eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

The eight factors of the path—namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these eight dharmas comprise twenty-four types. [End.]

The nine fetters are: the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.

Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings: there are sentient beings with form who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, namely humans and certain devas; this is called the first abode of sentient beings.
There are beings with form who have diverse bodies but a single perception; namely, those who were first created as the Brahmā deities. This is called the second abode of sentient beings.
There are beings with form who are uniform in body but diverse in perception; these are the Ābhāsvara devas, and this is called the third abode of beings.
There are beings with form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception; these are the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and this is called the fourth abode of beings.
There are sentient beings with form who are without perception; these are the sentient beings of the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva-deva), which is called the fifth abode of sentient beings.

There are sentient beings without form who, having transcended all perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance, and having completely ceased perceptions of diversity, contemplate the sphere of infinite space and enter and abide in the sphere of infinite space—namely, the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana-deva). This is called the sixth abode of sentient beings.

Formless beings, having transcended the sphere of infinite space, enter and abide in the sphere of infinite consciousness; these are the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness, known as the seventh abode of sentient beings.

As for formless beings, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, they enter and abide in the sphere of nothingness; these are the gods of the sphere of nothingness, which is called the eighth abode of sentient beings.

As for formless beings, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, they enter and abide in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this refers to the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called the ninth abode of sentient beings. Thus ends the nine categories consisting of eighteen types.

The ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are as follows: the earth universal base, which arises as a single sign, extending upward, downward, and in all directions, without duality and immeasurable; this is called the first universal base.

The spheres of totality (kasiṇa) of water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, and space; and the sphere of totality of consciousness—these arise as a single characteristic, above, below, and in all directions, non-dual and immeasurable. These are called the ten spheres of totality.

The ten factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) refer to the untrained right view, up to and including untrained liberation and untrained knowledge and vision of liberation; these ten factors comprise twenty types in total.

The eleven dharmas refer to form, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*); feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, each being either with outflows or without outflows; and unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus ends the section on the eleven kinds of the eleven dharmas.
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) refer to the eye-base and the form-base, up to the mind-base and the mental-object-base; thus the twelve phenomena consist of twelve kinds.
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), as explained in detail in the previous "Chapter on the Analysis of the Seven Matters," consist of eighteen kinds.

The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are as follows: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, male faculty, female faculty, life faculty, mind faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Thus ends the enumeration of the twenty-two factors as the twenty-two [faculties].
The ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) and the ninety-eight phenomena (*dharma*) have been fully explained.
What are the phenomena of suchness (*tathatā-dharma*)?
They refer to all phenomena as they are known by the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), according to their respective natures.
What is meant by "according to what is appropriate"?

It means that the knowledge of suffering knows it; the knowledge of the origin of suffering knows it; the knowledge of the cessation of the origin knows it; the knowledge of the path to cessation knows it; and the knowledge of the path, as well as the knowledge of the wholesome and so forth, also know them.

Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation—all these phenomena are known by the knowledge of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*), according to their respective natures; this is called the dharma of suchness.
What are the phenomena cognized by consciousness?
They refer to all phenomena that are cognized and discriminated by consciousness, according to their respective natures.
What does "according to their respective natures" mean?

That is to say: eye-consciousness cognizes forms; ear-consciousness cognizes sounds; nose-consciousness cognizes odors; tongue-consciousness cognizes tastes; body-consciousness cognizes tangibles; and mind-consciousness cognizes mental phenomena.

The eye and forms are cognized by eye-consciousness; the ear and sounds are cognized by ear-consciousness; the nose and odors are cognized by nose-consciousness; the tongue and tastes are cognized by tongue-consciousness; the body and tangibles are cognized by body-consciousness; and the mind and mental phenomena are cognized by mind-consciousness.
All these phenomena are conceptualizations of consciousness; according to their respective natures, they are called "phenomena of consciousness.
What is the "penetration of reality" (*tattvārtha*)?
By "penetration of reality" is meant wisdom (*prajñā*); it is that wisdom which penetrates all those phenomena according to their respective natures.

What is meant by "according to what is appropriate"? It refers to the fact that the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) both pertain to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of suffering; the patience regarding origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) both pertain to the object-condition of origin; the patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) both pertain to the object-condition of cessation; and the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-jñāna*) both pertain to the object-condition of the path. Furthermore, wholesome contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-kuśala-prajñā*) also pertains to the object-condition of suffering, as well as to the object-conditions of origin, cessation, the path, space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
All these phenomena are pervasive and illuminating; according to their respective applications, they are called pervasive and illuminating phenomena (*paryāpanna-dharma*).
What are conditioned phenomena (*pratyaya-dharma*)?
They refer to all phenomena that serve as conditions, namely the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), according to their respective applications.

What is meant by "according to their respective applications"? It means that visual consciousness and its associated mental factors take visible forms as their object; auditory consciousness and its associated mental factors take sounds as their object; olfactory consciousness and its associated mental factors take odors as their object; gustatory consciousness and its associated mental factors take tastes as their object; tactile consciousness and its associated mental factors take tangibles as their object; and mental consciousness and its associated mental factors take [all phenomena] as their object.

The conditions for the eye and forms and eye-consciousness; the conditions for the ear and sounds and ear-consciousness; the conditions for the nose and odors and nose-consciousness; the conditions for the body and tangibles and body-consciousness; and the conditions for the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness—all phenomena—namely, the mind and mental factors, are called the "conditioned phenomena."
What are the dominant factors (*adhipati-dharma*)?

They refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) acting as dominant conditions for one another, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) acting as dominant conditions for conditioned phenomena; these are called dominant factors.
What are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*)?
They are the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What are non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*)?
It refers to one base (*āyatana*) and a portion of another base.
What are the phenomena that are visible?
It refers to one base.
What are the invisible phenomena?
They are the eleven bases (āyatana).
What are the resistant phenomena?
That is, the ten bases (āyatana).
What are the non-resistant phenomena?
That is, the two bases.
What are the phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*)?
They are the ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
What are the phenomena without outflows (*anāsrava-dharma*)?
That is to say, a portion of two bases (*āyatana*).
What are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)?
They are eleven bases and a portion of one base.
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
They are a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
What are phenomena associated with contention (*saraṇa-dharma*)?
This refers to the ten bases (āyatana) and a portion of two bases.
What are the dharmas free from contention?
They refer to a portion of two bases.

As it is with phenomena that involve contention, so it is with phenomena free from contention; with mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena; with phenomena that lead to entry [into the Dharma] and those that do not; with defiled phenomena and undefiled phenomena; and likewise with phenomena based on the household life and phenomena based on the essential way of renunciation.
What are mental factors?
They are one base (āyatana).
What are non-mental factors?
It refers to the eleven bases (āyatana).
What are mental factors (caitasika-dharma)?
It refers to those phenomena that are associated with the mind (citta-samprayukta).
What, then, are they? They are the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), and their associated aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
What are the factors that are not mental states (acaitasika-dharma)?
That is to say, those phenomena that are dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta). What, then, are they?
They are matter (rūpa), mind (citta), formations dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

As it is with mental factors (*cittadharma*), so it is with non-mental factors (*acittadharma*). It is the same for factors associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and factors dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
What are the factors coexistent with the mind (*cittasahabhū*)?
This refers to those factors that share in eleven bases (*āyatana*) with the mind, excluding the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
What are the factors not shared in common with the mind?
They are the mind-base, or those factors that do not share in the eleven bases with the mind.
What are the mental concomitants (cittānuparivartin-dharma)?
They are those phenomena that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind. What, then, are they?

This refers to all mental factors (caitta-dharma), as well as the precepts associated with the Path (mārga-samvara) and those associated with meditative concentration (samādhi-samvara); the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of that mind and those factors are called the phenomena that follow the mind (cittānuvartin-dharma).
What are the phenomena that do not follow the mind?
They are those phenomena which do not arise together with the mind, do not abide together with it, and do not cease together with it. What, then, are they?

This refers to: (1) all other matter, excluding the mental factors, the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samvara*) and those associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*); (2) all other formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), excluding those that follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*); and (3) the mind itself and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are the phenomena that are causes of mind?
They are: for one who has entered the state of transcendence and departure from birth, with the exception of that first untainted mind;

or any other minds, as well as any other ordinary persons who are definitely destined for transcendence and departure from birth, with the exception of their future first untainted mind—namely, those other minds and a portion of the eleven bases (*āyatana*) that serve as causes of mind.
What are the phenomena that are not causes of mind?
They are: the first untainted mind of one who has entered the state of transcendence beyond the stage of ordinary birth;
and the first future untainted mind of other ordinary persons who are definitely destined for transcendence beyond the stage of ordinary birth.
Furthermore, [this includes] that which is non-mental, or the eleven bases (*āyatana*) in part that are not mental causes.
What are the factors that follow immediately after the mind (*cittānantaradharma*)?

They are: whatever other minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) have arisen or will arise following the mind; and the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), whether they have already arisen or will arise. These are called the factors that follow immediately after the mind.
What are the phenomena that do not follow immediately after the mind?

They are: with the exception of those mental states and mental factors that follow immediately after the mind, all other mental states and mental factors; with the exception of those formations dissociated from the mind that follow immediately after the mind, all other formations dissociated from the mind, as well as form and the unconditioned.
What are mental factors that take mind as their object?
They are those mental factors associated with the mental consciousness that take mind as their object.
What are mental factors that do not take mind as their object?

This refers to: with the exception of those associated with the mind-consciousness that take [objects] as their conditions, all others associated with the mind-consciousness that do not take [objects] as their conditions; matter associated with the five consciousnesses; and unconditioned phenomena and formations dissociated from the mind.
What are the phenomena predominant over the mind?
They are the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are the phenomena not predominant over the mind?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are the phenomena that are the fruits of the mind?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are phenomena that are not the fruit of the mind?
They are space and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are phenomena that are the retribution of the mind?
That is to say: if the mind consists of a portion of eleven bases (āyatana) obtained as karmic retribution, excluding the base of sound.
What is not a dharma that is the retribution of the mind?
It is the base of sound.
Excluding a portion of the eleven bases acquired as the retribution of mind,
what are the dharmas of karma?
They are bodily karma, vocal karma, and the karma of volition.
What are non-action dharmas?
They refer to other forms (rūpa) excluding bodily and vocal actions;
and other formations (saṃskāra) excluding volitional action (cetanā).
Excluding the remaining three aggregates—feeling and so forth—as well as the unconditioned.
What are the factors associated with volition?
They are those factors that are associated with *cetanā* (volition).
What, then, are those?
They are all minds and mental factors, with the exception of volition (*cetanā*).
What are the factors not associated with karma?
That is to say, which phenomena are dissociated from volition? They are:
matter, volition, mental factors dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned.
What are the factors co-existent with karma?
They are the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), and, excluding volition (*cetanā*), a portion of the eleven sense-bases that are co-existent with karma.
What are the factors not co-existent with karma?
This refers to volitional action (*cetanā-karma*), excluding the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the portions of the eleven bases that are not co-existent with action.
What are the phenomena that follow along with action (*karmānuvartin-dharma*)? They are those phenomena that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with volition.
What, then, are they? They are all minds and mental factors, with the exception of volition;

as well as the precepts associated with the Path or associated with meditative concentration, or that volitional karma itself, along with the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of those phenomena. These are called the dharmas that follow along with karma.
What are the phenomena that do not follow along with karma?
They are those phenomena which do not arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*). What, then, are they?
That is to say: excluding mind, mental factors, and bodily and vocal actions that follow from karma, whatever other matter there may be;
and excluding formations dissociated from mind that follow from karma, whatever other formations dissociated from mind there may be, as well as volition and the unconditioned.
What are the phenomena that have karma as their cause?

They refer to the volitional formations (*cetanā*) of one who has entered the state of transcending and departing from the realm of birth—excluding those initial outflow-free (*anāsrava*) volitional formations—and any other volitional formations;

as well as the volitional formations of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are certain to proceed toward transcending and departing from the realm of birth—excluding those initial future outflow-free volitional formations—and any other volitional formations.
And the mind-base (*manāyatana*), as well as a portion of the eleven bases that have karma as their cause.
What are the phenomena that do not have karma as their cause?
They are the first untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*) of one who has transcended and entered the state of being free from birth.

Furthermore, regarding other ordinary persons who are certain to transcend and emerge from the state of birth, their first future untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*)—if it is not the cause of karma—is comprised of a portion of eleven bases (*āyatana*), excluding the mind base (*manāyatana*).
What are phenomena that follow in sequence from karma?
They are those phenomena that follow in sequence from the mind.
What are phenomena that do not follow in sequence from karma?
That is to say, if a dharma does not follow immediately after the mind,
how can it take karma as its object?
It refers to the eye, ear, and mind, which, in association with their respective groups of consciousness, take karma as their object.

What are the phenomena that are not associated with the three consciousness-bodies having karma as their condition? They are: those associated with the three consciousness-bodies having karma as their condition—excluding the eye and so forth;

the remaining phenomena associated with the three consciousness-bodies that do not have karma as their condition; the forms associated with the three consciousness-bodies of the nose, tongue, and body; and the unconditioned phenomena and formations dissociated from mind.
What are phenomena predominant by way of karma?
They are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena not predominant by way of karma?
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are the fruits of karma?
They refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are phenomena that are not the fruit of karma?
They are space and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are phenomena that are the retribution of karma?
That is to say, if a portion of eleven bases (*āyatana*) is obtained as the maturation of karma, with the exception of the sound base (*śabdāyatana*).
What are the factors that are not the maturation of karma?
They are the sound base, or that portion of the eleven bases which is not obtained as the maturation of karma.
What are existent phenomena?
They are the tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
What are non-existent phenomena?
That is to say, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*)?
That is to say, tainted mind and mental factors (*sāsrava-citta-caitta*).
What are the factors not associated with existence?
They are the untainted mind and mental factors, matter, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind.
What are the factors that exist and are co-existent?
This refers to tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) or untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) that arise simultaneously with tainted phenomena.
What are non-associated phenomena?
This refers to all other untainted phenomena, excluding tainted phenomena and those untainted phenomena that are associated.
What are phenomena that both have concomitants and have causes?
They are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
What are phenomena that neither have concomitants nor have causes?
This refers to untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are phenomena that possess sequence?

It refers to those tainted minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arising in succession, as well as other minds and mental factors that have already arisen or will arise, and the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) that have already arisen or will arise; these are called phenomena that possess sequence.
What are the dharmas that do not possess sequential order?
They are: with the exception of those mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) that possess sequential order, all other mental states and mental factors;

with the exception of those formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that possess sequential order, all other formations dissociated from mind, as well as form (rūpa) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
What are phenomena that have existence as their object?
They are those associated with the five consciousnesses and those associated with the mental consciousness that has existence as its object.
What are phenomena that do not have existence as their object?

This refers to that which is associated with consciousness other than that associated with the five sensory consciousnesses and their objects, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
What are the phenomena that possess sovereignty?
They are the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are the phenomena that do not possess sovereignty?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are phenomena that possess results (*saphala-dharma*)?
They are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), or those which are realized through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) as the severance of various fetters (*saṃyojana*).
What are phenomena that do not have a fruit?
They are those other than contaminated phenomena and uncontaminated phenomena that have a fruit; namely, the remaining uncontaminated phenomena.
What are phenomena that entail retribution?
That is to say, there are portions of eleven bases (āyatana) obtained through retribution, excluding the base of sound.
What are the non-retribution-producing dharmas?
They are the base of sound, or those portions of the eleven bases that are not obtained through retribution.
What are the dharmas to be abandoned through knowledge?
They are two types of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge.
What are the phenomena known by wisdom?
They are all phenomena that are known by wisdom.
What are the phenomena not known by wisdom?
This means that if one seeks such dharmas, they cannot be found.
What are the dharmas to be abandoned through realization?
They are the dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What are the phenomena not to be abandoned by the knowledge of abandonment?
They are the untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
What are the phenomena to be cultivated?
It refers to wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are non-cultivated phenomena?
They refer to unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena (*akuśala-avyākṛta-dharma*), as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is the realization of the Dharma?
It refers to two kinds of realization of the Dharma:
realization through wisdom and realization through attainment.
What are phenomena realized through wisdom?
They are all phenomena realized by wisdom.
What are phenomena not realized through wisdom?
This means that if such dharmas are sought, they cannot be found.
How, then, does one realize the dharma?
It is said that when wholesome dharmas depend upon meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) to realize the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) divine eye and divine ear, this is called "realization."
What are the dharmas not to be realized?
