They are all indeterminate (avyākṛta) and unwholesome (akuśala) dharmas, with the exception of the non-obscured indeterminate divine eye and divine ear.
What are the dharmas to be cultivated (bhāvanīya)?
That is to say, wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are non-cultivated phenomena (*anucitadharma*)?
They are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are dharmas with fault?
They are unwholesome dharmas and obscured-unspecified dharmas.
What are dharmas without fault?
This refers to wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) and non-obscured neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
As with phenomena that are faulty, so it is with phenomena that are faultless, black phenomena, white phenomena, phenomena subject to decline, and phenomena not subject to decline.
What are the obscured phenomena?
They are the defiled phenomena.
What are the non-obscured phenomena?
That is to say, non-defiled dharmas.
What are determinate dharmas?
They are wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas.
What are indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*)?
They are those phenomena other than wholesome and unwholesome ones.
What are arisen phenomena (*utpanna-dharma*)?
This refers to past and present phenomena (*dharma*).
What are non-arising phenomena?
They refer to future phenomena that do not arise and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are phenomena that arise in the present?
They are those future phenomena which will necessarily arise when they manifest before one.
What are phenomena that do not arise in the present?
This refers to all other future dharmas—excluding those that are destined to arise when they become present—as well as past and present dharmas and unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the dharmas that have already ceased?
This refers to past phenomena.
What are non-extinguished phenomena?
They are future and present phenomena, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is the phenomenon that ceases in the present? It refers to any phenomenon that ceases while currently existing. What is the phenomenon that does not cease in the present?
It refers to any phenomenon that does not cease while currently existing.
This refers to all other present phenomena—excluding those that are currently manifesting and ceasing—as well as past and future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are non-conditionally-arisen phenomena?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

As it is with the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), so it is with the dharma that is not dependently originated; with the dharma produced by conditions (*pratyayaja*) and the dharma not produced by conditions; with the causal dharma (*hetudharma*) and the non-causal dharma; with the dharma possessing a cause (*sahetuka*) and the dharma lacking a cause; and likewise with the dharma arisen from causes (*hetusamutthita*) and the dharma not arisen from causes.
What are factors associated with causes?
They are all mind and mental factors.
What are factors not associated with causes?
They are form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
What are the phenomena that are fetters?
They are the nine fetters.
What are the non-fettering phenomena (*asaṃyojanadharma*)?
They are all other phenomena, excluding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
What are the phenomena that give rise to fetters (*saṃyojanotpādaka-dharma*)?
They are the tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
What are the phenomena that are not fetters of birth?
They are the untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
What are the phenomena that are objects of clinging?
They are the four types of clinging.
What are the phenomena that are not objects of clinging?
That is to say, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are phenomena that are felt (*vedita-dharma*)?
They are those phenomena which are comprised within their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
What are non-appropriated phenomena?
They are those phenomena not comprised within intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
What are phenomena that arise through grasping?
That is to say, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas.
What are the dharmas that arise without grasping?
That is to say, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
What are phenomena that are afflictions?
They are those phenomena that arise from the fetters.
What are phenomena that are not afflictions?
That is to say, if a phenomenon is not produced by the fetters (paryavasthāna),
what are defiled phenomena (kliṣṭadharma)?
They are unwholesome phenomena (akuśaladharma) and obscured-unspecified phenomena (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
What are the non-defiled phenomena?
They are wholesome phenomena and non-obscured neutral phenomena.
What are the defiled phenomena?
That is to say, they are tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). What are non-defiled phenomena?
That is to say, they are untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)?
They are all phenomena that are afflictions (*kleśa*).
What are the phenomena that are not envelopments?
That is to say, they are not the dharmas that are afflictions (*kleśa*).
What are the dharmas characterized by entanglement (*paryavasthāna*)?
They are the defiled mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
What are the phenomena that do not abide as envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)?
They are unpolluted mind, mental factors, form, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What are the phenomena produced by envelopments?
That is to say, they are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
What are phenomena not produced by entanglements (*paryavasthāna*)?
That is to say, they are uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What are phenomena with objects?
They are all minds and mental factors.
What are phenomena without objects?
That is to say: form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
What are phenomena associated with vitarka?
Those phenomena which are associated with vitarka.
What are phenomena that are without vitarka?
They are those phenomena that are dissociated from vitarka.
What are phenomena with vicāra?
That is to say, if a phenomenon is associated with insight (*vipaśyanā*),
how could it not be a phenomenon possessing insight?
It means that if a phenomenon is dissociated from insight.
What is the dharma that is pleasant?
It refers to any dharma associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
What is the dharma that is not pleasant?
That is to say, if a dharma is not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), how is that dharma experienced?
It is said: if a dharma is associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*).
What are phenomena that are not objects of enjoyment?
They are those phenomena with which mental volition is not associated.
What are phenomena that possess a basis and possess an object?
That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that are without a basis and without an object?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are the dharmas that have a superior?
They are all conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*), as well as space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are the unsurpassed dharmas?
That is to say, the dharmas that are abandoned by cultivation. What are distant dharmas?
They are past and future dharmas.
What are proximate phenomena?
They are present phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
What are limited phenomena?
That is to say, if a phenomenon has a measurable result and its retribution can be measured, it is called a "measurable" phenomenon.
What is an "immeasurable" phenomenon?
It refers to a phenomenon that has an immeasurable result and whose retribution cannot be measured.
What are the phenomena that are views?
They are the eye-faculty, as well as the five false views, mundane right view, the view of one in training, and the view of one beyond training.
What are the phenomena that are not views?
That is to say, with the exception of the eye-faculty, it refers to other forms;

with the exception of the eight views, it refers to other phenomena subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as the other three aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are bases for views?
They are the phenomena that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What are the phenomena that are not bases for views?
That is, the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*).
What are the dharmas associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta*)?
That is, the eight dharmas associated with views.
What are the factors not associated with views?
They are those factors not associated with the eight views.
What are the factors of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)?

That is to say: the entry of hell-beings, the entry of animals, the entry of hungry ghosts, the entry of people from Uttarakuru, and the entry of beings in the Heaven of Non-conception—if one is born there by means of karma, this is called the dharma of ordinary persons.
What are the dharmas that are not those of ordinary persons?

They are: the four bases of psychic power, the four analytical knowledges, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, the absence of contention (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishless of the wishless (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita*), the signless of the signless (*animittā-animitta*), the cultivation of dhyāna and the knowledge of non-interruption (*anupadhiśeṣajñāna*), and entry into the Śuddhāvāsa heavens by birth through karma. These are called the dharmas that are not those of ordinary persons.
What are the dharmas common to ordinary persons?

They are those associated with the path or associated with meditative concentration which, in that particular realm of existence, can be possessed by both ordinary persons and noble ones, whether through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or through birth; these are called the dharmas common to ordinary persons.
What is the quality not shared with ordinary persons?
It is as described for the qualities not belonging to ordinary persons.
What is the determined quality?
That is to say: the five deeds of immediate retribution, the dharmas of training (śaikṣa), and the dharmas beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What are the non-fixed dharmas? That is to say:
excluding the five deeds of immediate retribution and the two types of dharmas of training, all other remaining contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
What are the phenomena that cause affliction?
They are unwholesome phenomena and obscured-unspecified phenomena.
What are the phenomena that do not cause affliction?
This refers to wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) and non-obscured neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
What are the phenomena that are faculties (*indriya-dharma*)?
They refer to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*) and those phenomena included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are subsumed under the faculties.
What are non-faculty phenomena (*anindriya-dharma*)?
They are the five external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) and those phenomena within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are not included among the faculties.
What are phenomena subsumed under the Noble Truths (*āryasatya-saṃgṛhīta-dharma*)?
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are the phenomena not included within the Noble Truths?
They are space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are phenomena with common characteristics?
They are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that are not common?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*)?
That is to say, all mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*).
What are the non-associated phenomena?
They are form, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind.
What are the resultant phenomena?
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are non-resultant phenomena?
They are space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are phenomena that possess results?
They are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that do not possess results?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are retributive phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*)?
They are the portions of the eleven bases (*āyatana*) obtained through retribution, excluding the sound base (*śabda-āyatana*).
What are the non-retribution dharmas?
They are the sense-base of sound, as well as a portion of the eleven sense-bases that are not obtained through retribution.
What are the retribution dharmas?
That is to say, unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas with outflows.
What are dharmas that do not have retribution?
That is to say, indeterminate dharmas and untainted dharmas.
What is the dharma of dependent origination?
It refers to all dharmas.
What is the dharma that is not dependent origination?
This means that such phenomena are unattainable.
What are phenomena with causes and conditions?
They are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that do not have causes and conditions?
They are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are emerging phenomena?

That is to say: wholesome precepts bound to the desire realm; wholesome right meditative attainments characterized by renunciation, tranquility, and seclusion bound to the form and formless realms; the dharmas of those in training; the dharmas of those beyond training; and analytical cessation.
What are the phenomena that are not "emergent" (*niḥsaraṇa*)?
They are: with the exception of the wholesome precepts bound to the desire realm, all other phenomena bound to the desire realm;

with the exception of the wholesome, right meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that are emergent, essential, and tranquil, which are bound to the form and formless realms, all other phenomena bound to the form and formless realms, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are phenomena that have emergence?
They are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What are phenomena that do not have emergence?
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). What are continuous phenomena?
They are those phenomena that have already arisen or are about to arise in successive segments.

What, then, are they? They are past and present dharmas, as well as future dharmas that are certain to arise when they manifest; these subsequent dharmas that continue in succession with preceding dharmas are called "successive dharmas."
What are non-continuous phenomena?

They refer to all phenomena other than past and present phenomena, as well as future phenomena that are destined to arise in the present; specifically, they are the remaining future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is the phenomenon of continuity?
It refers to those phenomena that have already arisen in discrete segments. What, then, are they?

This refers to past and present phenomena, excluding the five aggregates of an Arhat at the final moment of death; if there are other past or present phenomena such that a preceding phenomenon induces a subsequent continuity, these are called phenomena with continuity.
What are the phenomena that do not constitute a continuity?
They are the five aggregates at the final moment of death of an Arhat in the past or present, as well as future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; these two categories comprise them all.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.

Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas, from the sixth chapter, "The Section on Classification and Compendium," Part Two: What are wholesome dharmas?
They refer to the five aggregates of wholesomeness and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are unwholesome phenomena?
They are the five unwholesome aggregates.
What are indeterminate phenomena?
That is to say: the five aggregates that are indeterminate (avyākṛta), as well as space (ākāśa) and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
What are the dharmas of training (śaikṣadharma)?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one in training.
What are the dharmas of one beyond training?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one beyond training.
What are the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
They are the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are the dharmas to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-dharma*)?

This refers to those dharmas abandoned by the patience of immediate succession (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?

It means that the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), the dharmas associated with them, and the non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them are abandoned.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation?
They are those phenomena that are abandoned through cultivation by one who has entered the path of seeing and attained the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*). How are they abandoned?

This refers to the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, their associated mental factors, the bodily and vocal actions they give rise to, the formations dissociated from mind that they produce, and all non-defiled out-flowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
What are the dharmas that are not to be abandoned?
They are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
What are the dharmas that have as their cause those to be abandoned by vision (darśana-heya)?
This refers to defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) and the retribution (*vipāka*) of those phenomena abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What are the phenomena whose causes are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetuka*)?
They are the phenomena abandoned through cultivation; that is, such phenomena are abandoned [in this manner].
What are the factors that are not subject to abandonment?
They are the untainted conditioned factors (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are the factors that are visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*)?
That is to say, one base (āyatana).
What are the invisible and resistant phenomena?
That is to say, nine bases.
What are the invisible and non-obstructive dharmas?
They are the two bases (āyatana).
What are the resultant dharmas?
That is to say, it refers to a small portion of eleven bases (āyatana) acquired as retribution, excluding the base of sound.
What are non-retribution phenomena?
They are unwholesome phenomena, wholesome contaminated phenomena, and the base of sound.
What are the dharmas that are neither resultant nor non-resultant?
They are those other than the indeterminate resultant dharmas, namely, the remaining indeterminate dharmas and the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
What are the inferior dharmas?
That is to say: unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*) and obscured-neutral phenomena (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-dharma*).
What are intermediate phenomena?
They are wholesome contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) and non-obscured-neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-dharma*).
What are the superior dharmas?
They are the untainted conditioned dharmas and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are the minor dharmas?

It refers to little faith, little desire, and little resolve; the factors associated with these, the factors coexistent with them, and their material forms—namely, that which is slight, subtle, not much, and not extensive. These are called minor phenomena (*parīttadharma*).
What is the great dharma?

It refers to great faith, great aspiration, and great understanding; the dharmas associated with them, the dharmas co-existent with them, and their material forms—namely, those that are manifold, vast, boundless, limitless, and immeasurable, as well as space and analytical cessation. These are called the great dharma.
What are immeasurable phenomena (*apramāṇa-dharma*)?

They are immeasurable faith, immeasurable aspiration, and immeasurable resolve; their associated phenomena, their co-existent phenomena, and their material phenomena—which are manifold, vast, boundless, limitless, and immeasurable—along with space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These are called immeasurable phenomena.
What are phenomena that are agreeable to the mind?
They are those phenomena which are desired by the mind.
What are phenomena that are not agreeable to the mind?
That is to say, if a phenomenon is not desired by the mind.
What is a phenomenon that is neither desired nor undesired by the mind?
It refers to when the mind maintains equanimity toward a phenomenon.
What are phenomena associated with pleasure?
They are those phenomena that are associated with pleasant feeling.
What are phenomena associated with suffering?
That is to say, if a phenomenon is associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*),
how can it be a phenomenon concomitant with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
That is to say, if a phenomenon is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*).
What are the phenomena that arise together?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), because they possess the characteristic of arising.
What are the phenomena that abide together?
This refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of abiding.
What are phenomena that perish simultaneously?
This refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of cessation.
What are phenomena that do not arise simultaneously?
They are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they lack the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
What are phenomena that do not abide simultaneously?
This means that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) do not possess the characteristic of abiding.
Why are they not phenomena that perish simultaneously?
This means that unconditioned phenomena do not possess the characteristic of cessation.
What are the phenomena that arise together with the mind?
They are the portions of the eleven bases (*āyatana*) that arise together with the mind, excluding the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
What are the phenomena that abide together with the mind?
That is to say, those phenomena that follow the mind.
What are the phenomena that perish together with the mind?
They are the portions of the ten bases (*āyatana*) that perish together with the mind, excluding the sound base (*śabdāyatana*) and the mind base (*manāyatana*).
What are the phenomena that do not arise simultaneously with the mind?
They are the sense-base of the mind (manāyatana), and a portion of the eleven sense-bases that do not arise simultaneously with the mind.
What are the phenomena that do not abide simultaneously with the mind?
That is to say, those phenomena that do not follow the mind.
What are the phenomena that do not perish simultaneously with the mind?
They are the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), as well as a portion of the ten spheres that do not perish simultaneously with the mind.
What is the desire realm?

It refers to desire-greed and that which is associated with desire-greed—namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind arising from them.
What is the element of ill will (*vyāpādadhātu*)?

It refers to ill will and that which is associated with ill will—namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom, and the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom.
What is the element of harm?

It refers to harm and that which is associated with harm, namely: feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom; and the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom.
What is the realm of renunciation?

It refers to renunciation itself and that which is associated with renunciation: namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the bodily and vocal actions arising from them; the formations dissociated from mind arising from them; and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is the element of non-ill will?

It refers to non-ill will and that which is associated with non-ill will—namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom, and the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom.
What is the element of non-harming?

It refers to non-harming and that which is associated with non-harming—namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom, and the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom.
What is the desire realm?
It refers to those phenomena that are driven by the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and greed.
What is the form realm?
That is to say, those phenomena which are driven by the underlying tendency of desire for form.
What is the formless realm?
It refers to those phenomena which are driven by the underlying tendency of desire for the formless.
What is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
It refers to the desire realm and the form realm; this is called the form realm.
What is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The four formless [attainments] are called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What is the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)?
It refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is called the realm of cessation.
Furthermore, all material phenomena (rūpadharma) are called the form realm (rūpadhātu).

With the exception of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha), all other non-material phenomena (arūpadharma) are called the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Cessation through calculation and cessation not through calculation are called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
What is sensual existence?
It refers to those karmas bound to the desire realm that, conditioned by feeling, arise and bring about their future retribution.
What is existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*)?
It refers to when karma bound to the realm of form, conditioned by feeling, arises and brings about its future retribution.
What is existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*)?
That is to say, if there is karma bound to the formless realm that arises conditioned by feeling and will bring about its retribution in the future.
What is the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) associated with the desire realm, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*) bound to the desire realm; these are called the outflow of desire.
What are the outflows (āsrava)?

Excluding the ignorance associated with the realms of form and formlessness, the remaining fetters (saṃyojana), bonds (bandhana), proclivities (anuśaya), afflictions (kleśa), and entanglements (paryavasthāna) associated with the realms of form and formlessness are called the outflows.
What is the outflow of ignorance?
It refers to the delusion regarding the three realms, being shrouded in darkness and lacking knowledge.
What is the past world?

That is to say, if formations have already arisen and been originated, have been produced and been reproduced, have evolved and been evolved, have existed, have passed away, have been exhausted and transformed, and are categorized as belonging to the past, having reached the ultimate limit of the past, this is called the past time.
What is the future time?

It refers to those formations that have not yet arisen, have not yet fully arisen; have not yet been born, have not yet fully been born; have not yet occurred, have not yet already occurred; which do not yet exist, are not yet present; which are future, are ultimately future, and are subsumed within the future time—this is called the future time.
What is the present time?

It refers to those formations that have now arisen and are arising, have been produced and are being produced, have turned and are turning, have already come to be, are already abiding in the present, and have not yet reached their end or transformation; being present, having reached the culmination of the present, and being subsumed within the present time—this is called the present time.
What is the matter spoken of as past?
It refers to past formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is the matter spoken of as future?
This refers to future formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is the "matter" (*vastu*) spoken of in relation to the present?
It refers to present formations.
What are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)?

They are as follows: the suffering of suffering pertains to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the suffering of change pertains to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and the suffering of conditioned formations pertains to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Furthermore, painful sensations are suffering through the nature of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); pleasant sensations are suffering through the nature of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations are suffering through the nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, formations that are not desired are suffering through the nature of suffering; formations that are desired are suffering through the nature of change; and formations that are neither desired nor undesired are suffering through the nature of conditioned formations.
What are phenomena with vitarka and vicāra?
They are those associated with vitarka and vicāra.
What are phenomena without vitarka but with vicāra?
That is to say: if a dharma is dissociated from vitarka (applied thought) and associated with vicāra (sustained thought).
What are dharmas without vitarka and without vicāra?
That is to say: if a dharma is dissociated from both vitarka and vicāra.
What is the stage with vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to the desire realm up to the Brahma-world, as well as untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What is the stage without vitarka but with vicāra?
This refers to having already attained the state of Mahābrahmā and untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) during the intermediate stage of meditative cultivation.
What is the stage without vitarka and without vicāra?
It refers to all the Ābhāsvara [heaven], all the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], all the Bṛhatphala [heaven], all the formless realms (*ārūpya*), and untainted dharmas.
What is bodily action?
It refers to bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
What is verbal action?
That is to say, vocal action and non-informative action.
What is mental karma?
It is volitional karma.
What is wholesome karma?
It refers to wholesome bodily and verbal actions, as well as wholesome mental volitions.
What is unwholesome karma?
This refers to unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as unwholesome mental volitional action (*cetanā-karma*).
What is neutral action?
It refers to neutral bodily and vocal actions, as well as neutral mental volitional action.
What is the karma of those in training (śaikṣa)?
It refers to the karma of body and speech of those in training, as well as the karma of volition (cetanā) of those in training.
What is the karma of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
This refers to the bodily and vocal karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as the mental karma of one beyond training.
What is karma that is neither of training nor beyond training?
This refers to the contaminated (sāsrava) bodily and vocal karma, as well as the contaminated mental karma.
What is karma to be abandoned by vision?

It refers to that karma which is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How is it abandoned?
This refers to the volitional karma associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing.
What is karma to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to that karma which is abandoned through cultivation by a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the path].
How is it abandoned?

It refers to the volitional karma associated with the ten proclivities (*daśānuśaya*) that is to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the bodily and vocal karma produced thereby, and non-defiled out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*).
What is non-abandonable karma?
This refers to untainted (anāsrava) bodily and vocal karma, as well as untainted mental karma (*cetanā-karma*).
What is karma to be experienced in the present life?

It refers to karma that is performed and nurtured in this very birth, such that the retribution for that karma is experienced in this very life and not in another birth; this is called karma to be experienced in the present life.
What is karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*)?
It refers to karma that is performed and nourished in this life, yet its retribution is experienced in the second life; this is called karma to be experienced in the next life.
What is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*)?

That is to say, if karma is performed and nourished in this life, yet its retribution is experienced only in the third or fourth life, or even after passing through many lifetimes before it is experienced, this is called "karma to be experienced later."
What is karma that results in pleasant feeling?
It refers to wholesome karma associated with the desire realm, up to and including wholesome karma of the third dhyāna.
What is karma that results in painful feeling?
This refers to unwholesome karma.
What is karma that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
It refers to wholesome karma of the fourth dhyāna stage, up to and including wholesome karma associated with the formless realm. This concludes the three dharmas.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of the body?
It refers to the ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental objects; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of feeling?
This refers to the six groups of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, and likewise feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness: the group of eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
It refers to non-material phenomena not subsumed under feeling, which are included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); this is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.

Furthermore, when the body is predominant, the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) paths that arise therein are called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
When the mind and mental factors are predominant, the wholesome outflowing and non-outflowing paths that arise therein are called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, wisdom that takes the body as its object is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The wisdom that takes as its object feeling, mind, and phenomena is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
What is the right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) for the purpose of abandoning evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen?

It refers to the cultivation of the superior path for the abandonment of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen, which gives rise to wholesome states, both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*); this is called the right effort for the purpose of abandoning evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.

What is the right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) for preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising through skillful means? It refers to the cultivation of the path of supremacy (*adhipatimārga*) to prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, thereby giving rise to wholesome states, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*). This is called the right effort for preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising through skillful means.
What is the right effort to cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise?

It refers to the diligent cultivation of unarisen wholesome dharmas so that they arise as the path of supremacy, producing both contaminated and uncontaminated wholesome states; this is called the right effort to cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise through diligent cultivation.

What is the right effort of realizing through wisdom (*prajñā-sākṣātkriyā-samyakpradhāna*) for the sake of maintaining, not losing, fulfilling, cultivating, increasing, and expanding wholesome states that have already arisen?

It refers to the superior path of generating wholesome states—both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)—by diligently cultivating those wholesome states that have already arisen so as to maintain them, prevent their loss, fulfill their cultivation, increase them, and expand them through the realization of wisdom. This is called the right effort of realizing through wisdom for the sake of maintaining, not losing, fulfilling, cultivating, increasing, and expanding wholesome states that have already arisen.
What is the basis for supernormal power consisting in the concentration of desire and the purification of conduct?

It refers to the wholesome, outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states that arise through the predominance of desire on that path; this is called the basis for supernormal power consisting in the concentration of desire and the purification of conduct.
What is the basis for psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting in the accomplishment of the pure cultivation of concentration through wisdom?

It refers to the wholesome, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states produced by that path, wherein wisdom is predominant; this is called the basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the pure cultivation of concentration through wisdom.
What is the first dhyāna?
It refers to the five aggregates of wholesome states subsumed under the first dhyāna.
What are the second, third, and fourth dhyānas?
That is to say, the wholesome five aggregates (pañca-skandhāḥ) subsumed within the fourth dhyāna.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ).
What is the noble truth of the origin?
It refers to the cause of the outflows (*āsrava*).
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
That is, it is cessation through analytical knowledge.
What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
It refers to the dharmas of training and the dharmas beyond training.
What is loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?

It refers to loving-kindness itself and that which is associated with loving-kindness: namely, the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom; and the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are also like this.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?

It refers to that which is associated with equanimity: namely, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom; and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) arising therefrom.
What is the sphere of infinite space?

It is said that the sphere of infinite space is of two kinds: meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*). These include the mental factors associated with them, namely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
As it is with the sphere of infinite space, so it is with the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness.
What is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?

It is said that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is of two kinds: namely, meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*). Whatever perception, volition, formations, and consciousness are associated with those [two], this is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains by begging?

It refers to the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) states arising from that path, which have as their predominant condition the activity of being content with whatever robes one obtains by begging; this is called the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains by begging.
What is meant by "obtaining food through begging as it is given, as well as bedding and seating, and delighting in solitude and delighting in the cultivation of the noble lineages"?

It refers to the wholesome, with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), that arise on the path through the predominance of obtaining food through begging as it is given, bedding and seating, and delighting in solitude and delighting in the practice; this is called "obtaining food through begging as it is given, as well as bedding and seating, and delighting in solitude and delighting in the cultivation of the noble lineages."
What is the fruit of the śramaṇa that is srotāpanna?
It is said that there are two kinds of the fruit of srotāpanna: conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the conditioned fruit of srotāpanna?

It refers to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*); those dharmas of training (*śaikṣadharma*) that have been attained, are being attained, or will be attained—these are called the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛtaphala*) of stream-entry.
What is the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛtaphala*) of stream-entry?

This refers to the realization of the fruit of *srotāpanna*; whether the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have already been abandoned, are being abandoned now, or will be abandoned in the future, this is called the unconditioned fruit of *srotāpanna*.
As it is with the fruit of the *śrāmaṇya* for a *srotāpanna*, so it is likewise for the fruit of the *śrāmaṇya* for a *sakṛdāgāmin* and the fruit of the *śrāmaṇya* for an *anāgāmin*.
What is the fruit of arhatship for a śramaṇa?
It is said that the fruit of arhatship is of two kinds:
conditioned and unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of an arhat?

It refers to the realization of the fruit of arhatship; whatever dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) have been attained, are being attained, or will be attained—this is called the conditioned fruit of an arhat.
What is the unconditioned fruit of arhatship?

It refers to the realization of the fruit of arhatship; whether those fetters have been abandoned, are being abandoned now, or will be abandoned in the future, this is called the unconditioned fruit of arhatship.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
It is the untainted knowledge that knows the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm; it is explained in detail as in the previous "Chapter on the Five Dharmas.
This applies likewise up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*)?
It refers to the immovable wisdom (*acalajñāna*) being well able to discern that ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?
This refers to the Immovable Wisdom (*acalajñāna*) being well able to discern those bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
What is eloquence (*pratibhāna*)?
It refers to the Immovable Wisdom not giving rise to obstructive conceptions regarding those verbal expressions.
What is analytical exposition according to circumstances?
It refers to the unshakable wisdom that is uninterrupted, undispersed, and characterized by definitive mastery.
What are its causes and conditions?
It refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

It refers to past and present minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), excluding the final mind and mental factors at the moment of death of an Arhat; all other past and present minds and mental factors [constitute it].
What are the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)?
They refer to all phenomena as objects.
What is gross material food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra)?

That which is of the nature of solid food: because of that food, the sense faculties increase, the four great elements increase, and it provides nourishment and protection, becoming sufficient and clear; this is called solid food.
What is the nutriment of contact?

It refers to conditioned by tainted contact, the growth of the sense faculties, the growth of the four great elements, the nourishment of the sense faculties, and their protection and maintenance, as previously described.
What is the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*)?
It refers to the increase of the sense faculties and the increase of the four great elements conditioned by outflow-tainted volition, as explained in detail previously.
What is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*)?
This refers to the nourishment of the sense faculties and the great elements through consciousness conditioned by outflows (*sāsrava*), as explained in detail previously.
What is the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*)?

It refers to all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the desire realm, excluding the five views and ignorance associated with the desire realm; these are called the flood of desire.
What is the flux of existence (*bhava-āsrava*)?

It refers to the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, excluding the five views and ignorance associated with those two realms; this is called the flux of existence.
What is the flood of views?
It refers to the five views; these are called the flood of views.
What is the flood of ignorance?
This refers to the ignorance that is dark regarding the three realms, like a flowing stream;
the yokes (*yoga*) are also like this.
What is the clinging to sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*)?

That is to say, excluding the five views bound to the desire realm, the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the desire realm are called the grasping for sensual pleasure (*kāma-upādāna*).
What is the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*)?

This refers to four views, excluding one view—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the view that grasps at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). These are called the "grasping at views.
What is the "grasping at precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
This refers to one view, excluding the other four views; namely, the attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). What is that?

It refers to when a person wrongly grasps the characteristics of rules and observances, regarding them as purification and as being liberation itself, thereby giving rise to views and convictions; this is called the attachment to rules and observances.
What is the grasping for a self (*ātma-grāha*)?

It refers to all other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, excluding the five views bound to those same realms; this is called the grasping for a self.
What are past phenomena?
They are the five aggregates of the past.
What are future phenomena?
That is to say, the five aggregates of the future.
What are present phenomena?
They are the five aggregates of the present.
What are the phenomena that are neither past, future, nor present?
They are the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
What are the phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktadharma*)?
This refers to the five aggregates (skandhas) bound to the desire realm.
What are the phenomena bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates bound to the form realm.
What are the phenomena associated with the formless realm?
They are the four aggregates associated with the formless realm.
What are the unassociated phenomena?
This refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are the factors that have wholesome causes (*kuśala-hetuka-dharma*)? They are wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the retribution of wholesome phenomena.
What are the phenomena that have unwholesome causes?
They are the defiled phenomena bound to the desire realm and the retribution of unwholesome phenomena.
What are the phenomena that have neutral causes?
This refers to indeterminate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*).
What are phenomena that have neither wholesome causes nor unwholesome causes nor indeterminate causes?
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are phenomena that have an object-condition (*sālambana-dharma*)?
They are the mind and mental factors associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that take an object.
What are phenomena that lack an object-condition (*anālambana-dharma*)?

That is to say, [factors] associated with the five consciousnesses, or those associated with the mental consciousness, take as their object form, the unconditioned, or formations dissociated from mind.
What are the factors that have objects as their conditions and those that do not have objects as their conditions?

That is to say: if they are associated with mental consciousness, they take as objects the mind and mental factors; if they are dissociated from the mind, they take as objects form and the unconditioned.
What are the phenomena that are neither objects of objective conditions nor objects of non-objects-of-objective-conditions?
This concludes the four dharmas: form, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind.
What are the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*)?
They are explained in detail as previously set forth in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Seven Matters."
What is the hell realm (*niraya-gati*)?
It refers to hell-beings who, by virtue of their single nature, single category, and individual selfhood, have attained a location, attained an object, and attained an entrance;
or it refers to the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced by those hell-beings in that place—this is called the hell realm.
The destinies of animals and hungry ghosts are also like this.
What are the destinies of gods and humans?

They refer to those who are gods or humans, possessing a single nature, a single category, and a single individuality; they have attained their respective locations, attained their respective objects, and attained their respective spheres of entry.
If gods or humans, born in this or that realm, possess non-obscured neutral form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, this is called the realm of gods and humans (*devamanuṣyagati*).
What is the group of afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya-kleśa-skandha*)?

This refers to the aggregate of afflictions that are abandoned by the patience regarding the non-interruption of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?
It means the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*darśana-heya*), along with the aggregate of afflictions associated with them.
What is the category of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya-kleśa-nikāya*)?

It refers to that category of afflictions which is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption regarding the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-akṣānti*), etc., for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?
This refers to the group of afflictions associated with the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering.
What is the group of afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation?

It refers to those groups of afflictions that are abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) regarding cessation for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?
It refers to the group of afflictions associated with the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
What is the group of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*)?

This refers to the category of afflictions (*kleśa-skandha*) that are abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth on the path of humans for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How are they abandoned?
It means that the twenty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and their associated categories of afflictions are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
What is the body of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to that body of afflictions which is to be abandoned through cultivation by one who has seen the tracks of training. How is it abandoned?
This refers to the aggregate of afflictions associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation.
What are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*)?
They are all the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which is derived from the four great elements.
What are mental phenomena?
They are the six groups of consciousness, from the group of eye-consciousness up to the group of mind-consciousness.
What are the phenomena associated with the mind?
That is to say, which dharmas are associated with the mind? What are they? They are:

feeling, perception, volition, contact, mindfulness, desire, resolve, attention, concentration, wisdom, faith, diligence, initial mental application (*vitarka*), sustained mental application (*vicāra*), and so forth, up to the afflictions, fetters, and envelopments, as explained at length in the previous "Chapter on the Five Dharmas."
What are the formations dissociated from mind?
They are those phenomena that are dissociated from the mind. What, then, are they?

This refers to all acquisitions (*prāpti*) up to the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), as explained in detail in the previous "Chapter on the Five Dharmas" (*Pañcadharmavarga*).
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?

They are the three unconditioned phenomena: space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This concludes the five dharmas.
What is the earth element?
It is characterized by solidity.
What is the water element?
That is to say, the characteristic of moisture.
What is the fire element?
That is to say, the characteristic of heat.
What is the wind element?
It is characterized by lightness and motion.
What is the space element?
This refers to form that is limited by space.
What is the element of consciousness?
It refers to the five groups of consciousness and the contaminated mental consciousness.
What are the phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering?

They are those abandoned by the patience of non-interruption regarding suffering and so forth, belonging to those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma; they are explained in detail as previously set forth in the "Analysis of the Bases" (*Vibhaṅga-āyatana-varga*).
The same applies to origination, cessation, the path, and cultivation.
What are the dharmas that are not to be abandoned? They are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas. This concludes the six categories of dharmas.
What is the latent tendency of sensual desire?
It is as explained for sensual desire.
What is the latent tendency of ill will?
This refers to causing affliction and harm to sentient beings.
What is the latent tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*)?
It refers to craving for the realms of form and formlessness.
What is the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*)?
It refers to the experience of the mind’s fluctuation between loftiness and lowness.
What is the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*)?
This refers to the ignorance that is dark and deluded regarding the three realms.
What is the proclivity of views?
It refers to the five false views.
What is the latent tendency of doubt?
It refers to the lack of clear understanding regarding the Truths.
What is the first station of consciousness?
This refers to sentient beings with form who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, namely humans and certain devas; this is called the first station of consciousness.
What is the first sequential enumeration?

That is to say, the first station of consciousness consists of the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are associated with or dissociated from that [consciousness]; this is called the first station of consciousness.

There are sentient beings who possess form, having diverse bodies but a single perception—namely, those who were the first to arise as Brahmā-deities; this is called the second station of consciousness.
What is the second sequential enumeration?

It refers to the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Whatever is associated or dissociated with it—whether form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*)—this is called the second station of consciousness.

There are beings with form who have a single type of body but diverse perceptions; these are the Ābhāsvara devas. This is called the third station of consciousness, and so on, up to "this is called the third station of consciousness," as explained in detail above.

There are beings with form who possess a single type of body and a single type of perception; namely, the Śubhakṛtsna devas. This is called the fourth station of consciousness, and so forth, up to "this is called the fourth station of consciousness," as explained in detail above.

As for formless beings, having transcended all perceptions of form, having transcended perceptions of sensory obstruction, having reached the culmination of perceptions of obstruction, and being free from perceptions of diversity, they contemplate the sphere of infinite space and dwell in the base of infinite space; these are called the gods of the sphere of infinite space, and this is known as the fifth station of consciousness.
What is the fifth sequential enumeration?

It refers to the fifth station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) associated with that [consciousness]; if there are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, these are called the fifth station of consciousness.

As for the beings of the formless realm, having already transcended the sphere of infinite space, they abide in the immeasurable consciousness and enter the sphere of immeasurable consciousness; that is, the gods of the sphere of consciousness. This is called the sixth station of consciousness. ... [repeated] ... up to: this is called the sixth station of consciousness, as explained in detail above.

As for formless beings who have already transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell in the sphere of nothingness—the gods of the sphere of nothingness—this is called the seventh station of consciousness. This is called the seventh station of consciousness; the detailed exposition is as above.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness?

It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; associated with untainted mental attention, it consists of mindfulness, constant mindfulness, mindfulness without forgetfulness, non-dispersed mindfulness, and perpetual non-forgetfulness. This is called the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, contemplates its origin as its origin, contemplates its cessation as its cessation, and contemplates the path as the path; being associated with untainted mental attention, they investigate, select, and discern the characteristics of phenomena, determining their specific and general characteristics. This wisdom that is awakened, intelligent, and characterized by the practice of observation is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena.
What is the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the noble disciple who, regarding suffering, contemplates suffering, and so on up to regarding the path, contemplates the path; being associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), he applies the skillful means of desire and energy for deliverance, maintaining a courageous and resolute mind, acting with swiftness and without interruption—this is called the awakening factor of energy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the noble disciple who, up to and including being associated with untainted mental attention, experiences a state of mental gladness and exultation, superior joy, a mind of resolute happiness, and that which is capable of joy and finds joy; this is called the factor of enlightenment of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the noble disciple, up to being associated with untainted mental attention, whether it be physical tranquility, mental tranquility, or the state of being tranquilized by bliss; this is called the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
What is the factor of enlightenment of concentration?

It refers to the noble disciple’s state of mind associated with untainted mental attention, wherein the mind abides, abides evenly, abides joyfully, and abides firmly; it is undistracted, unconfused, and focused in one-pointedness. This is called the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
What is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; being associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), if the mind is even, evenly sustained, and abides without grasping, this is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. Thus ends the seven factors.
What is the first sphere of liberation?
It refers to having the perception of internal forms while externally perceiving forms; this is called the first sphere of liberation.
What is the first successive attainment in the sequence of enumeration?

That is to say, the first sphere of liberation: when one enters meditative absorption, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness therein are called the first sphere of liberation.
Having no perception of internal form, one perceives external forms; this is called the second sphere of liberation.
What is the second successive attainment in the sequence of enumeration?
It refers to the second sphere of liberation.
If one enters meditative attainment, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called the second sphere of liberation.

To dwell having personally realized the liberation through the perception of purity is called the third base of liberation; this continues up to the third successive attainment (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), as explained in detail above.

Transcending all perceptions of form, transcending perceptions of resistance, and having completely transcended perceptions of diversity, one attends to the sphere of infinite space and enters the sphere of infinite space; this is called the fourth liberation.
What is the fourth successive attainment in the sequence?

It refers to the fourth sphere of liberation; whether it is the entry into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or the wholesome perception, volition, formations, and consciousness, this is called the fourth sphere of liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the fifth stage of liberation (*vimokṣa*).
The successive attainments up to the fifth are explained in detail as above.

The sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, up to the seventh meditative attainment, are explained in detail as above; this is called the seventh stage of liberation.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells having realized the cessation of perception and feeling through bodily witness; this is called the eighth liberation.
What is the eighth successive attainment in the sequence of the serial order?

This refers to the eighth stage of liberation: whether entering meditative absorption or attaining liberation, if the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), the perception of subtle causes (*sūkṣmahetusaṃjñā*), and the perception of subtle sequential succession (*sūkṣmānupūrvyasaṃjñā*) are no longer continuous, unaccomplished, and have ceased, this is called the eighth stage of liberation.
What is the first sphere of mastery?

It refers to having the perception of internal forms, while externally perceiving limited forms, whether beautiful or ugly; one generates the contemplative perception that "those [forms] are mastered," and this is called the entry into the first sphere of mastery.
What is the sequential continuity and numerical order of the successive attainments (*samāpatti*) of the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)?

Regarding the first sphere of mastery: if one enters into attainment, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness [that arise] are called the entry into the first sphere of mastery.

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives externally many forms, whether beautiful or ugly; by generating the contemplative perception regarding these spheres of mastery, this is called the entry into the second sphere of mastery.
This continues up to the second meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), as explained in detail above.
This continues up to the seventh sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) meditative attainment, as explained in detail above.
This is called the entry into the seventh sphere of mastery.

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as white—white in color, with the appearance of white, and emitting white light—just like the color of an *utpala* flower, or like the whiteness of a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī, which is white in color, with the appearance of white, and emits white light.

In this way, a bhikṣu, having no perception of internal forms, perceives external forms as white—white in color, with a white appearance, and emitting white light; thus, he generates the contemplative perception of that sphere of mastery. This is called the entry into the eighth sphere of mastery.
What is the eighth successive attainment in the sequence of enumeration?

It refers to the eighth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); when one enters meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are called the entry into the eighth base of mastery.
What is right view?

It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; who, associated with untainted mental attention, exercises discernment, selection, and the examination of characteristics regarding phenomena; who possesses wisdom, awakening, and intelligence, and engages in the investigation of wisdom—this is called right view.
What is right intention?

It refers to the noble disciple who, up to and including the contemplation of the Path as the Path, possesses a mind associated with untainted mental attention; whether it be the awakening of the mind, the successive awakening, the awakening to form, the further awakening to form, the frequent awakening, the awakening of intention, or equal intention—this is called right intention.

What is right speech? It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; associated with untainted mental attention, they eliminate the four verbal transgressions of wrong livelihood and other evil verbal actions. Through the untainted cessation through cultivation, they do not perform and do not commit them. They maintain restraint and protection, guarding themselves; they do not engage in evil conduct nor commit offenses. Abiding in a firm embankment, abiding in firm non-transgression—this is called right speech.
What is right action?

It refers to the noble disciple who, up to the point of contemplating the path regarding the path, possesses a mind associated with untainted mental attention. With the exception of wrong livelihood and the three types of bodily misconduct, all other unwholesome bodily actions are extinguished through the influx-free state (*anāsrava*). He does not perform them, does not engage in them, and remains steadfastly non-transgressing. As previously explained for right speech, this is called right action.
What is right livelihood?

It refers to the noble disciple who, up to the point of contemplating the path regarding the path, possesses a mind associated with untainted mental attention. As previously explained, having abandoned the bodily and verbal evils of wrong livelihood, they attain the cessation through the untainted [path], neither performing nor committing them; as described in detail above, this is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?

It refers to the noble disciple who, up to the point of contemplating the path as the path, possesses a mind associated with untainted mental attention. As explained in detail regarding the factor of enlightenment of energy, this is called right effort.
Right Livelihood is explained at length as in the case of the awakening factor of mindfulness; this is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?

It refers to the noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path, associated with untainted mental attention; the full explanation is as in the awakening factor of right concentration. Thus ends the eight factors.
What is the fetter of sensual desire?
It refers to craving for the three realms.
What is the fetter of ill will?
This refers to the affliction and harming of sentient beings.
What is the fetter of pride?
It refers to the seven types of pride.
What is the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to the delusion regarding the three realms, being obscured by darkness and lacking knowledge.
What is the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
That is to say, the three views:
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
What is the fetter of clinging to others (parāmarśa-saṃyojana)?
It refers to two views:
the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
What is the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*)?
This refers to the failure to clearly understand the Truths (satya).
What is the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana)?
It refers to the intensification and expansion of a jealous mind.
What is the fetter of stinginess?
It refers to the mind’s grasping and firm attachment.
What is the first abode of sentient beings?

This refers to sentient beings possessing form, with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, namely devas and humans; this is called the first abode of sentient beings, and it is called the first in the sequential enumeration.
What are called the abodes of sentient beings?
It refers to those places where sentient beings dwell, where they take birth and enter; these are called the abodes of sentient beings.
What are the second, third, and fourth abodes of sentient beings?
This is as explained at length regarding the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
What is the fifth abode of sentient beings?
It refers to sentient beings who possess form but are without ideation (*asaṃjñin*), namely the Heaven of No-Ideation (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); this is called the fifth abode of sentient beings.
The fifth sequential enumeration is as explained extensively above.

What is the sixth abode of sentient beings? It refers to formless sentient beings who, having transcended all perceptions of form, have transcended perceptions of resistance, and have reached the culmination of perceptions of resistance; this continues up to the eighth abode of sentient beings, which is explained at length in the same manner as the latter three stations of consciousness.
What is the ninth abode of sentient beings?

It refers to formless sentient beings who, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, enter and abide in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—namely, the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. This is called the ninth abode of sentient beings.
The sequence, continuity, and enumeration are as explained extensively above.
This concludes the nine abodes of sentient beings and the nine dharmas.
What is the first universal base (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?

This refers to the earth-kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa), wherein a single sign arises, extending upward, downward, and in all directions, without duality and immeasurable; this is called the first base of totalization (kasiṇāyatana).
What is the first successive attainment (anupubbābhisamaya) through the sequence of counting?

This refers to the first universal base (*kasiṇa*): when one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called the earth universal base.
As it is with the earth universal base, so it is with the water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white universal bases.

The sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness arise as a single characteristic, being non-dual and immeasurable above, below, and in all directions; these are called the ten spheres of totality.
What is the sequential continuity and numerical order of the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) as they are correctly attained?
It refers to the ten universal bases: when one enters correct attainment, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are called the ten universal bases.
The unlearned right view up to the unlearned right concentration are as explained in the section on the factors of the path.
What is unlearned right liberation?

It refers to the noble disciple who, up to the point of contemplating the path, possesses the unlearned mental application associated with contemplation of the path; it is that mind which has been liberated or is being liberated.
What is the liberation of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) characterized by correct knowledge and vision?
It refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna); this concludes the ten factors.
What is contaminated form (sāsrava-rūpa)?

This refers to form that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and arises from grasping (*upādāna*). That is to say, regarding this form—whether past, future, or present—one gives rise to desire, or gives rise to it now, or will give rise to it; likewise for anger or delusion, various mental factors (*caitasika*) give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), giving rise to them now or will give rise to them. This is called form with outflows.
This applies likewise even to contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*).
What is uncontaminated form (*anāsrava-rūpa*)?

It refers to form that is uncontaminated and not produced from grasping (*upādāna*). That is to say, whether this form is past, future, or present, if desire should arise but does not, or if anger, delusion, or other mental afflictions (*caitasika-kleśa*) should arise but do not, this is called uncontaminated form.
In this way, it extends even to untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), which is likewise.
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
They are the three unconditioned [phenomena]:
The eleven factors—space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation—are concluded.
What are the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*)?
They are as extensively explained in the previous "Chapter on the Seven Matters," concluding the twelve factors and eighteen factors.
What is the eye-faculty?
It is as described for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
Likewise, this continues up to the body-faculty, which is as described for the body-base (*kāyāyatana*).
What is the female faculty?
It refers to a specific portion of the body faculty.
The male faculty is likewise.
What is the life-faculty?
It refers to the life-force within the three realms.
What is the mind-faculty?
That which is called mind, thought, and consciousness— what, then, is that?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness, namely, visual consciousness up to mental consciousness.
