The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity are explained in detail as previously set forth in the "Chapter on the Seven Matters.
What is the faculty of faith?

That is to say, based on the wholesome dharmas that give rise to faith through renunciation and tranquility, there is superior faith and right reflection; this purification of the mind through various practices, various activities, and various reflections is called the faculty of faith.
What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?

It refers to the emergence of wholesome dharmas that are essential for liberation and characterized by tranquility; if one applies the means of diligence with desire, courageously collects the mind, and remains constantly unremitting, this is called the faculty of diligence.
What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
It refers to the mindfulness and constant recollection that arise from the wholesome dharmas of renunciation and tranquility; this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?

That is to say, when the mind arises from the essential departure [from suffering] and tranquility within wholesome dharmas, and is free from distraction, abiding well and established in equanimity, this is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?

That which arises from the renunciation, tranquility, and wholesome dharmas—namely, the discernment of phenomena, illumination, investigation, decisiveness, and thorough understanding—is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?

Regarding those who have transcended and emerged from the state of ordinary beings: if they possess the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) while still in training—meaning that while their faculties follow through faith or follow through Dharma, they have not yet attained the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths, but are on the verge of attaining it—this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyajñendriya*).
What is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)?

It refers to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) of those who have attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths and are still in training (*śaikṣa*). That is to say, for those who are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or those who are bodily witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*), having already attained clear realization, there arises immediately thereafter that which is predominant regarding the Four Noble Truths; this is called the faculty of one who has already known.
What is the faculty of one who has nothing further to know (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?

It refers to an Arhat who has exhausted all outflows and fetters; it is the faculty of wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), meaning that through this faculty he attains liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*) or double liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*), abides in happiness in the present life, and gives rise to the superior state of immediate succession. This is called the faculty of one who has nothing further to know. The twenty-two factors are now complete.
What are the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)?

They are as follows: thirty-six latent tendencies bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), thirty-one latent tendencies bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and thirty-one latent tendencies bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This concludes the ninety-eight factors.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.

Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.

Chapter Six, Part Three: The Classification of Categories. The objects of cognition (*jñeya-dharma*), consciousness (*vijñāna-dharma*), the objects of cognition as a whole (*sarva-jñeya-dharma*), the conditions (*pratyaya-dharma*), and the predominant factors (*adhipati-dharma*).

The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) are subsumed [within these categories]; they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) act as their drivers.

Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are subsumed within eleven elements, eleven bases, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. They are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragānuśaya*) pertaining to the two realms of desire and form, as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are governed by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal.

Visible phenomena (*sanidarśanadharma*) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*)—and cognized by two consciousnesses. They are governed by all pervasive latent dispositions of the desire and form realms, as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The invisible phenomena (*anidarśana-dharma*) are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The resistant phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements, ten bases, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses. They are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as by the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*).

Non-obstructive (*apratigha*) dharmas are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)—cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent tendencies.

Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are not the objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by six consciousnesses, and are all driven by the underlying tendencies.

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The phenomena associated with contention (*saraṇa-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). All underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as their drivers.

The phenomena free from contention (*araṇa-dharma*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not underlie them.

As with the phenomena involving contention, so it is with the phenomena free from contention; likewise for mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena, phenomena that enter [the path] and those that do not, defiled phenomena and undefiled phenomena, phenomena based on the household life and phenomena based on the essential departure [from it].

Mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Non-mental phenomena (*acittadharma*) are subsumed under eleven elements, eleven bases, and four aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies.

Mental phenomena (citta-dharma) are comprised within one element, one base, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

Non-mental phenomena (a-citta-dharma) are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and three aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies.

As it is with mental factors (citta-dharma), so it is with non-mental factors (a-citta-dharma); the same applies to factors associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta) and factors dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta).

Factors co-existent with the mind (citta-sahabhū) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie them.

Dharmas not co-existent with the mind are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and three aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that follow the movement of the mind are comprised within one element, one base, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and cognized by one consciousness, and are driven by all latent dispositions.

Dharmas that do not follow the mind (*acittānuvartin*) are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the three aggregates (*skandhas*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñānas*), cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), and driven by all latent proclivities (*anuśayas*).

Dharmas that are causes of the mind (*cittahetuka*) are comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—cognized by the six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent proclivities.

Dharmas that are not causes of mind are subsumed under thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges and cognized by six consciousnesses; they are driven by all pervasive latent proclivities of the three realms as well as by those latent proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation.

Mental sequential phenomena (*cittānuparivartin*) are comprised of eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Non-mental sequential phenomena are comprised of eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies.

Conditioned mental phenomena (*cittasamprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have conditioned objects as their conditions.

Non-conditioned mental phenomena (*cittaviprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all proclivities.

Dharmas predominant over the mind (*cittādhipati*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas not predominant over the mind are comprised of one element, one base, and are not subsumed within any aggregate. They are known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not driven by any underlying tendencies.

Dharmas that are the fruits of mind are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) act as their drivers.

Dharmas that are not the fruits of mind are comprised within one element, one base, and are not comprised within any aggregate; they are known by one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and cognized by one consciousness; latent proclivities do not act as their drivers.

The mental resultant phenomena (*cittavipākadharmas*) are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātus*), eleven bases (*āyatanas*), and five aggregates (*skandhas*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñānas*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by the five consciousnesses (*vijñānas*). They are driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the three realms, as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

Non-mental resultant factors (*cittavipāka-dharma*) are subsumed under eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) act upon them.

Resultant factors of karma (*karmadharma*) are subsumed under three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and cognized by three consciousnesses—namely, eye, ear, and mind consciousness; all latent dispositions act upon them.

Non-karmic factors (*akarmadharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Factors associated with karma (*karmasaṃprayuktadharma*) are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—cognized by one consciousness, and driven by all latent tendencies.

Dharmas not associated with karma are comprised within eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

Dharmas coexistent with karma are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions underlie them.

Dharmas not co-existent with karma are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and are driven by all latent proclivities (anuśayas).

Dharmas that follow along with karma are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and cognized by one consciousness, and are driven by all latent proclivities.

Dharmas that do not follow along with karma (*akarmānuvartin*) are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that have karma as their cause (*karmahetuka*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all underlying tendencies.

Dharmas that are not caused by karma are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas); they are influenced by all pervasive latent proclivities (anuśayas) of the three realms as well as those latent proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation.

The dharma of karma-succession (karma-anupūrva) is subsumed under eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha); it is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) underlie it.

The dharma of non-karma-succession is subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; it is known by ten knowledges and cognized by six consciousnesses; all latent dispositions underlie it.

Conditioned by karma (*karmapratyaya*), phenomena are subsumed under five elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have conditioned things as their object.

Non-conditioned by karma phenomena are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all proclivities.

The phenomena predominant by karma (*karmādhipateya-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

The non-karma-dominant dharma is not subsumed within one element, one base, or the aggregates; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not influenced by the underlying tendencies.

Dharmas that are karmic results (*karmaphala*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that are not karmic results are subsumed within one element, one base, and are not included in any aggregate; they are known by one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), cognized by one consciousness, and are not driven by latent tendencies.

The dharma of karmic retribution is comprised of seventeen elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by the five consciousnesses; and it is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (anuśayas) of the three realms as well as those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation.

That which is not a dharma of karmic retribution is comprised within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas); it is known by ten knowledges (jñānas) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas); it is driven by all latent tendencies (anuśayas).

That which is a dharma of existence is comprised within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and cognized by six consciousnesses; it is driven by all latent tendencies.

Non-existent dharmas (*abhāvadharma*) are subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are not the objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Associated dharmas (*saṃprayuktadharma*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*); they are cognized by one consciousness, and are all driven by the underlying tendencies.

Non-associated dharmas are comprised within thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges and cognized by six consciousnesses; they have outflowing objects and are driven by the underlying tendencies.

There are phenomena that are shared (*sādhāraṇa*), which are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*) excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The non-existent and the common-to-all dharmas are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are not influenced by the underlying tendencies.

The dharmas that are concomitant and possess causes are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (anuśayas).

That which is neither concomitant nor a causal dharma is subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; it is cognized by one consciousness, and it is not that which is activated by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

There is a category of dharmas that are sequential: they are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*);

it is driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Existence (*bhāva*) is subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—and cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by the underlying tendencies that take existence as their object.

Non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed under thirteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Phenomena with predominance (*adhipati-dharma*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)—cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent tendencies.

There is no dharma that possesses predominance which is not subsumed within one element, one base, or one aggregate; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is not influenced by the underlying tendencies.

Dharmas that possess fruit are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all latent proclivities.

The dharma that is not a fruit is comprised within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is not driven by the underlying tendencies.

The dharmas that are retribution (vipāka-dharma) are comprised within seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight cognitions (jñāna), excluding the cognition of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the cognition of the path (mārga-jñāna); they are cognized by the five consciousnesses (vijñāna). They are driven by all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the three realms, as well as by the proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya).

Dharmas that are not subject to retribution (avipāka-dharma) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and driven by all latent tendencies (anuśayas).

Dharmas that are objects of knowledge (jñeya-dharma) are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent tendencies.

Those dharmas not known by wisdom (*jñāna*) are not subsumed within the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), or aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by wisdom, not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Those dharmas to be abandoned through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all underlying tendencies.

Dharmas not to be abandoned by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*); they are cognized by one consciousness, and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not underlie them.

The practice of cultivation (bhāvanā) is subsumed under the ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); it is cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). It is influenced by all pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the three realms, as well as by the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya).

The non-cultivated dharma (*abhāvanādharma*) is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie it.

Dharmas realized through wisdom (*prajñā-sākṣātkṛta*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas not realized through wisdom are not subsumed within the elements, bases, or aggregates; they are not known by wisdom, not cognized by consciousness, and not driven by the underlying tendencies.

The attainment of the realization of the Dharma is subsumed within the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six sense-fields (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three realms, as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Non-acquisition (aprāpti) is comprised within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) underlie it.

The conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms.

Non-practiced phenomena (*aśaikṣadharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

Dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas without outflows (*anāsrava*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the three realms as well as those underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As it is with dharmas that are blameworthy, so it is with dharmas that are blameless; with black dharmas and white dharmas; with dharmas subject to decline and dharmas not subject to decline; and likewise with dharmas that are obscured and dharmas that are unobscured.

The dharma of "recording" (dharmānusmaraṇa) is subsumed within ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by ten knowledges (jñāna) and cognized by three consciousnesses (vijñāna). It is driven by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm, by all pervasive latent dispositions of the form and formless realms, and by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They include all [dharmas] of the form and formless realms, as well as the two types of view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm; they are driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragasaṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*).

Dharmas that have already arisen are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all the underlying tendencies (anuśayas).

The unarisen phenomena (*anutpanna-dharma*) are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

As with the arisen phenomena, so it is for the unarisen phenomena, the presently arising phenomena, the not presently arising phenomena, the already ceased phenomena, the not already ceased phenomena, the presently ceasing phenomena, and the not presently ceasing phenomena.

The law of dependent origination is subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by the six consciousnesses; and it is driven by all underlying tendencies.

That which is not a dependent origination dharma is not subsumed under any single element (dhātu), single base (āyatana), or aggregate (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not that which is driven by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

As it is with the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), so it is with the dharma that is not dependently originated; with the dharma produced by conditions (*pratyayaja*) and the dharma not produced by conditions; with the causal dharma (*hetudharma*) and the non-causal dharma; with the dharma possessing a cause (*sahetuka*) and the dharma lacking a cause; and likewise with the dharma arisen from causes (*hetusamutthita*) and the dharma not arisen from causes.

Factors associated with causes (*hetu-saṃprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Factors not associated with causes (*ahetu-saṃprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under eleven elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*); they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by those underlying tendencies that have out-flowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya*).

The dharma of fetters (saṃyojana) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). With the exception of the unique ignorance (avidyā) that takes the untainted (anāsrava) as its object, it is driven by all remaining proclivities (anuśaya).

Non-fettering phenomena (*asaṃyojana-dharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Fettering phenomena (*saṃyojana-dharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses, and are driven by all underlying tendencies.

The non-arising fetters (*asaṃyojana*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are not activated by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The phenomena that are objects of grasping (*upādāna*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one sense-base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

The phenomena that are not objects of grasping (*anupādāna*) are subsumed under three elements, two sense-bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are not underlain by the underlying tendencies.

The dharma of feeling (vedanā-dharma) is subsumed under nine elements (dhātu), nine bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledges of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the path (mārgajñāna)—and is cognized by the five consciousnesses (vijñāna). It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya) within both the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).

Non-appropriated phenomena (*anupādāna-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Appropriated phenomena (*upādāna-janaka-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and cognized by six consciousnesses, and are driven by all latent tendencies.

The phenomena that are not subject to grasping are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; they are cognized by one consciousness, and the latent dispositions do not underlie them.

Defiled phenomena (*kleśa-dharma*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*);

they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them. Non-defiled phenomena are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and all underlying tendencies underlie them.

Defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Non-defiled phenomena (*akliṣṭa-dharma*) are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies.

There are defiled phenomena (sāsrava-dharma), which are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie them.

The non-defiled dharmas are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledges of suffering and its origin; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are not the objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The phenomena that are *paryavasthāna* (envelopments) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) act upon them.

The phenomena that are not *paryavasthāna* are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions act upon them.

Dharmas that are *paryavasthāna* (active defilements) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that are not *paryavasthāna* are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by those underlying tendencies that have out-flowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*).
Dharmas arising from the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) are explained at length as being like the *sāsrava* (tainted) dharmas.
Dharmas not arising from the *paryavasthānas* are explained at length as being like the *anāsrava* (untainted) dharmas.

Dharmas with objects (*sālambana*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that are without object (anālambana) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna); they are cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and they are driven by the proclivities (anuśaya) that have out-flowing (sāsrava) objects.

Dharmas with vitarka are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all latent proclivities of the desire and form realms.

Dharmas that are not accompanied by vitarka are comprised within thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

As it is with dharmas that are not accompanied by vitarka, so it is for those that are accompanied by vitarka, as well as for those that are accompanied by vicāra and those that are not accompanied by vicāra.

The dharma of "pleasurable" (sukha) is subsumed under two bases (āyatana), three aggregates (skandha), and two realms (dhātu). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). It is driven by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm (rūpa-dhātu). Regarding the desire realm (kāma-dhātu), with the exception of the ignorance (avidyā) associated with doubt that takes the untainted (anāsrava) as its object, it is driven by all other latent dispositions of the desire realm.

Dharmas that are not to be delighted in (*anabhinandaniya*) are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that are to be enjoyed (*paribhogika*) are comprised within eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)—cognized by one consciousness, and driven by all latent tendencies.

Dharmas that are not objects of enjoyment are comprised within eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and are governed by all underlying tendencies (anuśayas).

Dharmas that have an objective basis and an object are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and cognized by six consciousnesses, and are governed by all underlying tendencies.

The phenomena that are without object and without condition are not subsumed under any single element (*dhātu*), any single sense-base (*āyatana*), or any aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The dharmas with superior (sottara) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all proclivities (anuśaya) exert their influence over them.

The unsurpassed dharma is not subsumed under any single element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Distant phenomena (*dūradharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

Near phenomena (*antika-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by the six consciousnesses, and all underlying tendencies underlie them.
As with distant phenomena (*dūradharma*), so it is with near phenomena (*āsannadharma*), finite phenomena (*parimāṇadharma*), and infinite phenomena (*aparimāṇadharma*).

Visible phenomena (*dṛśyadharma*) are subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take out-flowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) as their condition, as well as by the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the views that take non-out-flowing objects (*anāsravālambana*) as their condition.

Non-objects of vision (*adṛṣṭa-dharma*) are comprised within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Objects of vision (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna-dharma*) are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all underlying tendencies.

The phenomena that are not objects of vision (*adṛṣṭa-sthāna-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not underlie them.

Dharmas associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects as their condition, as well as by the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with those [knowledges] that take uncontaminated objects as their condition.

Dharmas not associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); they are governed by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) except for those that take the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object and those associated with views.

The dharmas of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are governed by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms.

It is not a dharma of ordinary beings; it is comprised within eleven elements, ten bases, and five aggregates; it is known by ten knowledges and cognized by four consciousnesses; and it is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation.

The dharmas common to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. They are driven by all the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms.

It is not a dharma shared with ordinary beings; it is comprised of eleven elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by four consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and it is influenced by all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation.

The determined dharma (*niyata-dharma*) is subsumed under five elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The non-fixed dharma is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas); it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), and is cognized by the six consciousnesses; all latent proclivities (anuśayas) function with respect to it.

Dharmas that cause affliction (*saṃkleśika*) are comprised within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that do not cause affliction (*asaṃkleśika*) are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Root-dharmas (*indriya-dharma*) are subsumed under thirteen elements (*dhātu*), seven bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all proclivities (*anuśaya*) exercise their influence over them.

Non-root-dharmas (*anindriya-dharma*) are subsumed under six elements, six bases, and three aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and all proclivities exercise their influence over them.

Dharmas subsumed under the Noble Truths are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges, cognized by six consciousnesses, and driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas not subsumed under the Noble Truths are subsumed within one element and one base, are not subsumed within any aggregate, are known by one knowledge—namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)—are cognized by one consciousness, and are not driven by any latent dispositions.

The common phenomena (*sādhāraṇadharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and they are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The non-common dharmas are not subsumed under any single element (dhātu), sense-base (āyatana), or aggregate (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are not activated by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

Associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Non-associated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*) are subsumed under eleven elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*); they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by those underlying tendencies that take the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object.

Fruitional phenomena (*phala-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) exercise their influence over them.

Non-fruitional phenomena are comprised of one element, one base, and are not subsumed within any aggregate; they are known by one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and cognized by one consciousness; latent dispositions do not exercise their influence over them.

Dharmas that possess fruit are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all latent tendencies (anuśayas).

Dharmas that do not possess a fruit are not subsumed under any single *dhātu*, *āyatana*, or *skandha*. They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by a single consciousness. They are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The dharma of retribution (vipāka-dharma) is comprised of seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by the five consciousnesses (vijñāna). It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the three realms, as well as by the latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya).

Non-resultant phenomena (*avipāka-dharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Resultant phenomena (*savipāka-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements, four bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—cognized by three consciousnesses, and driven by all underlying tendencies of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), as well as the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*).

The dharmas that are not subject to retribution (avipāka-dharma) are comprised within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by ten knowledges (jñāna) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna). They include all [dharmas] of the form and formless realms, as well as all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) and those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya) among the two types of self-view (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) in the desire realm. These are the proclivities that drive and bind.
Conditioned phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) are explained in detail as they are known by wisdom (*jñeya-dharma*).
Unconditioned phenomena (*apratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) are explained in detail as they are not known by wisdom (*ajñeya-dharma*).
Phenomena that have causes and conditions (*sahetupratyaya-dharma*) are explained in detail as phenomena that possess results (*saphala-dharma*).
Non-existent causal factors (*ahetupratyaya-dharma*) are explained in detail as non-existent resultant factors (*aphala-dharma*).

Factors that emerge (*niryāṇa-dharma*) are subsumed under five elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); they are driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as by latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*).

The non-emergent dharma is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by the six consciousnesses; and it is driven by all latent tendencies (anuśayas).

There are phenomena that emerge, which are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie them.

There is no dharma that emerges [from this], which is not subsumed within any realm (*dhātu*), any sense-base (*āyatana*), or any aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds, as well as the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The dharma of continuity (saṃtati) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all latent tendencies (anuśaya) underlie it.

Non-continuous phenomena (*asaṃtati-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by ten cognitions (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

As with continuous phenomena, so it is for non-continuous phenomena, for phenomena that possess continuity, and for phenomena that do not possess continuity; thus ends the pair of these two categories of phenomena.

Wholesome dharmas are subsumed within ten elements, four bases, and five aggregates; they are known by ten knowledges and cognized by three consciousnesses; they are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation.

Unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*). They are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They include all [factors] of the form and formless realms, as well as all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*)—specifically those associated with the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—and those latent tendencies abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The dharmas of training (śaikṣa-dharma) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are not the objects of the proclivities (anuśaya).
The dharmas of no-more-training (aśaikṣa-dharma) are likewise.

Dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses; all proclivities (anuśaya) exercise their influence over them.

The factors abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). All latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by seeing are activated by them.

The dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. They are driven by all the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as by all the pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

Dharmas that are not subject to abandonment (*aprahātavya*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are not driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas whose causes are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-hetuka*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases, and five aggregates. They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by six consciousnesses, and are driven by all underlying tendencies.

The factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as by all pervasive latent proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

The dharmas that are not causes for cessation are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not governed by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The visible and resistant phenomena (*sanidarśana-sapratigha-dharma*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*). They are cognized by two consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The invisible and impinging dharmas are subsumed under nine elements (dhātu), nine bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and are cognized by the five consciousnesses. They are driven by all-pervasive proclivities (anuśaya) pertaining to both the desire and form realms, as well as by the proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation.

The invisible and non-obstructive dharmas are subsumed under eight elements (dhātus), two bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas) and cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna); they are driven by all latent dispositions (anuśayas).

The resultant (vipāka) dharmas are subsumed under seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—and cognized by five consciousnesses; they are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions of the three realms as well as those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Non-resultant phenomena (*avipāka-dharma*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm, all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms, as well as those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

That which is neither a result of retribution nor a dharma that is not a result of retribution is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It includes all [factors] of the form and formless realms, as well as all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)—namely, those pertaining to the two views of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm—and those proclivities abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Inferior phenomena (*hīna-dharma*) are comprised within ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*);

they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Intermediate phenomena (*madhya-dharma*) are comprised within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*).

The superior dharmas (*uttara-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin; they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are not governed by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The minor dharmas (*parīttaka-dharma*) and the great dharmas (*mahadgata-dharma*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by six consciousnesses, and are governed by all latent dispositions.

Infinite phenomena (*ananta-dharma*), agreeable phenomena (*manāpa-dharma*), disagreeable phenomena (*amanāpa-dharma*), and neither-agreeable-nor-disagreeable phenomena (*naiva-manāpa-na-amanāpa-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas associated with pleasure (*sukha-sahagata*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). Furthermore, they are driven by all latent dispositions of the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*), with the exception of those doubt (*vicikitsā*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with that doubt.

Dharmas associated with suffering (*duḥkha-sahagata*) are subsumed under eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by seven cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) as well as the cognitions of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) exercise their influence over them.

Dharmas associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and three aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that arise together, abide together, and cease together are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

It is not a dharma that arises simultaneously, does not abide simultaneously, nor ceases simultaneously; it is not subsumed within any single element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Mental concomitants (citta-sahabhū-dharmas) are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and are driven by all underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

Dharmas coexistent with the mind are subsumed under one element, one base, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas coexistent with the cessation of the mind are subsumed under ten elements, ten bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by five consciousnesses; and they are driven by all latent tendencies.

Those phenomena that do not arise together with the mind, do not abide together with the mind, and do not cease together with the mind are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the three aggregates (skandhas); they are known by ten knowledges (jñānas), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and driven by all latent proclivities (anuśayas).

The desire realm is comprised of ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. It is driven by the proclivities (anuśaya) that have the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects of the desire realm as their condition.
As with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), so it is with the realm of ill-will (*vyāpādadhātu*).

The realm of cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*) is subsumed within five elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path; it is cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the desire realm as well as by those proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The factors pertaining to the realm of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*) are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are influenced by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the three realms as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The element of non-ill will and the element of non-harming are subsumed within ten elements, four bases, and five aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by three consciousnesses; and they are driven by all pervasive latent tendencies of the three realms as well as by latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation.

The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
