It is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is subsumed under fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). It is cognized by four consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm act as its drivers.

The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is subsumed under three elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). It is known by six knowledges (jñāna)—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (nirodhamārgajñāna)—and is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). All latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm are active within it.

That which is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—comprising the desire realm and the form realm—is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñānas*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), and all latent proclivities (*anuśayas*) of both the desire and form realms act as its fetters.

Regarding the statement that "the four formless [attainments] are called the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)": it is comprised within the three realms, two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (nirodhamārgajñāna)—and is cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm act as their enablers (paryavasthāna).

Regarding the statement that "cessation through calculation and cessation not through calculation are called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)," it consists of one element, one base (*āyatana*), and is not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is not activated by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

All material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are termed the "form realm" (*rūpadhātu*). They are subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*). They are cognized by six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are governed by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragakleśa*) of both the desire and form realms, as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

Those non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*), excluding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), are called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). They are comprised of eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Regarding the statement that "cessation through calculation and cessation not through calculation are called the element of cessation (nirodhadhātu)": it consists of one element, one base, and is not subsumed within the aggregates (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is not activated by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is comprised of eighteen elements (*dhātus*), twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and five aggregates (*skandhas*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding subsequent cognition (*anvayajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*). All latent dispositions (*anuśayas*) of the desire realm act as its drivers.

The existence of form (rūpabhava) is comprised of fourteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (nirodhamārgajñāna). It is cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna) and is driven by all the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the form realm.

The formless existence (ārūpyabhava) is subsumed under three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), and the knowledges of cessation and the path; it is cognized by one consciousness, and all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm act as its proclivities.

The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

The *sāsrava* (with outflows) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) act as its proclivities (*anuśerate*).

The outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) is comprised within one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). With the exception of those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object, all other latent dispositions act as fetters upon it.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*, Fascicle Six *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*,
Fascicle Seven Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra (Vasumitra)
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas, Chapter Six, Part Four:

"The Analysis of Inclusion. The phenomena of the three times and the teaching concerning the three times are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśayas*) act as their drivers.

The suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*). It is driven by all the latent dispositions (*anuśayas*) of the desire realm.

The suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is comprised of fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*); it is cognized by four consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm.

The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is subsumed under three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by six knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*) and is driven by all the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm.

Furthermore, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna)—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). It is driven by all the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm.

The suffering inherent in the transformation of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā-pariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm; and it is driven by all latent dispositions of the desire realm, with the exception of doubt conditioned by the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the ignorance associated therewith.

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is suffering by way of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). It is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas with vitarka and vicāra are subsumed under eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); they are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna); and they are governed by all latent proclivities (anuśaya) pertaining to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).

Dharmas without vitarka but with vicāra are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all latent proclivities of the desire and form realms.

Dharmas without vitarka and vicāra are subsumed under thirteen elements (dhātus), twelve bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by ten cognitions (jñānas) and cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñānas). They are driven by all latent tendencies (anuśayas) of the form and formless realms, as well as by those latent tendencies of the desire realm that have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana).

The stage with vitarka and vicāra is subsumed under the eighteen dhātus, the twelve āyatanas, and the five skandhas. It is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. It is governed by all the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the two realms of desire and form.

The stage of non-discursive thought with discursive investigation (*avitarkavicāra-bhūmi*) is subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The stage without vitarka and vicāra is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and is cognized by four consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the realms of form and formlessness (rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu) act as their drivers.

The bodily action (kāyakarma) is subsumed under two elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna). It is cognized by two consciousnesses (vijñāna). It is driven by all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) and proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya) within both the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).
As with bodily action (*kāyakarman*), so it is with vocal action (*vākkarman*).

Mental action (*manaskarman*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Wholesome karma is subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and two aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by three consciousnesses; and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities of the three realms as well as by proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation.

Unwholesome karma is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by the three consciousnesses; it is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

Indeterminate karma is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. It comprises all [defilements] of the form and formless realms, as well as all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin and the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), along with those proclivities abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The training (śaikṣa-karma) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and the proclivities (anuśaya) do not adhere to it.
As with the training, so it is with the state beyond training (aśaikṣa-karma).

Karma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is subsumed under the three realms, the three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by three consciousnesses; it is driven by all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).

Karma abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-karma) is comprised within one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha); it is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and all proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned by insight are its driving forces.

The karma to be abandoned by cultivation is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by three consciousnesses; and it is driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation as well as all pervasive latent dispositions.

The uninterrupted karma (*anantarya-karma*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not underlie it.

Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman*) are subsumed within the three realms (*dhātu*), the three bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm, by all pervasive latent dispositions of the form and formless realms, and by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The karma of pleasant feeling is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by three consciousnesses; and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within both the desire and form realms.

Karma that results in painful feeling is subsumed under the three realms, three bases, and two aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as well as the knowledges of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by three consciousnesses. It is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

Karma that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-jñāna). It is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the form and formless realms, as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation. This concludes the three dharmas.

The foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna). It is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna). It is influenced by all pervasive latent proclivities (sarvatragakleśa) and those latent proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya) within both the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).

The foundation of mindfulness of feelings is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all latent tendencies.

The foundation of mindfulness of mind is comprised of seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all latent tendencies.

The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one sense-base (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, the wholesome—whether outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)—arising from that path through the predominance of the body; and the wholesome—whether outflowing or non-outflowing—arising from that path through the predominance of sensation, mind, and phenomena; as well as the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) and the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*): these are comprised of three elements, two sense-bases, and five aggregates. They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness; they are driven by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the three realms and by those underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Dhyāna is subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities of the form realm as well as proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation.

The Truth of Suffering is subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by the six consciousnesses; and it is driven by all latent tendencies.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.

The Truth of Cessation is not subsumed under any element (dhātu), sense-base (āyatana), or aggregate (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origination, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is not activated by any underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and is not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path; they are cognized by one consciousness, and are influenced by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the form realm as well as those underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness are subsumed within three elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are governed by all the underlying tendencies of the formless realm.

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subsumed under three elements, two bases, and four aggregates; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is governed by all the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm.

The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); they are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatragakleśa) of the three realms as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya).

The conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not the objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya are not comprised within any realm, sense-base, or aggregate; they are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not influenced by the underlying tendencies.

Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by six knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is not activated by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness, and it is not that which is activated by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The knowledge of others' minds is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities of the form realm as well as by proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation.

Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of those defilements (anuśaya) that are associated with views and have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object, all other defilements act as its proclivities.

The remaining knowledges (*jñāna*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*).

They are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). The analytical skill of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*) and the analytical skill of eloquence (*pratibhānapratibhāna*) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate. They are known by nine knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are influenced by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the three realms as well as those underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness. They are influenced by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The condition of cause (hetu-pratyaya) is subsumed under the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). It is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie it.

The condition of contiguity (samanantara-pratyaya) is subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates. It is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness (the mental consciousness), and all underlying tendencies underlie it.

The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha). They are known by ten knowledges (jñāna), cognized by six consciousnesses (vijñāna), and driven by all latent tendencies (anuśaya).

Edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), three bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by four consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire realm as well as the proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*).

The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) and the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*) are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The consciousness nutriment (*vijñānāhāra*) is comprised within seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*);

it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is driven by all proclivities (*anuśaya*). The flux of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges, excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as well as the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all proclivities of the desire realm.

The outflowing (sāsrava) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all the proclivities (anuśaya) of the form and formless realms.

The outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) that take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), excluding those associated with views that take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one sense-base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). With the exception of those [afflictions] that take the untainted as their object, they are driven by all other underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As with the *āsava*, so too are the *yoga*.

The grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

The clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is comprised of one element (*dhātu*), one sense-base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and which have out-flowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), with the exception of those associated with views and those *avidyā* (ignorance) that have out-flow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).

The clinging to precepts (śīlavrata-parāmarśa) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, by all pervasive underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of origin, and so on, up to the underlying tendencies with outflows as their objects to be abandoned through the vision of the path.
The grasping of self (*ātmagrāha*), as explained in detail, is like the outflows (*āsrava*).

Past phenomena, future phenomena, and present phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by the six consciousnesses; and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

It is not a dharma of the past, future, or present; it is comprised within one element, one base, and is not included within any aggregate (skandha). It is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is not that which is activated by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

Dharmas bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm act as their drivers.

Dharmas bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) are subsumed under fourteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). They are known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (nirodhamārgajñāna). They are cognized by the four consciousnesses (vijñāna) and are driven by all the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the realm of form.

Dharmas bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed under three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by six knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). They are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*) and are driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm.

Dharmas that are non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are not governed by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dharmas that have wholesome causes (*kuśala-hetu*) are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases, and five aggregates. They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by six consciousnesses, and are governed by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms as well as the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Unwholesome causal phenomena (*akuśala-hetu-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven types of knowledge—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

Dharmas that are indeterminate causes are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). They are known by eight cognitions, excluding the cognition of cessation and the cognition of the path, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) underlie them.

Dharmas that are neither causes of the wholesome, nor causes of the unwholesome, nor causes of the indeterminate are comprised within one element, one base, and are not included among the aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

There are dharmas that have objects as their conditions (*sālambana-dharma*). They are subsumed under the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness; and they are driven by the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that take conditioned phenomena as their objects.

Dharmas that do not have an object-condition (*anālambana*) are comprised within eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all proclivities (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

Dharmas that both have and do not have an object-condition are comprised within three elements, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; they are cognized by one consciousness; and all proclivities underlie them.

Dharmas that are neither with an object-condition nor without an object-condition are subsumed under eleven elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha). They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, and are cognized by the six consciousnesses. As for the proclivities (anuśaya) that have out-flowing objects, they are driven by these four categories; thus ends this section.

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is subsumed under eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate. It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*). It is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatragakleśa*) and those underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) are subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and three aggregates. They are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); they are cognized by one consciousness; and all latent proclivities (anuśaya) underlie them.

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is comprised by seven elements (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna); and it is driven by all latent tendencies (anuśaya).

The aggregate of material form (rūpa-skandha) is comprised by eleven elements, eleven bases, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by six consciousnesses; and it is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya).

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations are comprised within one element, one base, and three aggregates; they are known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and are cognized by one consciousness; all proclivities (anuśaya) underlie them.

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*);

it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). The destinies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges, excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path; they are cognized by six consciousnesses; and they are driven by all latent dispositions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The heavenly realm (*devagati*) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms act as its fetters.

The body of afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya-kleśa-kāya) is comprised of one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). It is driven by all proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as by all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya).

The group of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya-kleśa-skandha) is comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all latent proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin, as well as by all pervasive latent proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).

The body of afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by the proclivities (anuśaya) associated with outflows that are abandoned through the vision of cessation, as well as by all pervasive proclivities.

The body of afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya-kleśa-skandha) is comprised of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna). It is driven by the proclivities (anuśaya) that take contaminated objects as their conditions (sāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing, as well as by all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya).

The body of afflictions abandoned through cultivation is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; it is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation, as well as by all pervasive latent dispositions.

Material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are as explained under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are as explained under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

These mental phenomena are subsumed within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*); they are known by nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) underlie them.

The formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) are subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna). They are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna) and are driven by the proclivities (anuśaya) that have out-flowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana).
Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the detailed exposition is as follows, concluding with the five factors that are neither fruits nor fruit-producing dharmas.

The earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is subsumed under one element, one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and is cognized by two consciousnesses. It is driven by all-pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within both the desire and form realms.
As it is with the earth element, so it is with the water element, the fire element, the wind element, and the space element.

The consciousness element is comprised within seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by eight knowledges—excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as by all the pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya*).

The phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed within the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin, as well as by all the pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*).

The phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya-dharma*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the path, as well as by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

The dharmas abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are subsumed under the three realms, two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned by the path of seeing, as well as by all the universal proclivities (*sarvatragānuśaya*).

The factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-dharma*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight cognitions (*jñāna*), excluding the cognition of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the cognition of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). They are cognized by the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

The dharmas that are not subject to abandonment (*aprahātavya*) are subsumed under the three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), and are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); thus ends the section on the six dharmas.

The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) and the latent tendency of ill will (*pratighānuśaya*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding subsequent cognition (*anvayajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. These latent tendencies are those that bind through objects with outflows (*sāsrava*) within the desire realm.

The latent tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is the latent tendency that conditions the outflow-tainted objects of the form and formless realms.

The latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is activated as a latent tendency with respect to the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of the three realms.

The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of those [latent tendencies] that take the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object, it is driven by all other latent tendencies.

The proclivities of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) are comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; they are cognized by one consciousness; and they consist of the proclivities of views that take contaminated objects as their conditions, as well as the ignorance associated with views that takes uncontaminated objects as its condition.

The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It consists of the latent tendencies that are abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) which take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt that takes uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).

The first station of consciousness is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas). It is known by seven types of knowledge—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. All latent dispositions (anuśayas) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) act as its drivers.

The second station of consciousness is comprised of fourteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path; it is cognized by four consciousnesses (vijñāna), and is governed by all the proclivities (anuśaya) of the form realm.

The third and fourth stations of consciousness are subsumed under eleven elements, ten bases, and five aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) act as their drivers.

The fifth, sixth, and seventh stations of consciousness are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; they are known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness, and all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) act as their drivers.

The Chapter on the Seven Factors of Enlightenment is subsumed under one element, one base, and two aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Thus ends the section on the seven factors.

The first stage of liberation, as well as the second and third stages of liberation, are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all-pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the form realm and by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The liberation of the sphere of infinite space, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the liberation of the sphere of nothingness are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm as well as those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*) is subsumed under three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*). It is known by six knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). It is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as well as those proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The liberation of the sphere of the cessation of perception and feeling is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the formless realm as well as those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are subsumed under three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). They are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). They are driven by all pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and by those proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Among the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), right speech (samyagvāk), right action (samyakkarmānta), and right livelihood (samyagājīva) are subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The remaining factors of the path are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). This concludes the eight factors.

The fetter of greed (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness, and they are driven by the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects of the three realms as their domain.

The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) that acts as a proclivity toward the outflow-tainted objects of the desire realm.

The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) is as described for the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*). The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is as described for the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*).

The fetter of clinging to others (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is driven by the underlying tendencies that are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and which have outflows as their object (*sāsrava-ālambana*).

The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one sense-base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness. It consists of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) which take the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) as their object, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt that takes the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) as its object.

The two fetters of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire realm as well as by those proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The first abode of sentient beings is like the first station of consciousness.
The second abode of sentient beings is like the second station of consciousness.
The third, fourth, and fifth abodes of sentient beings are like the third, fourth, and [fifth] stations of consciousness.
The remaining abodes of sentient beings are like the other stations of consciousness; thus ends the section on the nine dharmas.

The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) are subsumed under two bases (*āyatana*), four aggregates (*skandha*), and three realms. They are known by six knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). They are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*) and are influenced by all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Among the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), right speech, right action, and right livelihood are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are not driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The remaining dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are as explained for the other factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*). [Thus] the ten factors are concluded.

Contaminated form (*sāsrava-rūpa*) is comprised within eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by the six consciousnesses. It is governed by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) belonging to both the desire and form realms.

The contaminated (sāsrava) feelings (vedanā), perceptions (saṃjñā), and formations (saṃskāra) are comprised within one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and three aggregates (skandha). They are known by eight knowledges (jñāna), excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); they are cognized by one consciousness (vijñāna), and are all driven by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) is as previously described for the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*).

Uncontaminated form (*anāsrava-rūpa*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), as well as the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not that which is driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The untainted (anāsrava) feeling, perception, and formations are subsumed under one element, one base, and three aggregates; they are known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and are cognized by one consciousness; they are not the objects of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*), and it is not that which is driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as explained at length in the section on "non-fruit phenomena" among the eleven dharmas, they are concluded here.

The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

As it is with the eye base, so it is with the ear base, nose base, tongue base, body base; the eye element, ear element, nose element, tongue element, body element; and the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty.

The form base (*rūpāyatana*) is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). It is known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*). It is cognized by two consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of both the desire and form realms, as well as by the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

As with the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), so it is with the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*), and the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).

The sense-base of odor (*gandhāyatana*) is comprised within one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding the knowledge of inference (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and is cognized by two types of consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the desire realm as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
As with the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*), so it is for the taste-base (*rasāyatana*), the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), and the taste-element (*rasadhātu*).

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) is subsumed under seven elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As with the *manāyatana* (mind-base), so it is with the *manodhātu* (mind-element) and the *manendriya* (mind-faculty).

The *dharmāyatana* (dharma-base) is comprised of one element, one base, and four aggregates; it is known by ten knowledges, cognized by one consciousness, and is the object of all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As with the *dharmāyatana*, so too is the *dharmadhātu*; thus ends the section on the twelve factors (*dvādaśa-dharma*).

The *cakṣurvijñānadhātu* is subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*); and it is influenced by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragakleśa*) as well as those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As with the eye-consciousness element, so it is with the ear-consciousness element and the body-consciousness element.

The nose-consciousness element is subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is influenced by all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.
As with the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), so it is with the tongue-consciousness element (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*).

The mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is comprised within two elements, one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). This concludes the eighteen dharmas.

The female faculty (*strī-indriya*) is comprised of one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire realm as well as by proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As with the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), so it is with the male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*).

The life faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms and by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm, as well as by all pervasive latent tendencies and those to be abandoned through cultivation of the desire realm.

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the desire realm as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).

The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm; and, with the exception of doubt conditioned by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and the ignorance associated therewith in the desire realm, it is driven by all other latent tendencies of the desire realm.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive latent proclivities of the three realms as well as those latent proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As with the faculty of faith, so it is with the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is comprised within the three realms, two bases, and three aggregates; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not influenced by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

As with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), so it is with the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). This concludes the twenty-two factors.

The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven cognitions—excluding inferential cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are activated by all underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering that are bound to the desire realm, as well as by all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). These are the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin that are bound to the desire realm, as well as all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

The proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). With the exception of the non-common ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) that takes the untainted as its object (*anāsrava-ālambana*) among those proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of cessation bound to the desire realm, they are all driven by the proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of cessation bound to the desire realm, as well as by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

The proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of the non-common ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*) that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object and is to be abandoned by the path of vision pertaining to the desire realm, they are all driven by the proclivities to be abandoned by the path of vision pertaining to the desire realm and by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatragānuśaya*).

The proclivities (anuśaya) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation are comprised within one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all proclivities of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as by all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya).
As it is with those bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
The distinction for the form realm is that dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is excluded.
The distinction for the formless realm is that six knowledges know [these objects], excluding dharma-knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledges of cessation and the path.
The remainder is as explained above. This concludes the ninety-eight *anuśayas*.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
