Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body, it may be retributive or non-retributive.
What is retributive?
This refers to the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows applications of mindfulness regarding the body.
What is without retribution?
This refers to the indeterminate and the outflow-free applications of mindfulness regarding the body.
As it is with the application of mindfulness to the body, so it is with the applications of mindfulness to sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Three [of these] arise from causes and conditions and are comprised within the mundane; one is analytical.
As for the application of mindfulness to phenomena, if it is conditioned, it arises from causes and conditions and is comprised within the mundane.
If they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are not produced by causes and conditions and are not included within the world.
One is included among the forms (*rūpa*), and three are included among the designations (*nāman*).
One is included among the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), and two are included among the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*); this is the classification.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either comprised within the internal bases or comprised within the external bases.
What is comprised within the internal bases?
It refers to the five internal bases.
What is comprised by the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)?
It refers to the five external bases and a portion of one external base.
All of these are known by wisdom (*jñāna*).
If it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is known through the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-parijñā) and is abandoned;
if it is without outflows (anāsrava), it is not known through the knowledge of abandonment and is not abandoned.
Question:
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, how many should be cultivated and how many should not be cultivated?
Answer: All of them should be analyzed.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body, it is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to the wholesome foundation of mindfulness of the body.
What is not to be cultivated?
It refers to the foundations of mindfulness of the body that are unwholesome or indeterminate.
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, so it is with the foundations of mindfulness of feeling and of the mind.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena that consists of wholesome conditioned dharmas.
What are those that should not be cultivated?
They are the foundations of mindfulness regarding unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena, as well as space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation.
Question:
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are defiled and how many are undefiled?
Answer:
All should be analyzed accordingly.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either defiled or undefiled.
What is defiled? It refers to that which is obscured.
What is meant by "not defiled"? It means being non-obscured.
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, so it is with the foundations of mindfulness of feeling, mind, and phenomena.
Third, regarding the "fruit" and that which "has a fruit," there is a distinction.
In the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one may have three propositions concerning that which is a fruit but does not have a fruit.
That which is a fruit but does not have a fruit refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
That which is both a fruit and possesses a fruit refers to the foundations of mindfulness that are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
That which is neither a fruit nor possesses a fruit refers to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Three are non-appropriated (*anupātta*); one is to be distinguished.
The application of mindfulness to the body may be either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What is appropriated?
It refers to the nature of the internal sense bases as appropriated.
What is "not felt"?
It refers to that which is not felt by its own nature.
Three [elements] are not produced from the four great elements; this is one type of discrimination.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either derived from the four great elements or not derived from the four great elements.
What is derived from the four great elements?
It refers to nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
What is not derived from the four great elements?
It refers to a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
Three are with superior [states], as is one type of discernment (*pravicaya*).
The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is either surpassable or unsurpassable.
What is surpassable?
It refers to the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha), the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), space (ākāśa), and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha).
What is the unsurpassed?
It is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it does not exist [as such].
First, it is dissociated from causes; second, it is associated with causes; third, it is to be distinguished.

Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it consists of mental factors (*caitasika*), it is associated with causes; if it consists of non-mental factors (*acaitasika*), it is dissociated from causes.
A portion of the wholesome bases includes a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness, and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes a portion of the wholesome bases.
A portion of the unwholesome bases includes a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness, and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes a portion of the unwholesome bases.

A portion of the indeterminate bases (avyākṛtāyatana) includes a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness likewise includes a portion of the indeterminate bases.
A portion of the taints (āsravāyatana) includes a portion of one foundation of mindfulness, and a portion of one foundation of mindfulness likewise includes a portion of the taints.

A portion of the contaminated bases (*sāsrava-āyatana*) includes a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes a portion of the contaminated bases.

A portion of the uncontaminated bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) includes a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness, and a portion of the four foundations of mindfulness also includes a portion of the uncontaminated bases.
The three [foundations of mindfulness] are either past, future, or present; this is their distinction.
As for the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), if it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is either past, future, or present;
if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Question:
Of the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
Answer:
All [foundations of mindfulness] should be analyzed.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to a portion of the three bases (*āyatana*).
What is unwholesome?
It refers to a portion of the three bases.
What are the indeterminate [factors]? They are said to be eight bases (āyatana) and a portion of three bases.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with wholesome mental volition.
What is unwholesome?
This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with unwholesome mental attention.
What is the indeterminate?
This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with indeterminate mental attention.
As with the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, so it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
As for the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
This refers to the wholesome aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). What is unwholesome?
It refers to the unwholesome aggregates of perception and formations.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
It refers to the indeterminate aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question:
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are bound by the realms?
Answer:
All should be analyzed accordingly.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to two bases and a portion of nine bases.
What is bound to the realm of form?
It refers to a portion of nine bases.
What is unbound?
That is to say, it is a portion of one base (āyatana):
the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna), which is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with mental volition bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with mental attention bound to the form realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with mental attention bound to the formless realm.
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to the application of mindfulness to feelings associated with untainted mental attention.
As it is with the application of mindfulness to feelings, so it is with the application of mindfulness to the mind.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations associated with the desire realm.
What are those associated with the form realm?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations associated with the form realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of formations that are bound to the formless realm.
What is that which is unbound?
That is to say: the untainted aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the unconditioned.
Question:
Of the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are of the learner (śaikṣa), how many are of the adept (aśaikṣa), and how many are neither of the learner nor of the adept?
Answer: All should be analyzed.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either trainee (śaikṣa), or beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither trainee nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
What is that which pertains to training (*śaikṣa*)?
It refers to a small portion of one sense base (*āyatana*).
What is that which pertains to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to a portion of one sense base (*āyatana*).
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
It refers to ten sense bases and a portion of one sense base.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is either of one in training (śaikṣa), or of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither of one in training nor of one beyond training.
What is that of one in training?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with the mental attention of one in training.
What is that which pertains to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) associated with the mental attention of one beyond training.
What is that which pertains neither to one in training nor to one beyond training?
This refers to the foundation of mindfulness of sensation associated with tainted mental attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*).
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of sensation, so it is with the foundation of mindfulness of mind.
The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena may be of the learner (*śaikṣa*), of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither of the learner nor the non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What is the learner (śaikṣa)?
It refers to the aggregates of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha) of the learner.
What is the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa)?
This refers to the aggregates of perception and formations of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is neither of training nor beyond training?
It refers to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Question:
Of the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are abandoned by vision, how many are abandoned by cultivation, and how many are not to be abandoned?
Answer:
All should be analyzed.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either to be abandoned through cultivation or not to be abandoned.
What is to be abandoned through cultivation?
This refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is not subject to abandonment?
It refers to a portion of one base.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is either abandoned through insight, abandoned through cultivation, or not abandoned.
What is abandoned through insight?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling that is abandoned by the patience of immediate realization for those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma.
How are they abandoned through vision?
It refers to the application of mindfulness on feelings associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by vision.
How are they abandoned through cultivation?
This refers to the application of mindfulness to feeling practiced by one in training who has seen the tracks [of the path] and is abandoning [defilements]. How is it abandoned?

It refers to the application of mindfulness to feeling associated with the ten proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the untainted yet impure application of mindfulness to feeling that is subject to outflows.
What is non-abandonment?
It refers to the foundation of mindfulness of sensation that is untainted (*anāsrava*).
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of sensation, so it is with the foundation of mindfulness of mind.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is either abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), or not abandoned.
What is abandoned by insight?
It refers to that which is abandoned by the patience of immediate realization (anantarya-jñāna-kṣānti) for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
How are they abandoned through seeing?

It refers to the eight-and-eighty latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by seeing, the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) arising from them.
How are they abandoned through cultivation?

This refers to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) practiced by one in training who has seen the tracks [of the path] and abandons through cultivation. How is it abandoned?

It refers to the application of mindfulness to phenomena associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom, the formations dissociated from mind arising therefrom, and the untainted (i.e., non-defiled) application of mindfulness to phenomena that are still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is non-abandonment?
It refers to the application of mindfulness to untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).

One is neither mind nor mental factor (*caitta*) and is not associated with the mind; one is a mental factor and is associated with the mind; one is exclusively mind; and one is discernment (*prajñā*).

Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it has an object, it consists of mental factors (*caitasika*) and that which is associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*);
if it has no object, it is neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with the mind.
One type is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling; one type is associated with feeling but not concomitant with the mind; these are the two distinctions.

As for the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is either concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling, or neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling.

Regarding "mental concomitants that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling": this refers to bodily and vocal karma that follows the mind; the remainder are neither mental concomitants that follow the mind nor associated with feeling.

As for the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be a mental concomitant that follows the mind but is not associated with feeling; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
Those that follow the mind but are not associated with feeling (*vedanā*) refer to the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the mind.
Those that both follow the mind and are associated with feeling refer to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and its associated aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Those that neither follow the mind nor are associated with feeling refer to all other formations dissociated from the mind, excluding those formations dissociated from the mind that do follow the mind, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
As it is with feeling, so it is with perception and mental formations, excluding their own intrinsic natures.
Question:
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, how many proceed in accordance with the factors of enlightenment but are not associated with insight?
Answer: All [categories] should be analyzed.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is either concomitant with vitarka but not associated with vicāra, or neither concomitant with vitarka nor associated with vicāra.

Regarding those that follow from vitarka but are not associated with vicāra: these refer to the bodily and vocal karmas that follow from vitarka. All others neither follow from vitarka nor are they associated with vicāra.
As for the foundation of mindfulness of feeling, it may be with both vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the application of mindfulness of feeling associated with mental attention that is with vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka but with vicāra"?
That is to say, the application of mindfulness to feelings associated with mental attention that is without vitarka but with vicāra.
What is without vitarka and without vicāra?
It is the application of mindfulness to feelings associated with mental attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
As with the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), so it is for the foundation of mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are four permutations concerning those factors that follow the movement of initial inquiry (*vitarka*) but are not associated with investigation (*vicāra*).

Those that follow the movement of initial inquiry but are not associated with investigation are: formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow the movement of initial inquiry, as well as investigation itself when it is associated with initial inquiry.

Regarding those associated with *vipaśyanā* (insight) but not following after *vitarka* (applied thought): this refers to *vitarka* itself, or those mental factors associated with *vipaśyanā* but dissociated from *vitarka*, namely the application of mindfulness to mental phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding those that follow after *vitarka* and are also associated with *vipaśyanā*: this refers to the application of mindfulness to mental phenomena associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought).

That which neither follows through with vitarka nor is associated with vicāra refers to: all other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) excluding those formations dissociated from mind that follow through with vitarka; vicāra that is not associated with vitarka; the application of mindfulness to mental phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) consisting of mental factors not associated with either vitarka or vicāra; and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
Question:
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are views but not bases of views?
Answer:
All [bases] should be analyzed.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is either a basis for views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*) or not a view; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
That which is a basis for views but is not a view refers to nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
That which is both vision and a basis for vision refers to one base (āyatana).
That which is neither vision nor a basis for vision refers to a portion of one base.
As for the application of mindfulness to feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna), if it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is a basis for vision but not vision itself.
If it is untainted (anāsrava), it is neither vision nor the locus of vision.
As with the application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna), so it is for the application of mindfulness to the mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna).
Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna), there are four permutations: it may be vision but not the locus of vision, and so forth.
"Vision that is not a basis for vision" refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
"A basis for vision that is not vision" refers to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) consisting of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) that are not subsumed under vision.
That which is both a view and a basis for views refers to the five views and mundane right view.
That which is neither a view nor a basis for views refers to the foundations of mindfulness consisting of untainted phenomena that are not subsumed under the category of views.
Question:
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are based on the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and how many are not based on the view of a self-identity?
Answer:
All should be analyzed in this way.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body: if it is defiled, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is its cause, but it is not the cause of that view;
if it is undefiled, the view of a self-body is not its cause, nor is it the cause of that view.

Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of feelings: either the view of a self-identity is its cause while it is not the cause of the view of a self-identity; or the view of a self-identity is its cause and it is also the cause of the view of a self-identity; or the view of a self-identity is not its cause and it is also not the cause of the view of a self-identity.

"Self-view is the cause of those, but those are not the cause of self-view" means: excluding the past and present latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that are associated with the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*); excluding all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are associated with the foundation of mindfulness of feeling; excluding the future foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with self-view; excluding the arising, abiding, alteration, and cessation of self-view, as well as the arising, abiding, alteration, and cessation of the factors associated with it; and [excluding] whatever other defiled foundations of mindfulness of feeling there may be.
"Self-view is the cause of those, and they are also the cause of self-view" refers to those aforementioned factors that have been excluded.
"Self-view is not the cause of those, nor are they the cause of self-view" refers to the untainted application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
As with the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, so it is with the foundation of mindfulness of mind.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena: sometimes bodily view is its cause but it is not the cause of bodily view; thus, three propositions are to be formulated.

"Self-view is the cause of those, but those are not the cause of self-view" means: excluding the past and present *anusayas* abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and their associated *smṛtyupasthānas*; excluding all pervasive *anusayas* (*sarvatraga*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and their associated *smṛtyupasthānas*; excluding the future *smṛtyupasthānas* associated with self-view; excluding the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of self-view and the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of its associated factors; and including all other defiled *smṛtyupasthānas*.
"Self-view is the cause of those, and they are also the cause of self-view" refers to those aforementioned factors that have been excluded.
"Self-view is not the cause of those, nor are they the cause of self-view" refers to the applications of mindfulness consisting of non-defiled dharmas.
Question:
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are karma and not the maturation of karma?
Answer:
All should be analyzed.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be either karma or not a karmic retribution; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
That which is karma but not a karmic retribution refers to the karma of body and speech.
That which is karmic retribution but not karma refers to the application of mindfulness to the body born of retribution (*vipākaja*).

That which is neither karma nor karmic retribution refers to the remaining applications of mindfulness to the body, excluding both karma and the application of mindfulness to the body born of retribution.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling may be karmic retribution, not karmic action;
or it may be neither karmic action nor karmic retribution.
"Karma-resultant but not karma" refers to the foundations of mindfulness born of retribution (*vipākaja*). The remainder are neither karma nor karma-results.
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, so it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are four permutations concerning that which is karma but not the maturation of karma.
That which is karma but not the maturation of karma refers to volitional karma (*cetanākarma*) not subsumed under maturation.
That which is the maturation of karma but not karma refers to those phenomena included in the application of mindfulness to phenomena that arise as maturation and are not subsumed under volition.
That which is both karma and the retribution of karma refers to volitional karma born of retribution (*vipākaja-cetanā-karma*).

That which is neither karma nor the retribution of karma refers to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) excluding both karma and the phenomena that are the retribution of karma, as well as other applications of mindfulness to phenomena.
Two are concomitants of karma but are not karma; two are to be analyzed.
Regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is either karma that is not a concomitant of karma, or it is to be treated in three propositions.
That which is karma but not a concomitant of karma refers to bodily and vocal karma other than those bodily and vocal karmas that are concomitants of karma.
That which is both karma and concomitant with karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that is concomitant with karma.

That which is neither karma nor concomitant with karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that is not concomitant with karma, as well as the mindfulness foundations (smṛtyupasthāna) of body that are concomitant with karma, and other instances of the mindfulness foundation of body.
Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are three propositions concerning that which is either karma or non-karma but concomitant with karma.
That which is karma and concomitant with non-karma refers to volitional action (*cetanākarma*).

That which is concomitant with karma but not karma refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), as well as those formations within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are concomitant with karma but are not subsumed under volition.

That which is neither karma nor concomitant with karma refers to the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) excluding both karma and those dharmas concomitant with karma; it is the remaining mindfulness of phenomena.
Three are non-derived matter (anupādāyarūpa), and one is non-visible matter (anidarśana-rūpa). This is the analysis.

Regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is either derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) that is not visible matter (*anidarśana-rūpa*); this constitutes three propositions.
That which is derived matter and not visible matter refers to the eight bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
That which is derived matter and is also visible matter refers to one base (āyatana).
That which is neither derived matter nor visible matter refers to a portion of one base.
Three are non-derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and non-obstructive matter (*apratigha-rūpa*); one is to be analyzed.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is either derived matter and non-obstructive matter; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
That which is derived matter but not obstructive matter refers to a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
That which is obstructive matter but not derived matter refers to a small portion of one base.
Derived matter that is also resistant matter refers to the nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
All of these are profound and difficult to comprehend; they are difficult to comprehend and profound.
Question:
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are wholesome causes and not wholesome? Answer: [All four are wholesome causes and wholesome.]
All [categories] should be analyzed.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be either a wholesome cause or not wholesome; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
That which is a wholesome cause but not itself wholesome refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body that arises as the maturation (*vipākaja*) of wholesome karma.
That which is wholesome and has a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

That which is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause refers to the application of mindfulness of the body other than that produced as a result of wholesome karma, namely, the remaining indeterminate and unwholesome applications of mindfulness of the body.
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, so it is with the foundations of mindfulness of feeling and of the mind.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are four permutations concerning that which is wholesome and not caused by the wholesome.
That which is wholesome and not caused by the wholesome refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
That which is wholesome but not a wholesome cause refers to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) born of wholesome retribution.
That which is both wholesome and a wholesome cause refers to the application of mindfulness on conditioned wholesome phenomena (*saṃskṛta-kuśala-dharma*).

That which is neither wholesome nor a wholesome cause refers to all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) applications of mindfulness on phenomena, excluding those born of wholesome retribution.
Question:
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are unwholesome or have unwholesome causes?
Answer:
All [categories] should be analyzed.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be "not unwholesome despite having an unwholesome cause"; this constitutes three propositions.
That which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body that arises as the retribution of the unwholesome.
That which is unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome application of mindfulness on the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the application of mindfulness on the body that arises as the maturation of an unwholesome state, as well as other neutral (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome applications of mindfulness on the body.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three propositions concerning that which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome.

That which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feeling born of the retribution of the unwholesome, as well as the foundation of mindfulness of feeling associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm.
That which is unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome foundations of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).

That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the foundations of mindfulness of feeling that are other than those born of the retribution of the unwholesome, as well as those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm; it includes all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome foundations of mindfulness of feeling.
As with the foundation of mindfulness of feeling, so it is with the foundation of mindfulness of mind.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three propositions concerning that which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome.

That which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena born of the retribution of the unwholesome, as well as the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm.
That which is unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause refers to the application of mindfulness to unwholesome phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).

That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the application of mindfulness to phenomena other than those born of the retribution of the unwholesome, as well as those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm; it includes all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome applications of mindfulness to phenomena.
Question:
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are indeterminate (avyākṛta) but not causes of the indeterminate?
Answer: [None.]
All [categories] should be analyzed.

Regarding the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), it may be that which has an indeterminate cause (*avyākṛtahetu*) but is not itself indeterminate; this constitutes three propositions (*trikoti*).
That which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate refers to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) mindfulness of the body.
That which is indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause refers to the indeterminate application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
That which is neither indeterminate nor has an indeterminate cause refers to the wholesome application of mindfulness of the body.
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, so it is with the foundations of mindfulness of feeling and mind.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are four permutations: that which is indeterminate but not the cause of the indeterminate.
That which is indeterminate but not the cause of the indeterminate refers to space (ākāśa) and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
That which is the cause of the indeterminate but is not itself indeterminate refers to the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) consisting of unwholesome dharmas.
That which is indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause refers to the indeterminate applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding conditioned phenomena.
That which is neither indeterminate nor has an indeterminate cause refers to the wholesome applications of mindfulness.
Third, regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and being with cause (*sahetuka*):
the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is, if conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), both an object-condition and with cause;
if unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is neither an object-condition nor with cause.
First, that which is neither a sequential [condition] nor a condition as a sequential object is analyzed into three parts.

Regarding the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), it may be a sequential condition but not a condition as a sequential object; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.

Regarding those that are sequential but not sequential conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*): these refer to the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) that will necessarily arise when it is present in the future, as well as the mindfulness of feeling at the final moment of death of an Arhat in the past or the present.

That which is both successive and a condition by way of succession refers to all other past and present applications of mindfulness regarding sensation, excluding the final application of mindfulness regarding sensation at the moment of death of a past or present Arhat.

That which is neither sequential nor a condition by way of sequential object refers to the mindfulness of feelings that will necessarily arise in the present from the future, as well as other instances of the mindfulness of feelings in the future.
As with the mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), so it is with the mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three propositions concerning that which is sequential but not a condition by way of being a sequential object-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

That which is sequential but not a condition by way of being a sequential object-condition refers to: (1) future mental factors of the mindfulness of phenomena that are certain to arise in the present; (2) past and present mental factors of the mindfulness of phenomena at the final moment of death of an Arhat; and (3) those mental factors of the mindfulness of phenomena associated with the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), whether already arisen or yet to arise.

That which is both sequential and a sequential condition (samanantarapratyaya) refers to all other past and present mental factors of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), excluding the final mind and mental factors at the moment of death of a past or present Arhat.

That which is neither sequential nor a sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) refers to: with the exception of those future mental factors of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) that are destined to arise in the present; other future mental factors of the application of mindfulness to phenomena; with the exception of sequential mind-dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), other mind-dissociated formations; and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

First, there are those that are object-conditions but not possessing-conditions; second, there are those that are both object-conditions and possessing-conditions. Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): if it pertains to mental phenomena, it is both an object-condition and a possessing-condition; if it pertains to non-mental phenomena, it is an object-condition but not a possessing-condition.
Third, regarding the predominating condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and that which possesses predominance:
the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is distinguished as follows. If it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is both a predominating condition and possesses predominance;
if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is a predominating condition but does not possess predominance.
Question:
Of the four foundations of mindfulness, how many are outflows (*āsava*) and how many are concomitants of the outflows (*āsavasānuvattin*)?
Answer:
All should be analyzed as follows:
regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body, if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a flow but not a stream;
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a stream nor a flow.
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, so it is with the foundations of mindfulness of feeling and of the mind.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are three categories based on whether they follow the fluxes (*āsrava*) or are not the fluxes themselves.

Those that follow the fluxes but are not the fluxes refer to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena consisting of out-flowing (*sāsrava*) factors that are not themselves included within the fluxes.
"Outflows as well as those that follow outflows" refers to the four outflows (*catvāra oghāḥ*).
"Neither outflows nor those that follow outflows" refers to the application of mindfulness to untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
"Truths" refers to the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*).
Question: What are the four?
Answer:

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of the cessation [of suffering], and the noble truth of the path [leading to the cessation of suffering].
Question:
Of these Four Noble Truths, how many are material (rūpa) and how many are non-material (arūpa)?
Answer:
One is non-material; three discern the Truth of Suffering as being either material or non-material.
What is material?
It refers to the ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is non-form?
It refers to one base (*āyatana*) and a portion of another base.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
The bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the Truth of the Path are material; the remainder are non-material.
Two [of these] are invisible; two are to be analyzed.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, they are either visible or invisible.
How is it visible?
It refers to one base (āyatana).
How is it invisible?
That is to say, the eleven bases (*āyatana*).
As with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Two are non-obstructive (*apratigha*); two are differentiated (*vikalpita*).
The Truth of Suffering is either with resistance (*sapratigha*) or without resistance (*apratigha*).
What is meant by "with resistance"? It refers to the ten bases (*āyatana*).
What is the non-resistant?
It refers to the two bases (*āyatana*).
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Two are with outflows (*sāsrava*), two are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Three are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Two are without retribution (*avipāka*), two are to be analyzed (*vibhajya*).
The Truth of Suffering is either retributive or non-retributive.
What is retributive?
It refers to wholesome and unwholesome suffering.
What is that which has no retribution?
It refers to the indeterminate (avyākṛta) truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya).
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
Three are produced from causes and conditions and are comprised within the world; one is not produced from causes and conditions and is not comprised within the world.
One is comprised within name (*nāman*); three are discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The Truth of Suffering is either comprised within form (*rūpa*) or comprised within name.
What is comprised by form?
It refers to the ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is comprised by name?
This refers to one base (*āyatana*) and a portion of another base.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Within the Truth of the Path, bodily and vocal actions are subsumed under the category of form (*rūpa*), while the remainder are subsumed under the category of name (*nāman*).
First, the threefold discrimination is comprised within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is either comprised within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) or comprised within the external bases.
What is comprised within the internal bases?
That is to say, the six internal bases.
What is included within the external bases?
That is to say, the six external bases.
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination.
Regarding the mind, mentation, and consciousness subsumed under the truth of the path: those are subsumed within the internal bases, while the remainder are subsumed within the external bases.
All are known by knowledge (*jñāna*).
Two are both known by the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) and are abandoned; two are not known by the knowledge of abandonment and are not abandoned.
One is to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*), one is not to be cultivated; these two are to be analyzed.
The truth of suffering is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to the wholesome truth of suffering.
What should not be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate aspects of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
Two are defiled, and two are differentiated.
Regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is either defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or undefiled (*akliṣṭa*). What is defiled?
That is to say, it is obscured. What is non-defiled?
That is to say, it is unobscured.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
One fruit is not possessed of a fruit; three fruits are possessed of fruits.
Two are not to be felt; two are to be analyzed.
The truth of suffering is either experienced or not experienced.
What is meant by "experienced"? It refers to experience by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
What is non-feeling?
It refers to that which is not feeling by its own nature.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
One [category] is not composed of the four great elements; three are discriminative.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is either composed of the four great elements or not composed of the four great elements.
What is composed of the four great elements?
This refers to nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
What is not derived from the four great elements?
This refers to one base and a portion of two bases.
As with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Those comprised within the Truth of the Path consist of bodily and vocal karma produced by the four great elements; the remainder are not produced by the four great elements.
Three have something superior to them; one is unsurpassed.
Two are associated with causes, and two are not associated with causes.
First, those dissociated from causes; third, those that are discriminative.
Those factors included within the Truth of Suffering that are form and formations dissociated from mind are dissociated from causes; the remainder are associated with causes.
As with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.

Regarding the bodily and vocal actions and formations dissociated from mind subsumed under the Truth of the Path, they are dissociated from their causes; the remainder are associated with their causes.
The wholesome sphere (kuśalāyatana) subsumes the two truths and a portion of the two truths; the two truths and a portion of the two truths also subsume the wholesome sphere.
The unwholesome sphere (akuśalāyatana) subsumes a portion of the two truths; a portion of the two truths also subsumes the unwholesome sphere.
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) but is not a truth (*satya*).
That which is included within the indeterminate bases but is not a truth refers to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is included within the truths but is not an indeterminate base refers to two of the truths and a portion of the other two truths.
That which is included within the indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) and is also a truth refers to a portion of the two truths.
That which is neither included within the indeterminate bases nor is a truth is an impossibility.
The *āsravasthāna* (bases of outflows) subsume a portion of the two truths, and a portion of the two truths also subsumes the *āsravasthāna*.
The *sāsravasthāna* (bases of that which is with outflows) subsume the two truths, and the two truths also subsume the *sāsravasthāna*.
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) but is not a truth (*satya*).
That which is included within the untainted bases but is not a truth refers to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is included within the truths but is not an untainted base refers to the two truths [the conventional and the ultimate].
Those that are both included within the untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and are truths (*satya*) refer to the two truths.
That which is neither included within the untainted bases nor is a truth is an impossibility.
Three [of these] are either past, future, or present; one is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Two are wholesome; two are to be analyzed.
The truth of suffering is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
This refers to the five aggregates that are wholesome and subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What are the unwholesome?
They refer to the five aggregates that are unwholesome and subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the five aggregates that are subsumed under the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) and are indeterminate.
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
Two are unconditioned; two are to be analyzed.
The truth of suffering is either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
This refers to the five aggregates associated with the desire realm, which are subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What are those associated with the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates associated with the form realm, which are subsumed under the truth of suffering.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the four aggregates bound to the formless realm, which are subsumed under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
Three are neither-learner-nor-non-learner; one is to be analyzed.
The truth of the path is either learner or non-learner.
What is learner?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one in training.
What are those of one beyond training?
That is to say, the five aggregates of one beyond training.
Two are not to be abandoned; two are to be analyzed.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, it is either to be abandoned by seeing or abandoned by cultivation.
What is abandoned by seeing?

If the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is abandoned by the patience of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryakṣānti*) of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), how is it abandoned?

It refers to the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), the truth of suffering associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) arising therefrom.
What is abandonment through cultivation?
It is that which is abandoned through cultivation by one who has seen the tracks of the Noble Truth of Suffering and is still in training (*śaikṣa*). How is it abandoned?

This refers to the truth of suffering associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) produced by them, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) produced by them, and the undefiled truth of suffering.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
One is neither mind nor mental factor nor associated with mind; these three are to be analyzed.
Those factors subsumed under the Truth of Suffering that are matter or formations dissociated from mind are neither mind nor mental factors nor associated with mind.

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, their associated aggregate of formations, and the mental factors associated with the mind—the mind, intellect, and consciousness are all simply the mind.
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of the origin.
The bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind that are subsumed under the Truth of the Path are neither mind, nor mental factors, nor associated with mind;

the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and their corresponding aggregate of formations are mental factors associated with mind; and mind, intellect, and consciousness are themselves the mind.
One [category] does not follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and is not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*); three [categories] are discriminative (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it may either follow the mind and not be associated with feeling; thus, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
That which follows the mind but is not associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal karma that follows the mind, as well as mental formations dissociated from the mind and feeling itself.
That which is associated with feeling but does not follow the mind refers to the mind, mentation, and consciousness.
That which follows the mind and is also associated with feeling refers to the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and its associated aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
That which neither follows the mind nor is associated with feeling refers to all other material phenomena (rūpa), excluding those bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind;
and it refers to all other formations non-associated with the mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), excluding those that follow the mind.
As with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Regarding the Truth of the Path, there are four permutations concerning that which is concomitant with the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*).

That which is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal actions concomitant with the mind, as well as mental formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and feeling itself.
Those associated with feeling but not following the mind are the mind, mentation, and consciousness.
Those that follow the mind and are also associated with feeling are the aggregate of perception and its associated aggregate of formations.
That which neither follows the mind nor is associated with feeling refers to those formations dissociated from mind that do not follow the mind, as well as other formations dissociated from mind.
As with feeling (*vedanā*), so it is with perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), excluding their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
One [type] does not follow through with investigation (*vitarka-anuvartin*) and is not associated with analysis (*vicāra-samprayukta*); this is the threefold discrimination.
Regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it either follows through with investigation but is not associated with analysis; thus, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are to be formulated.

That which is concomitant with initial mental application (*vitarka*) but not associated with sustained mental application (*vicāra*) refers to: bodily and vocal karma concomitant with initial mental application; formations dissociated from mind that are concomitant with initial mental application; and sustained mental application associated with initial mental application.

Regarding those associated with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) but not following after initial inquiry (*vitarka*): this refers to the mind and mental factors associated with contemplation that are dissociated from initial inquiry, which constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Regarding those that follow after initial inquiry and are also associated with contemplation: this refers to the mind and mental factors associated with both initial inquiry and sustained examination (*vicāra*), which constitute the Truth of Suffering.

That which neither follows from vitarka nor is associated with vicāra refers to: (1) other forms of bodily and vocal karma, excluding those that follow from vitarka; (2) other formations dissociated from mind, excluding those that follow from vitarka; (3) vicāra that is not associated with vitarka; and (4) the truths of suffering consisting of those mental states and mental factors that are neither associated with vitarka nor vicāra.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Regarding the Truth of the Path, there are four permutations concerning that which follows the awakening (bodha-anuvartin) but is not associated with insight (vipaśyanā-samprayukta).

That which follows the awakening but is not associated with insight refers to: bodily and vocal karma that follows the awakening; formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that follow the awakening; and insight that is associated with the awakening.

Those associated with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) but not following after initial inquiry (*vitarka*) refer to initial inquiry itself, or those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are associated with contemplation but not associated with initial inquiry.

Those that both follow after initial inquiry and are associated with contemplation refer to those mental states and mental factors associated with both initial inquiry and sustained examination (*vicāra*).

That which does not follow from vitarka (*vitarkānuparivartin*) and is also not associated with vicāra (*avicārasamprayukta*) refers to: bodily and vocal karma other than that which follows from vitarka; mental formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) other than those that follow from vitarka; vicāra that is not associated with vitarka; and those mental states and mental factors (*cittacaittadharma*) that are associated neither with vitarka nor with vicāra.
One is neither view nor the locus of a view; three are to be analyzed.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is either both a view and the locus of a view, or the locus of a view but not a view.

That which is both a view and the locus of a view refers to the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), the five views, and mundane right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*); the remainder are the locus of a view but not a view.
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination.

Regarding the truth of the path, that untainted wisdom included therein which is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is vision but not a basis for vision; all other [wisdom] is neither vision nor a basis for vision.
Regarding the two types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and that which is not its cause, and that which is also not the cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, there are two distinctions.

Concerning the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), either *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is its cause while it is not the cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*; or *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is its cause and it is also the cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*; or *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is not its cause and it is also not the cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.

Regarding the statement that "the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the cause for those [factors], but those are not the cause for the view of a self": this refers to all afflicted truths (duḥkhasatya), excluding: the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya) along with their associated factors in the past and present; all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudayadarśana-prahātavya) along with their associated factors in the past and present; the truth associated with the future view of a self; the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of the view of a self itself, as well as the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of its associated factors; and any other remaining afflicted truths.
Regarding "the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the cause of those, and those are also the cause of the view of a self," this refers to the aforementioned excluded factors.
Regarding "the view of a self is not the cause of those, nor are those the cause of the view of a self," this refers to the undefiled truth of suffering (aduṣṭa-duḥkhasatya).
As with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
One [category] is neither karma nor the fruit of karma; the other three are to be analyzed.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, there are cases that are karma but not the fruit of karma; thus, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are established.
That which is karma but not the retribution of karma refers to bodily and vocal karma, as well as volitional karma (cetanā-karma) that is not subsumed under retribution.
That which is the retribution of karma but not karma refers to the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) born of retribution that is not subsumed under volition.
That which is both karma and the retribution of karma refers to the karma of volition born of retribution (*vipākaja-cetanā-karma*).

That which is neither karma nor the retribution of karma refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) excluding both karma and the retribution of karma; that is, the remaining portions of the truth of suffering.
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination.

Regarding the truth of the path, bodily and vocal karma as well as volition (cetanā) subsumed within it are karma but not the retribution of karma; the remainder are neither karma nor the retribution of karma.
One [category] is neither karma nor concomitant with karma; three [categories] are to be analyzed.
Regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is either karma that is not concomitant with karma; this constitutes four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which is karma but not concomitant with karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that are not concomitant with karma, as well as other bodily and vocal karma and the karma of volition (*cetanā*).

That which is concomitant with karma but is not itself karma refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of consciousness, and the aggregate of formations that are concomitant with karma but are not comprised within volition (*cetanā*).
That which is both karma and concomitant with karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that are themselves concomitant with karma.
That which is neither karma nor concomitant with karma refers to the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) other than karma and that which is concomitant with karma.
As it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
Regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are four permutations concerning that which is either karma or not karma but follows after karma (*karmānuvartin*).
That which is karma but does not follow after karma refers to the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*).

That which follows after karma but is not karma refers to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), as well as those formations included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that follow after karma but are not themselves subsumed under volition.
That which is both karma and concomitant with karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that is concomitant with karma.
That which is neither karma nor concomitant with karma refers to those formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) other than those concomitant with karma.
First, there are non-derived matter and invisible matter; these are analyzed into three categories.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it may be derived matter that is invisible; thus, three propositions are established.
Derived matter that is not visible matter refers to eight bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
Derived matter that is also visible matter refers to one base.
That which is neither derived matter nor visible matter refers to one base (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
The bodily and vocal karma subsumed under the Truth of the Path is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and is not visible matter; the remainder is neither derived matter nor visible matter.
One part is neither derived matter nor obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*); this is the threefold classification.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering: there are four permutations concerning derived matter that is not obstructive matter.
That which is derived matter but not obstructive matter refers to a small portion of one base (āyatana).
That which is resistant matter but not derived matter refers to a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
That which is derived matter and also resistant matter refers to nine bases and a small portion of one base.
That which is neither derived matter nor obstructive matter refers to one base (*āyatana*) and a small portion of another base.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
The bodily and vocal actions subsumed under the Truth of the Path are derived matter and are non-obstructive matter; the remainder are neither derived matter nor obstructive matter.
All of these are profound and difficult to comprehend, and difficult to comprehend because they are profound.
First, that which is wholesome but not a cause of the wholesome; second, that which is both wholesome and a cause of the wholesome—these two are to be distinguished.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it may be a cause of the wholesome but not itself wholesome; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
That which is a wholesome cause but not wholesome refers to the Truth of Suffering arising from the maturation of wholesome karma.
That which is both wholesome and a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome Truth of Suffering.

That which is neither wholesome nor a wholesome cause refers to the Truth of Suffering other than that arising from the maturation of wholesome karma—namely, all other neutral (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) truths of suffering.
As with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Both are neither unwholesome causes nor unwholesome; both are to be analyzed.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, it may be an unwholesome cause but not unwholesome itself; thus, three propositions are to be formulated.

That which is not unwholesome but has an unwholesome cause refers to the Truth of Suffering arising as the retribution of the unwholesome, as well as the Truth of Suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm.
That which is both unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome Truth of Suffering.

That which is neither unwholesome nor the cause of the unwholesome refers to: the truth of suffering arising from the retribution of the unwholesome, excluding that; the truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm, excluding those; and all other neutral (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome truths of suffering.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
Both are neither indeterminate nor causes of the indeterminate; both are to be analyzed.
[This refers to] the Truth of Suffering.
Alternatively, there are three propositions regarding that which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate.
Regarding that which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate:
That which is unwholesome suffering-truth (duḥkhasatya) is [unwholesome].
That which is indeterminate and also has an indeterminate cause refers to indeterminate suffering-truth.
That which is neither indeterminate nor the cause of the indeterminate refers to the wholesome Truth of Suffering; as it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the others.
The Truth of Origination is also like this:
one is neither a condition by way of object nor possesses a cause;
three are both conditions by way of object and possess causes.
First, that which is neither a sequential [condition] nor a sequential-object condition (*samanantarālambanapratyaya*).
This is analyzed into three parts.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it may be a sequential condition but not a sequential-object condition; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭi*) are established.

That which is a sequential condition but not a sequential-object condition refers to: the suffering truth consisting of future mind and mental factors that are certain to arise in the present; the suffering truth consisting of past and present mind and mental factors at the final moment of death of an Arhat; and the mind and mental factors already arisen or yet to arise during the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding that which is both sequential and a sequential condition (*samanantarapratyaya*): this refers to all other past and present mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) belonging to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), excluding the final moments of mind and mental factors at the death of an Arhat in the past or present.

That which is neither sequential nor a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to: (1) with the exception of those future mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the Truth of Suffering that are destined to arise immediately; (2) other future mental states and mental factors of the Truth of Suffering, excluding sequential non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*); and (3) all other non-associated formations as well as matter (*rūpa*).
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.

Regarding the Truth of the Path, there are three categories concerning that which is either sequential but not a condition as a sequential object-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), or both sequential and a condition as a sequential object-condition.

That which is sequential but not a condition as a sequential object-condition refers to those future mental states and mental factors of the Truth of the Path that are destined to arise in the present.
That which is both sequential and a condition as a sequential object refers to the past and present mind and mental factors that constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

That which is neither sequential nor a condition as a sequential object refers to all future mind and mental factors constituting the Truth of the Path—excluding those that are currently manifest and bound to arise—as well as other future mind and mental factors constituting the Truth of the Path, and bodily and vocal actions, along with the mental concomitants (*cittānuvartin*) and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
First, regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) that is not the presence-condition (sahabhū-pratyaya), there are three categories.

Those conditioned factors included within the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya)—namely, matter (rūpa) and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra)—are object-conditions that are not presence-conditions; all others are both object-conditions and presence-conditions.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.

Regarding the Truth of the Path, bodily and vocal karma subsumed within it are object-conditions that are not possessors of objects; the remaining [factors] are both object-conditions and possessors of objects.
Three are both dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and possess dominance; one is a dominant condition but does not possess dominance.
Two are neither outflows (*āsrava*) nor concomitants of outflows; these two are to be analyzed.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is either both a flood (*ogha*) and a bond (*srota-anuśāyin*), or it is a bond but not a flood.
That which is both a flood and a bond refers to the four floods; the remainder are bonds but not floods.
As it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it is with the Truth of Origination.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*, Volume Nine; *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*, Volume Ten.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra;
translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.

Chapter Seven, Part Three of the *Sahasrapraśna-śāstra*: The Chapters on the Dhyānas, the Immeasurables, the Formless Realm, Samādhi, Meditative Concentration, Enlightenment, the Faculties, the Bases, the Aggregates, and the Elements.
"Meditative absorptions" (dhyāna) refers to the four dhyānas.
Question:
What are the four?
Answer:
They are the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
Question:
Regarding these four dhyānas, how many are material (rūpa) and how many are non-material (arūpa)?
Answer:
The bodily and vocal actions subsumed under dhyāna are material; the remainder are non-material.
All are invisible; all are non-resistant.
Question:
Of the dhyānas, how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer: All should be analyzed.
Dhyāna may be either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They are the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) comprised within dhyāna that are associated with outflows.
What are the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
This refers to the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) subsumed under dhyāna;
all of these are conditioned (saṃskṛta).
If they are tainted (sāsrava), they possess retribution (vipāka).
If they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they have no retribution (*avipāka*).
All that arises from causes and conditions is comprised within the worldly (*laukika*).
Bodily and vocal karma subsumed under dhyāna is comprised within form (*rūpa*); the remainder is comprised within name (*nāman*).
The mind and mental consciousness subsumed under dhyāna are included within the internal bases; the remainder are included within the external bases.
All are known by wisdom.
If they are with outflows (sāsrava), they are known by the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) and are abandoned.
If they are untainted (anāsrava), they are not known through the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) and are not subject to abandonment.
All are to be cultivated (bhāvayitavya); all are non-defiled (akliṣṭa); all are both fruits and possess fruits; all are non-appropriated (anupātta).
The bodily and vocal karma subsumed under dhyāna is composed of the four great elements; the remainder is not composed of the four great elements.
All of these are "with-remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa).
As for dhyāna, if it is with-outflows (sāsrava), it is "existent" (bhava).
If they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not exist [as such].
The bodily and vocal karma as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) included within dhyāna are dissociated from causes; the remainder are associated with causes.
The wholesome portion of the five bases subsumes the four dhyānas, and the four dhyānas likewise subsume the wholesome portion of the five bases.
They are not subsumed by the unwholesome bases, nor by the indeterminate bases, nor by the outflowing (sāsrava) bases.
There are four permutations regarding that which is included within the spheres of the outflows (sāsrava) but is not dhyāna.
That which is included within the spheres of the outflows but is not dhyāna refers to the five aggregates of the outflows (sāsrava-pañca-skandha) that are not subsumed under dhyāna.
That which is included within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) but not within the contaminated bases (*sāsrava-sthāna*) refers to the four uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
That which is included within the contaminated bases and is also a meditative absorption refers to the four contaminated dhyānas.

That which is neither included within the contaminated bases nor is a meditative absorption refers to the five uncontaminated aggregates (*skandha*) not subsumed under the dhyānas, as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the untainted (anāsrava) but is not dhyāna.
