Those that are neither included within the unwholesome bases nor are faculties are: the wholesome aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); the wholesome aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not included among the faculties, as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); the indeterminate aggregate of form and the aggregate of perception not included among the faculties; the indeterminate aggregate of formations not included among the faculties; and space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) but is not a faculty (*indriya*).

That which is included within the indeterminate bases but is not a faculty refers to: the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) not subsumed under the faculties; the indeterminate aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) not subsumed under the faculties; and space (*ākāśa*) as well as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Those included in the faculties but not in the indeterminate bases are the nine faculties and a portion of the five faculties.
Those included in the indeterminate bases and also in the faculties are the eight faculties and a portion of the five faculties.

Those which are neither included within the indeterminate bases nor are faculties are: the wholesome aggregates of form and perception; the wholesome aggregate of formations not included among the faculties, as well as analytical cessation; and the unwholesome aggregates of form and perception, and the unwholesome aggregate of formations not included among the faculties.
They are not included within the bases of the outflows (*āsravasthāna*).
Alternatively, there are cases where they are included within the bases of the outflows but are not faculties (*indriya*); these form four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

That which is included within the bases of the outflows but is not an faculty refers to the outflowing aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) that are not included among the faculties, as well as the outflowing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are not included among the faculties.
Those included within the faculties but not within the outflow-tainted bases (*sāsrava-āyatana*) are the three faculties and a portion of nine faculties.
Those included within the outflow-tainted bases and also included within the faculties are ten faculties and a portion of nine faculties.

That which is neither included within the contaminated bases nor is a faculty refers to the uncontaminated aggregate of form, the aggregate of perception, the uncontaminated aggregate of formations not subsumed under the faculties, and the unconditioned.
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the untainted (anāsrava) bases but is not a faculty (indriya).

That which is included within the untainted bases but is not a faculty refers to the untainted aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha), the untainted aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) not subsumed under the faculties, and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Those included among the faculties but not included among the untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) are the ten faculties and a portion of nine faculties.
Those included among both the untainted bases and the faculties are the three faculties and a portion of nine faculties.

That which is neither included within the uncontaminated bases nor is a faculty refers to the contaminated form aggregate and perception aggregate not included among the faculties, as well as the contaminated formation aggregate not included among the faculties.
All [factors] are either past, future, or present.
Eight are wholesome, eight are indeterminate, and six are to be analyzed.
The mind-faculty is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with wholesome mental volition.
What is unwholesome?
This refers to the mental faculty (manas) associated with unwholesome mental attention (manasikāra).
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the mental faculty associated with indeterminate mental attention.
As it is with the faculty of mind, so it is with the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
As for the faculty of grief, it is either wholesome or unwholesome.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the faculty of grief associated with wholesome mental attention.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the faculty of grief associated with unwholesome mental attention.
Four are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), three are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*), and fifteen are to be analyzed.
The eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
That is to say, the eye faculty is produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
What is meant by being bound to the form realm?
It means that the eye faculty is produced by the four great elements bound to the form realm.
As it is with the eye faculty, so it is with the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The life faculty is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to life bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
That is to say, the life-force bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
What is the life-force bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
It is the life-force bound to the formless realm.
The faculty of mind (manendriya) is either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental attention (manasikāra) that is bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental attention bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the formless realm?
This refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental attention bound to the formless realm.
What is non-bound?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with untainted (anāsrava) mental attention.

As it is with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), so it is with the faculties of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), faith (*śraddhendriya*), energy (*vīryendriya*), mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental volition bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). What is unbound?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with untainted (*anāsrava*) mental attention.
As with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), so it is with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Two are training (*śaikṣa*), one is beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*), ten are neither-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), and nine are to be analyzed.
The mental faculty (*manendriya*) is either training, or beyond-training, or neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
What is the faculty of mind associated with the mental application of training (*śaikṣa-manasikāra*)? It refers to the faculty of mind associated with the mental application of training.
The faculty of mind associated with the mental application of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*) is likewise.
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with tainted mental attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*).
As it is with the faculty of mind, so it is with the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as well as the faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Nine are to be abandoned by cultivation, three are not to be abandoned, and ten are to be distinguished.
As for the faculty of mind (*manas*), it is either to be abandoned by seeing, or to be abandoned by cultivation, or not to be abandoned.
What is to be abandoned by seeing?

If the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is abandoned through the "uninterrupted patience" (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth by those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), as explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Bases" (*Vibhaṅga-āyatana-varga*),
how is it abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
This refers to what was explained extensively above.
What is "non-interruption"?
It refers to the untainted faculty of mind (*anāsrava-manas-indriya*).
As it is with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), so it is with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

As for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), it is either to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), or to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
What is to be abandoned by vision?

If the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*),
how is it abandoned?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
What is abandonment through cultivation?
If the faculty of pleasure belongs to one who is a trainee (śaikṣa) and has seen the tracks [of the path], it is abandoned through cultivation. How is it abandoned?

This refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) associated with the five proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the undefiled, outflowing (*āsrava*) faculty of pleasure.
What is "not to be abandoned" (*aheya*)?
It refers to the twenty-eight instances of the undefiled faculty of pleasure; that is, the twenty-eight [instances] within the three dhyānas and the four noble truths.
Fifth, there are three types of contemplation in the third dhyāna and two types of contemplation in the desire realm, namely greed and ignorance.
The faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) is either abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not abandoned at all.
What is abandoned through vision?
If the faculty of joy is abandoned by the patience of immediate succession and so forth for those who follow by faith or follow by dharma.
How is it abandoned?
This refers to the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) associated with the fifty-two proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
It is the faculty of joy belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the tracks [of the path] and is abandoned through cultivation.
How is it abandoned?
It refers to the faculty of joy associated with the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the undefiled, out-flowing (*āsrava*) faculty of joy.
How is it not abandoned?

Regarding the fifty-two untainted factors associated with the faculty of joy (*anāsrava-prīti-indriya*): there are twenty-eight in the four truths of the second dhyāna; and in the desire realm, there is one view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), four wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), two clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), four clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), four greed (*rāga*), four pride (*māna*), and four ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for the six [factors]: there are two in the contemplation of the second dhyāna, three in the contemplation of the desire realm, and three consisting of greed, pride, and ignorance.
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is either abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through seeing?

It is that faculty of sorrow which is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How is it abandoned through seeing?
It refers to the faculty of grief associated with the sixteen proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing.
How is it abandoned through cultivation?
If the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is to be abandoned through cultivation by one who has entered the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), how is it abandoned?

It refers to the faculty of sorrow associated with the two proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the sixteen non-defiled faculties of sorrow: namely, four for each of the false views regarding the four truths of the desire realm, four for doubt, four for ill-will (*pratigha*), and four for ignorance (*avidyā*).
Second, there are two [factors] in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) that are to be abandoned through cultivation: ill-will and ignorance.
As for faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom: if they are with outflows (sāsrava), they are to be abandoned through cultivation;
if they are without outflows (anāsrava), they are not to be abandoned.
Eight [faculties] are neither mind nor mental factors nor associated with mind; ten are mental factors associated with mind; one is mind itself—thus they are distinguished into three categories.

The nine faculties or eight faculties subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known" consist of mental factors and those associated with mind; one faculty is mind itself.

Eight are neither concomitants of mind nor associated with feeling; one is associated with feeling but not a concomitant of mind; five are concomitants of mind but not associated with feeling; five are both concomitants of mind and associated with feeling; three are to be analyzed.

The three faculties subsumed under the faculty of "knowing the unknown," the faculty of "having known," and the faculty of "final knowledge" are as follows: one [the faculty of final knowledge] is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling; one [the faculty of having known] is associated with feeling but not concomitant with the mind; and five [the faculty of knowing the unknown and the four types of feeling] are both concomitant with the mind and associated with feeling.

Eight do not follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*) and are not associated with perception or formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra-samprayukta*); one is associated with perception and formations but does not follow the mind; ten follow the mind and are associated with perception and formations, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which constitutes the three types of discrimination (*vibhanga*).

The nine faculties or eight faculties subsumed under the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are concomitant with the mind and associated with perception and formations, excluding their own intrinsic nature. One faculty is associated with perception and formations but is not concomitant with the mind.
Two [elements] possess both vitarka and vicāra; eight possess neither vitarka nor vicāra; twelve are to be analyzed.
As for the faculty of mind (manas), it may possess both vitarka and vicāra, or possess vicāra without vitarka, or possess neither vitarka nor vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with mental application accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka but with vicāra"?
This refers to the mental faculty associated with volitional attention that is without vitarka and with vicāra.
What is [the mental faculty] without vitarka and without vicāra?
It refers to the mental faculty associated with volitional attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.

As it is with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), so it is also with the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; and likewise with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is with vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention that possesses vitarka and vicāra.
What is that which is without vitarka and without vicāra?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
As it is with the faculty of pleasure, so it is with the faculty of joy.
One [of the twelve bases] is both a view and a locus for views; nine loci for views are not views; and twelve are to be analyzed.
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*): if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a locus for views but not a view;
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a view nor a locus for views.

As it is with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), so it is with the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); the same applies to the faculties of faith (*śraddhendriya*), energy (*vīryendriya*), mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
Regarding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), it is either vision (*dṛṣṭi*) or not a basis for vision (*adṛṣṭisthāna*); thus, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*) are to be formulated.

That which is vision but not a basis for vision refers to the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
That which is a basis for vision but not vision refers to the tainted faculty of wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñendriya*) that is not subsumed under vision.
That which is both a view and a basis for views refers to mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
That which is neither a view nor a basis for views refers to the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) that is not subsumed under the category of views.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) are subsumed under [the category of] vision; they are vision but not the locus of vision. The remainder are neither vision nor the locus of vision.

The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*), which is subsumed under the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) but is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), is vision but not the locus of vision. The remainder are neither vision nor the locus of vision.
The sixteen [factors] are not the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), nor is the view of a self-identity their cause; this is explained through sixfold analysis.

The faculty of mind (*manendriya*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are explained in detail as in the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*): if it is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but the view of a self-identity is not its cause;
if it is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*), it does not have the view of a self-identity as its cause, nor is the view of a self-identity its cause.

Regarding the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), there are three propositions concerning its being the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) while the view of a self-identity is not its cause.

The first proposition—where the faculty of grief is the cause of the view of a self-identity, but the view of a self-identity is not its cause—refers to: (1) the faculty of grief associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, excluding those [proclivities]; (2) the faculty of grief associated with all-pervading (*sarvatraga*) proclivities abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, excluding those [proclivities]; and (3) any other afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) faculty of grief.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and for which the view of a self is also the cause refers to those factors previously excluded.
That which does not have the view of a self as its cause and for which the view of a self is also not the cause refers to the non-defiled faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Nine are neither karma nor the retribution of karma; one is the retribution of karma but not karma; twelve are to be analyzed.
As for the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is either the retribution of karma but not karma, or neither karma nor the retribution of karma.
"Karmic retribution that is not karma" refers to the eye-faculty born of retribution; the remaining [faculties] are neither karma nor karmic retribution.

As it is with the eye-faculty, so it is with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, male faculty, female faculty, mind-faculty, pleasure-faculty, joy-faculty, equanimity-faculty, and pain-faculty.
Eight are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; fourteen are concomitants of karma but not karma themselves.
Seven are derived matter that is not visible matter; fifteen are neither derived matter nor visible matter.
Seven are derived matter and obstructive matter; fifteen are neither derived matter nor obstructive matter.
All are profound and difficult to comprehend; difficult to comprehend and profound.
Eight are both wholesome and have wholesome causes; fourteen are to be analyzed.
As for the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is either a wholesome cause that is not itself wholesome, or it is neither a wholesome cause nor is it itself wholesome.

That which is a wholesome cause but not itself wholesome refers to the eye-faculty produced as the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma; the remainder are neither wholesome causes nor are they themselves wholesome.
As with the eye faculty, so it is with the ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, male faculty, female faculty, and life faculty.
As for the mind faculty, it may have a wholesome cause while not being wholesome itself; thus, three propositions are to be formulated.
That which is a wholesome cause but not wholesome refers to the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) arising from a wholesome retribution.
That which is both wholesome and a wholesome cause refers to a wholesome mind-faculty.

That which is neither wholesome nor a wholesome cause refers to all other unwholesome or indeterminate mind-faculties, excluding those arising from a wholesome retribution and the wholesome mind-faculty itself.
As it is with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), so it is with the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
As for the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), it is sometimes wholesome and has a wholesome cause, and sometimes it is not wholesome and does not have a wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome and has a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
That which is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) faculty of suffering.
As for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), it is either wholesome and has a wholesome cause, or neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause.
That which is wholesome and has a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
That which is neither wholesome nor has a wholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of grief.
Eight [faculties] are neither unwholesome nor have an unwholesome cause; fourteen are to be analyzed.
The eye-faculty is either (a) a cause of unwholesomeness but not itself unwholesome, or (b) neither a cause of unwholesomeness nor itself unwholesome.

Regarding (a) being a cause of unwholesomeness but not itself unwholesome: this refers to the eye-faculty born as the retribution of unwholesomeness; the remainder are neither a cause of unwholesomeness nor themselves unwholesome.
As with the eye faculty, so it is with the ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, male faculty, female faculty, and life faculty.
Regarding the mind faculty, it may be that which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome; thus, three cases are to be formulated.

That which is not unwholesome but has an unwholesome cause refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) arising as the retribution of the unwholesome, as well as the mental faculty associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm.
That which is both unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome mental faculty itself.

That which is neither unwholesome nor the cause of the unwholesome refers to: with the exception of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) arising from the retribution of the unwholesome, with the exception of the mental faculty associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm, and with the exception of the unwholesome mental faculty; it includes all other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome mental faculties.
The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is either unwholesome but not a cause of the unwholesome, or neither unwholesome nor a cause of the unwholesome.
That which is unwholesome but not a cause of the unwholesome refers to the unwholesome faculty of pleasure.
That which is neither unwholesome nor the cause of the unwholesome refers to the wholesome and the neutral faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Regarding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), it may be the cause of the unwholesome but not itself unwholesome; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.
That which is not unwholesome but has an unwholesome cause refers to the faculty of suffering born of the retribution of the unwholesome.
That which is both unwholesome and has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of suffering.

That which is neither unwholesome nor the cause of the unwholesome refers to the faculty of suffering born of the maturation of the unwholesome, as well as the unwholesome faculty of suffering itself—excluding these, it refers to all other indeterminate and wholesome faculties of suffering.
Regarding the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*): it may have an unwholesome cause but not itself be unwholesome; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are established.

As for that which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome: this refers to the faculty of joy associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm.
That which is unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*).

That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the faculty of joy associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm—excluding those—and, excluding the unwholesome faculty of joy, all other indeterminate or wholesome faculties of joy.
As it is with the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*), so it is with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
As for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), it is either unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause, or it is neither unwholesome nor does it have an unwholesome cause.
That which is unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the wholesome faculty of grief.
Eight [faculties] are neither indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor have an indeterminate cause; eight are indeterminate and also have an indeterminate cause; six are to be analyzed.

Regarding the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), there are three propositions concerning that which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate, and that which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause.
That which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate refers to the unwholesome mental faculty.
That which is both indeterminate and has an indeterminate cause refers to the indeterminate mental faculty.
That which is neither indeterminate nor the cause of the indeterminate refers to the wholesome faculty of mind.
As it is with the faculty of mind, so it is with the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is either a non-neutral cause that is not itself non-neutral, or it is neither non-neutral nor a non-neutral cause.
That which is a non-neutral cause but not itself non-neutral refers to the unwholesome faculty of sorrow.
That which is neither indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor has an indeterminate cause refers to the wholesome faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
It is entirely a condition by way of object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) and possesses a cause.
Eight [factors] are neither immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) nor object-conditions; fourteen are to be analyzed.

The mind-faculty (manas-indriya) is either a successive condition (anantara-pratyaya) or not a successive condition as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), as explained in detail in the case of the mindfulness foundation of feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).
The faculty of equanimity (upekṣā-indriya) is also like this.
The faculty of pleasure (sukha-indriya) is either a successive condition or not a successive condition as an object-condition; thus, three propositions (trikoṭika) are formed.
That which is a sequential condition but not a sequential-object-condition refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) that will necessarily arise in the future and present.
That which is both a sequential condition and a sequential-object-condition refers to the faculty of pleasure in the past and present.

Regarding those that are neither sequential nor objects of the sequential condition: this excludes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) that will necessarily arise in the future when it becomes manifest; it refers to all other future faculties of pleasure.

As with the faculty of pleasure, so it is for the faculties of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); and likewise for the faculties of faith (*śraddhendriya*), energy (*vīryendriya*), mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and wisdom (*prajñendriya*); and likewise for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Eight [conditions] are conditions as object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not conditions as possession (*samanvāgama*); fourteen are both conditions as object-conditions and conditions as possession.
All are conditions as predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and they also possess predominance.
Ten are concomitants (*anuvartin*) but not concomitants of the stream (*srotas*); three are neither concomitants nor concomitants of the stream; nine are to be analyzed.
Ninth: if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are outflows but not the flowing;
if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are neither the flowing nor the outflow.
"Entrances" (*āyatana*) refers to the twelve entrances.
Question:
What are the twelve?
Answer:
The detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Question:
Of these twelve bases (āyatana), how many are material (rūpa) and how many are non-material (arūpa)?
Answer:
It refers to ten [bases] as form, one as non-form, and one as a distinction.
Within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), there are both those that are form and those that are non-form.
What is form (*rūpa*)?
It refers to bodily and vocal actions within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); these are form, while the remainder are not form.
One [of these] is visible, and eleven are invisible.
Ten are with resistance (*sapratigha*), two are without resistance (*apratigha*).
Ten are with outflows (*sāsrava*), two are to be analyzed.
The sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) is either with outflows or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What is the tainted?
It refers to the sense-base of mind associated with tainted mental volition.
What is the untainted?
This refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) associated with untainted mental attention,
and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana), which may be either tainted (sāsrava) or untainted (anāsrava). What is tainted?
This refers to contaminated (sāsrava) bodily and vocal actions, as well as the contaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is uncontaminated (anāsrava)?
It refers to uncontaminated bodily and vocal actions, the uncontaminated aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Eleven [bases] are conditioned; one part of the *dharmāyatana* is either conditioned or unconditioned.
What is conditioned?
This refers to bodily and vocal karma within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
What is the unconditioned?
It refers to space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation.
Eight [bases] are without retribution; four are to be analyzed.
The base of visible form (rūpāyatana) is either with retribution or without retribution.
What is with retribution?
This refers to wholesome and unwholesome forms (rūpāyatana).
What is without retribution?
It refers to those other forms, excluding wholesome and unwholesome forms.
As with the sense-base of form, so it is with the sense-base of sound.
Regarding the sense-base of mind: is it retributive or non-retributive?
What is retributive?
This refers to the unwholesome, the wholesome, and the tainted mental bases (*manāyatana*).
What is without retribution?
This refers to the indeterminate and the untainted mental bases.
As it is with the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), so it is with the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Eleven [of the twelve bases] arise from causes and conditions and are comprised within the world; one part is discernment.

As for the sense-base of phenomena: if it is conditioned, it arises from causes and conditions and is comprised within the world; if it is unconditioned, it does not arise from causes and conditions and is not comprised within the world.
Ten are comprised within form (*rūpa*), one is comprised within name (*nāman*), and one is to be analyzed.
Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), bodily and vocal karma are comprised within form; the remainder are comprised within name.
Six are comprised within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), and six are comprised within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
All are known by wisdom (*jñāna*).
Ten are both known and abandoned by the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*); two are to be analyzed.
Second, if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) and are abandoned;
if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not known through the knowledge of abandonment and are not abandoned.
Eight are not to be cultivated (*abhāvya*); four are to be analyzed (*vibhajya*).
The sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to wholesome spheres of form.
What should not be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate form-base (*rūpāyatana*).
As it is with the form-base, so it is with the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) and the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is explained in detail as in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Spheres.
Eight are non-defiled; four are to be analyzed, as explained above.
Eleven are both results and possess results; one is to be analyzed.
Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there are cases where something is a result but not itself productive of a result; thus, three propositions are established.
That which is a result but not productive of a result refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
That which is both a result and productive of a result refers to conditioned phenomena within the sphere of mental objects.
That which is neither a fruit nor possesses a fruit refers to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Three are non-appropriated; nine are to be analyzed.
The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What is feeling?
It is feeling by its own nature.
What is non-feeling?
That is to say, it is not feeling by its own nature (*svabhāva*).
As it is with the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), so it is also with the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, visible-form-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-object-base.
The twelve bases (āyatana) are either derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta) or not derived from the four great elements.
What is derived from the four great elements?
It refers to nine bases and a portion of two bases.
What is not derived from the four great elements?
It refers to one base (āyatana) and a portion of two bases.
Eleven are with-outgoing (sopadhika); this is the analysis.
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is either with superior (*sottara*) or without superior (*anuttara*).
What is with superior?

It refers to bodily and vocal karma within the sphere of mental objects, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, along with space and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What is the unsurpassed? It refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Ten are "existent" (*bhava*), while two are "discriminated" (*vibhakta*).
Second, if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is "existence" (*bhava*);
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is not "existence.
Ten causes are dissociated (*viprayukta*), one cause is associated (*samprayukta*); this is the analysis.
The dharma-āyatana consists of those mental factors that are associated with causes and those non-mental factors that are dissociated from causes.
The wholesome sphere (kuśala-sthāna) subsumes a portion of four āyatanas, and a portion of those four āyatanas also subsumes the wholesome sphere.
The unwholesome sphere (*akuśalāyatana*) comprises a portion of four bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of those four bases also comprises the unwholesome sphere.
The indeterminate sphere (*avyākṛtāyatana*) comprises eight bases and a portion of four bases, and those eight bases and a portion of four bases also comprise the indeterminate sphere.
The outflows (*āsrava*) include a portion of one base (*āyatana*), and that portion of one base also includes the outflows.
The tainted (*sāsrava*) include ten bases and a portion of two bases, and those ten bases and portion of two bases also include the tainted.
The untainted bases (anāsrava-āyatana) encompass a portion of two bases, and those two bases also encompass a portion of the untainted bases.
Eleven [bases] are distinguished as being either past, future, or present.
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), if conditioned, is either past, future, or present;
if unconditioned, it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and four are to be analyzed, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Bases" (*Vibhaṅga-āyatana-varga*).
Two are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and ten are to be analyzed, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Bases."
Question:
Of the twelve bases (āyatana), how many are trainee (śaikṣa), how many are beyond-training (aśaikṣa), and how many are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training?
Answer:
The detailed explanation is as in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Bases" (*Vibhaṅga-āyatana-varga*).
Ten are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), two are analyzed; the detailed explanation is as in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Bases.
Ten are neither mind nor mental factors (*citta-caitta*) and are not associated with the mind; one is mind itself, and one is analyzed.
The dharma-base (dharmāyatana): if it has an object, it consists of mental factors associated with the mind; if it lacks an object, it consists of non-mental factors not associated with the mind.
Ten [bases] do not follow the mind and are not associated with feeling; one [base] is associated with feeling but does not follow the mind, namely, a portion of discrimination (prajñā).
Regarding the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), it is either concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling, or it is formulated in three propositions.

That which is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal karma concomitant with the mind, as well as mental formations dissociated from the mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) and feeling (vedanā).

That which follows the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and is associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*) refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and its associated aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

That which neither follows the mind nor is associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal actions that do not follow the mind, as well as other bodily and vocal actions; and, excluding those formations dissociated from the mind that follow the mind, it refers to other formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
As with feeling (*vedanā*), so it is with perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Ten [bases] do not follow through with vitarka (*vitarka-anuvartin*) nor are they associated with vicāra (*vicāra-saṃprayukta*); two are to be analyzed (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇīya*).
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it may be with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and with vicāra"?
It refers to the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) associated with mental application accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka but with vicāra"?
This refers to the sense-sphere of mind (manāyatana) associated with mental attention that is without vitarka but with vicāra.
What is without both vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to the sense-sphere of mind associated with mental attention that is without both vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), there are four permutations concerning that which follows the movement of initial inquiry (vitarka) but is not associated with investigation (vicāra).

That which follows the movement of initial inquiry but is not associated with investigation refers to: bodily and vocal karma that follows the movement of initial inquiry; formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) that follow the movement of initial inquiry; and investigation itself when it is associated with initial inquiry.

That which is associated with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) but does not follow from applied thought (*vitarka*) refers to applied thought itself, or those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are associated with contemplation but not associated with applied thought.
That which both follows from applied thought and is associated with contemplation refers to those mental states and mental factors associated with both applied thought and contemplation.

That which neither follows from vitarka nor is associated with vicāra refers to: bodily and vocal karma other than that which follows from vitarka; other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) other than those that follow from vitarka; vicāra that is not associated with vitarka; those mental factors and the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that are neither associated with vitarka nor vicāra; and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
One [of the bases] is both a view and a locus of views; nine loci of views are not views; two are to be analyzed.
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*): if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a locus of views but not a view;
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a view nor a locus of views.
Regarding the dharma-āyatana, there are four permutations concerning that which is "vision" (dṛṣṭi) but not the "locus of vision" (dṛṣṭisthāna).

That which is vision but not the locus of vision refers to the untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) included within the dharma-āyatana, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
"Views that are not view-places" refers to the inclusion of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) not subsumed under views.
"Both views and view-places" refers to the five views and mundane right view (*laukika-samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
"Neither view nor the locus of view" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma-entrances (*dharmāyatana*) not subsumed under view.
Eight [factors] are not the cause of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of a self-body is also not their cause; four [factors] are to be analyzed.
Regarding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*): if it is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it is caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), but the view of a self-identity is not its cause;
if it is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*), it is neither caused by the view of a self-identity, nor is the view of a self-identity its cause.
As it is with the sense-base of form, so it is with the sense-base of sound.
Regarding the sense-base of mind, the detailed explanation is as in the foundation of mindfulness of feeling.
Regarding the sense-base of phenomena, the detailed explanation is as in the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
Question: Among the twelve bases (āyatana), how many are karma and not the maturation of karma?
Answer: All should be analyzed.
The eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) is either karmic retribution but not karma, or neither karmic retribution nor karma.
That which is karmic retribution but not karma refers to the eye-base born of maturation; the remainder is neither karmic retribution nor karma.
As it is with the eye base, so it is with the ear base, nose base, odor base, tongue base, taste base, body base, tangible-base, and mind base.
The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is either karma that is not a karmic result, or it is divided into three categories.
That which is karma but not a karmic result refers to bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
That which is a karmic result but not karma refers to the sense-base of form born of maturation (vipākaja-rūpāyatana).
That which is neither karma nor the maturation of karma refers to the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) other than that which is produced by karma or born of the maturation of karma;
as well as the sense-sphere of sound (śabdāyatana), which may be either karma that is not the maturation of karma, or neither karma nor the maturation of karma.
Regarding that which is karma but not the retribution of karma: this refers to verbal action; the remainder is neither karma nor the retribution of karma.
As for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it may be karma but not the retribution of karma; thus, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
"Karma that is not karmic retribution" refers to bodily and vocal karma, as well as volitional karma (cetanā-karma) not subsumed under retribution.
"Karmic retribution that is not karma" refers to the factors included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that arise from retribution and are not subsumed under volition.
That which is both karma and the retribution of karma refers to volitional karma born of retribution (*vipākaja-cetanā-karma*).

That which is neither karma nor the retribution of karma refers to all other bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) apart from those factors that constitute karma and the factors born of the retribution of karma.
Eight [bases] are neither karma nor concomitants of karma; one is a concomitant of karma but not karma; three are to be analyzed.
As for the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), it is either karma that is not a concomitant of karma, or neither karma nor a concomitant of karma.
Regarding "karma that is not concomitant with karma": this refers to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), which is matter; the remainder is neither karma nor concomitant with karma.
The same applies to the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
As for the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is either karma or concomitant with karma; four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated.

That which is concomitant with karma but is not karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that is not concomitant with karma, as well as other bodily and vocal karmas and volitional karma (*cetanā-karma*).

That which is concomitant with karma but is not karma refers to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), as well as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) concomitant with karma that is not subsumed under volition.
That which is both karma and accompanied by karma refers to bodily and vocal karma that follows after karma.
That which is neither karma nor accompanied by karma refers to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) other than karma and those phenomena accompanied by karma.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), some are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) but not visible matter; this is formulated in three propositions.
As for those that are derived matter but not visible matter, they refer to eight bases and a portion of two bases.
That which is derived matter and also visible matter refers to one base (*āyatana*).
That which is neither derived matter nor visible matter refers to one base and a portion of two bases.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), there are those that are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) yet are non-obstructive matter (*apratigha-rūpa*).
This is explained through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). That which is derived matter yet is non-obstructive matter refers to a small portion of one base.
That which is resistant matter but not derived matter refers to a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
That which is derived matter and also resistant matter refers to nine bases and a small portion of one base.
That which is neither derived matter nor obstructive matter refers to one base (*āyatana*) and a small portion of another base.
All of this is profound and difficult to understand; it is difficult to understand because of its profundity.
Question:
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are both wholesome and have wholesome causes?
Answer:
All [bases] should be analyzed in this way.
As for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), it is either a wholesome cause that is not wholesome, or neither wholesome nor a wholesome cause.
That which is a wholesome cause but not wholesome refers to the eye-base born of the maturation of wholesome karma; the remainder are neither wholesome nor wholesome causes.
As it is with the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), so it is with the ear-base, nose-base, odor-base, tongue-base, taste-base, body-base, and tangible-base.
As for the form-base (*rūpāyatana*), it is either a wholesome cause that is not itself wholesome; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are to be formulated.
That which is a wholesome cause but not wholesome refers to the form bases (*rūpāyatana*) born of wholesome retribution.
That which is both wholesome and a wholesome cause refers to the wholesome form bases.
That which is neither wholesome nor a wholesome cause refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome form bases.
As it is with the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), so it is with the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
As for the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), it is either wholesome and has wholesome causes, or it is neither wholesome nor has wholesome causes.
That which is wholesome and has wholesome causes refers to wholesome sounds; the remainder are neither wholesome nor have wholesome causes.
The dharma-base (dharmāyatana) is either wholesome or not a cause of the wholesome; a detailed explanation is as given for the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Question:
Among the twelve bases (āyatanas), how many are unwholesome and also causes of the unwholesome?
Answer: All [categories] should be analyzed.
As for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), it is either not-unwholesome-caused but not unwholesome, or neither unwholesome nor unwholesome-caused.

That which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) born of the retribution of an unwholesome [action]. Other [bases] have neither an unwholesome cause nor are they themselves unwholesome.
As it is with the eye-base, so it is with the ear-base, nose-base, odor-base, tongue-base, taste-base, body-base, and tangible-base.
Regarding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), it may have an unwholesome cause but not itself be unwholesome; this constitutes three propositions.
That which has an unwholesome cause but is not itself unwholesome refers to the sense-base of form born of the retribution of the unwholesome.
That which is unwholesome and also has an unwholesome cause refers to the unwholesome form-base (*rūpāyatana*).
That which is neither unwholesome nor has an unwholesome cause refers to the indeterminate and wholesome form-bases.
The sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) is either unwholesome and also a cause of the unwholesome, or it is neither unwholesome nor a cause of the unwholesome.
That which is unwholesome and also a cause of the unwholesome refers to the unwholesome sound-base; the remainder are neither unwholesome nor causes of the unwholesome.
The mind-base (*manāyatana*) is as explained for the mind-faculty (*manendriya*).
The mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*) is as explained for the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Eight [of these] are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and are also causes of the indeterminate; four are to be analyzed.
Regarding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), there are three propositions concerning that which has an indeterminate cause (*avyākṛta-hetu*) but is not itself indeterminate.
That which has an indeterminate cause but is not itself indeterminate refers to unwholesome (*akuśala*) form-bases.
That which has an indeterminate cause and is also indeterminate refers to indeterminate form-bases.
That which is neither indeterminate nor a cause for the indeterminate refers to wholesome form-bases (*rūpāyatana*).
As with the form-base, so it is with the sound-base and the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
Regarding the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*), there are four permutations concerning that which is indeterminate but not a cause for the indeterminate.
That which is indeterminate but not a cause of the indeterminate refers to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is a cause of the indeterminate but is not itself indeterminate refers to the entry into unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma-praveśa*).
That which is indeterminate and also has an indeterminate cause refers to the entry into indeterminate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
That which is neither indeterminate nor has an indeterminate cause refers to the entry into wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*).
Eleventh: The object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) and that which has a cause (sahetuka) are partially distinguished.
As for the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana): if it is conditioned (saṃskṛta), it is both an object-condition and has a cause;
if it is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it is neither an object-condition nor does it have a cause.
The ten [bases] are neither immediate antecedents nor conditions as objects of an immediate antecedent; for these two, there is a distinction.
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it may be an immediate antecedent but not a condition as an object of an immediate antecedent; thus, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) are formed.

That which is a sequential condition but not a sequential-object condition refers to the future mental sphere (*manāyatana*) that is certain to arise when it becomes present, as well as the past and present final mental spheres at the moment of an Arhat’s death.

That which is both sequential and a sequential condition (samanantarapratyaya) refers to all past and present mental bases (manāyatana), with the exception of the final mental base at the moment of death of an Arhat in the past or present.

Regarding that which is neither sequential nor a sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*): this refers to the mental sense-base (*manāyatana*) of the future that is certain to arise in the present, excluding it;
as for other future mental sense-bases and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*), they may be sequential but not a sequential condition, or [neither], forming three propositions.

Those that are sequential conditions but not sequential-object conditions refer to: the mental factors and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) that will necessarily arise in the future as they manifest; the mental factors and the dharma-base of the final moment of consciousness at death of an Arhat in the past or present; and the mental factors and the dharma-base of the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), both those already arisen and those yet to arise.

Those that are both sequential and sequential-object conditions refer to all other past and present mental factors and the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), excluding the final mind and mental factors at the moment of death of an Arhat in the past or present.

That which is neither sequential nor a sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) refers to: with the exception of those future mental factors (*citta-dharma*) and the base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*) that are certain to arise in the present; other future mental factors and the base of mental objects; with the exception of sequential non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), other non-associated formations, bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Ten [bases] are object-conditions but not possessing-conditions; one is both an object-condition and a possessing-condition; this is the classification.

Regarding the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), if it is a mental factor (caitta), it is both an object-condition and a possessing-condition; the remainder are neither object-conditions nor possessing-conditions.
Eleventh: The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is both a dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) and possesses dominance (ādhipatya), with one distinction.
If it is conditioned (saṃskṛta), it is both a dominant condition and possesses dominance;
if it is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it is a dominant condition but does not possess dominance.
Ten [bases] are concomitants of the fluxes but are not themselves fluxes; two are to be analyzed.
As for the mind-base (*manāyatana*): if it is with-outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a concomitant of the fluxes but is not itself a flux;
if it is without-outflows (*anāsrava*), it is neither a flux nor a concomitant of the fluxes.
Regarding the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), there are three categories concerning that which conforms to the fluxes (āsrava) but is not itself a flux:
1. That which conforms to the fluxes but is not a flux refers to contaminated phenomena (sāsravadharma) not included within the fluxes themselves.
2. That which both enters into the fluxes and conforms to them refers to the four fluxes (catvāra āsravāḥ).
"Neither outflows nor concomitants of outflows" refers to the inclusion of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas not subsumed under the outflows.
*Saṃgītiparyāya-abhidharma-śāstra*, Volume 11;
*Saṃgītiparyāya-abhidharma-śāstra*, Volume 12.
The Venerable Vasumitra composed this;
translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.
From the remainder of Chapter Seven of the *Sāhasrikapraśna-śāstra*, "The Skandhas": "Skandha" refers to the five skandhas.
Question:
What are the five?
Answer:
The detailed explanation is as above.
Question:
Of these five aggregates (skandhas), how many are form (rūpa) and how many are non-form (arūpa)?
Answer:
One is material form; four are non-material.
Four are invisible; one is discernible.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either visible or invisible.
What is visible?
It refers to one base (āyatana).
What is the invisible?
It refers to nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
Four are non-obstructive; one is to be discerned.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either with resistance (sapratigha) or without resistance (apratigha).
What is with resistance?
It refers to the ten bases (āyatana).
What is non-resistant?
It refers to a small portion of one base (āyatana).
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What are the outflows (sāsrava)?
They are the ten bases (āyatana) associated with outflows and a portion of one base.
What are the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
It refers to a portion of one base (āyatana) and the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha),
which may be either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What is with outflows?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with outflowing mental attention.
What is the untainted?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with untainted mental attention.
As it is with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregates of perception and consciousness.
As for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
What is with outflows?
This refers to the aggregate of formations associated with outflowing minds and those dissociated from outflowing minds.
What is the untainted?
This refers to the aggregate of formations associated with untainted minds and those dissociated from untainted minds.
All things are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Question:
Among the aggregates (*skandha*), how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
Answer: All [categories] should be analyzed.
As for the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), it may be retributive (savipāka) or non-retributive (avipāka).
What is retribution?
It refers to the unwholesome aggregate of form and the wholesome, out-flowing aggregate of form.
What is non-retribution?
This refers to the aggregate of form that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
As it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
All of these arise from causes and conditions and are comprised within the worldly realm (*loka-saṃgṛhīta*).
One is comprised of form (*rūpa*), and four are comprised of name (*nāman*).
One is comprised of the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), and three are comprised of the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*); this is the classification.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either comprised within the internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) or comprised within the external bases (bāhyāyatana).
What is comprised within the internal bases?
It refers to the five internal bases.
What is comprised by the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)?
It refers to the five external bases and a portion of one external base.
All of these are known by wisdom (*jñāna*).
If it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) and is abandoned;
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is not known through the knowledge of abandonment and is not abandoned.
Question:
Regarding the aggregates (skandhas), how many should be cultivated and how many should not be cultivated?
Answer: All of them should be analyzed.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What is to be cultivated?
It refers to the wholesome aggregate of form.
What is not to be cultivated?
It refers to the unwholesome and the indeterminate form-aggregate (*rūpaskandha*).

As it is with the form-aggregate, so it is with the feeling-aggregate (*vedanāskandha*), perception-aggregate (*saṃjñāskandha*), consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), and formations-aggregate (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Question:
Among the aggregates (skandhas), how many are defiled (kliṣṭa) and how many are non-defiled?
Answer:
All [categories] should be analyzed.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either defiled (sāsrava) or undefiled (anāsrava). What is defiled?
This refers to the unwholesome aggregate of form and the obscured-unspecified aggregate of form.
What is not defiled?
It refers to the wholesome aggregate of form and the non-obscured-unspecified aggregate of form.

As it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is with the aggregates of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), and formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
All of these are both effects and possess effects.
Four are not to be clung to (*anupādānīya*); one is to be analyzed (*prabheda*).
The aggregate of form is either grasped or not grasped.
What is grasped?
That which is grasped by its own nature.
What is "not-feeling" (*anupagata*)?
It is that which is not feeling by its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Four [elements] are not derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); one part is discriminative (*vikalpita*).
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is either derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta) or not derived from the four great elements.
What is derived from the four great elements?
It refers to nine bases (āyatana) and a portion of two bases.
What is not derived from the four great elements?
It refers to a small portion of one base (*āyatana*).
All [of these] are surpassable (*sottara*).
Question:
Among the aggregates (skandhas), how many are existent (bhava) and how many are non-existent (abhava)?
Answer:
All [categories] should be analyzed:
if the aggregates (skandhas) are with outflows (sāsrava), they are existence (bhava);
if they are without outflows (anāsrava), they are not existence.
First, dissociation from causes; second, association with causes; third, analysis.
As for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): if it is a mental factor (*caitta*), it is associated with causes;
if it is not a mental factor, it is dissociated from causes.
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*) but is not an aggregate (*skandha*).
That which is included within the wholesome bases but is not an aggregate refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
That which is included within the aggregates but is not a wholesome base refers to the five aggregates that are unwholesome or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Those included within the wholesome bases (*kuśalāyatana*) that are also aggregates (*skandha*) refer to the five wholesome aggregates.
Those not included within the wholesome bases and not being aggregates refer to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
A portion of the five aggregates is included within the unwholesome bases (*akuśalāyatana*), and a portion of the five aggregates is also included within the unwholesome bases.
Alternatively, there are four permutations regarding that which is included within the indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) but is not an aggregate (*skandha*).
That which is included within the indeterminate bases but is not an aggregate refers to space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is included within the aggregates but is not an indeterminate base refers to the five aggregates that are wholesome or unwholesome.
That which is included in the indeterminate bases (*avyākṛtāyatana*) and is also an aggregate (*skandha*) refers to the five indeterminate aggregates.
That which is neither included in the indeterminate bases nor is an aggregate refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
One portion of one aggregate is included in the outflows (*āsrava*), and one portion of one aggregate also includes the outflows.
The *sāsrava-āyatana* (bases with outflows) subsumes a portion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and a portion of the five aggregates also subsumes the *sāsrava-āyatana*.
Alternatively, the *anāsrava-āyatana* (bases without outflows) subsumes that which is not an aggregate; these form four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those included within the untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) but not within the aggregates (*skandha*) are space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Those included within the aggregates but not within the untainted bases are the five tainted aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).
That which is included within the untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*) and is also an aggregate (*skandha*) refers to the five untainted aggregates.
That which is neither included within the untainted bases nor is an aggregate is a thing that cannot be found.
The aggregates (skandhas) are either past, future, or present.
The aggregates are either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
This refers to the five aggregates that are wholesome.
What are those that are unwholesome?
They refer to the five aggregates that are unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the five aggregates that are indeterminate.
These aggregates are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is that which is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the five aggregates bound to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the form realm?
This refers to the five aggregates associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What are those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
This refers to the four aggregates associated with the formless realm.
What is "unbound"?
It refers to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Question:
Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*): how many are in training (*śaikṣa*), how many are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither in training nor beyond training?
Answer:
All should be analyzed accordingly.
The aggregates (skandhas) are either those of one in training (śaikṣa), those of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), or those of neither training nor beyond training.
What are those of one in training?
They are the five aggregates of one in training.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) of one beyond training.
What is that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
That is to say, the five aggregates with outflows (sāsrava).
Question:
Of these aggregates, how many are abandoned by vision (darśana-heya) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?
Answer: All should be analyzed.
As for the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), if it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
If they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not to be abandoned.
What is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
It refers to ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
What is "not to be abandoned"?
It refers to a small portion of one *āyatana*.
As for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), it is either to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), or to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not to be abandoned at all.
What is abandonment through vision?

It is the abandonment of the aggregate of feeling by those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) through the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth. How is it abandoned?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It is the aggregate of feeling belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the path and abandon it through cultivation.
How is it abandoned?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with the ten proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the untainted yet out-flowing aggregate of feeling.
How is it not abandoned?
This refers to the untainted aggregate of feeling (*anāsrava-vedanā-skandha*). As with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregates of perception and consciousness.

As for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is either to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), or to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or not to be abandoned at all (*aheya*).
What is abandonment through vision (*darśana-prahāṇa*)?

It is when the form aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is abandoned by the patience of non-interruption (*ānantarya-kṣānti*) and so forth of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
How is it abandoned?

This refers to the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) associated with them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them.

What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? It is the aggregate of formations belonging to those who have seen the path and are training (*śaikṣa*), which is abandoned through cultivation.
How are they abandoned?

It refers to the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through cultivation, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) associated with them, the bodily and vocal actions produced by them, the formations dissociated from mind produced by them, and the non-defiled outflowing (*sāsrava*) aggregate of formations.
What is the non-abandonable?
It refers to the untainted aggregate of formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra-skandha*).

This is analyzed as follows: first, that which is neither mind (*citta*), nor mental factors (*caitta*), nor associated with mind; second, that which is both mental factors and associated with mind; third, that which is exclusively mind; and fourth, the classification [of these categories].

Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): if it is dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta*), it is neither mind, nor a mental factor (*caitta*), nor associated with mind; other mental factors are associated with mind.

There is a twofold classification: those that follow the movement of the mind alone and are not associated with feeling (*vedanā*), and those that follow the movement of the mind and are also associated with feeling.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is either concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*), or neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling.

That which is concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling refers to bodily and vocal actions that are concomitant with the mind; the remainder are neither concomitant with the mind nor associated with feeling.

Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), there are three propositions concerning those that are concomitant with the mind (*cittānuvartin*) but not associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*).
Those that are concomitant with the mind but not associated with feeling refer to the formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that are concomitant with the mind.
That which follows the mind and is also associated with feeling refers to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that is associated with the mind.

That which neither follows the mind nor is associated with feeling refers to the aggregate of formations dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha), excluding those formations dissociated from the mind that do follow the mind, as well as other such formations dissociated from the mind.
As it is with feeling (*vedanā*), so it is with perception (*saṃjñā*), excluding their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Question:
Among the aggregates (*skandha*), how many proceed in accordance with vitarka (*vitarka-anuvartin*) but are not associated with vicāra (*vicāra-saṃprayukta*)?
Answer: All [of these] should be analyzed.
As for the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), it is either accompanied by vitarka but not associated with vicāra, or neither accompanied by vitarka nor associated with vicāra.

Regarding those that follow from vitarka but are not associated with vicāra: these refer to the bodily and vocal actions that follow from vitarka. All others neither follow from vitarka nor are associated with vicāra.
As for the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), it may be with both vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka but with vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention that possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "without vitarka but with vicāra"?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention that is without vitarka but with vicāra.
What is without both vitarka and vicāra?
This refers to the aggregate of feeling associated with mental attention that is without both vitarka and vicāra.
As with the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), so it is with the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there are four permutations concerning those that follow from initial mental application (*vitarka-anuvartin*) but are not associated with sustained investigation (*vicāra-samprayukta*).

Those that follow from initial mental application but are not associated with sustained investigation refer to the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that follow from initial mental application, as well as sustained investigation itself when it is associated with initial mental application.
