It is known by one knowledge—namely, the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)—but it is not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), nor is it driven by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
As with the dharma-base, so too is the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).

The eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is subsumed under two elements, one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*); it is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the desire and form realms, as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is comprised of one element, but is neither included within the bases (*āyatana*) nor the aggregates (*skandha*); it is not known by knowledge (*jñāna*), not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As with the visual consciousness element, so it is with the auditory consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*) and the tactile consciousness element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*).

The nose-consciousness element (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) is subsumed under two elements, one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). It is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatragakleśa) of the desire realm, as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya).

That is, the nose-consciousness element (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) is comprised of one element, but is neither included in the bases (āyatana) nor in the aggregates (skandha). It is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and not driven by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
As it is with the nose-consciousness element, so it is with the tongue-consciousness element (jihvāvijñānadhātu).

The consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) is comprised within two elements, one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha); it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

The mind element (manodhātu) is comprised within one element, neither a base nor an aggregate; it is not known by any knowledge, not cognized by any consciousness, and not driven by any underlying tendency.

The female faculty (*strīndriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by six types of knowledge—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the desire realm, as well as by those proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The female faculty (strī-indriya) is not included within the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and not driven by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
As it is with the female faculty, so it is with the male faculty (puruṣa-indriya).

The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the three realms, as well as by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any knowledge (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any latent tendency (*anuśaya*).

The pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all latent tendencies of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), by all pervasive latent tendencies of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and by those latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any knowledge (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any latent proclivity (*anuśaya*).

The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all latent proclivities of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is driven by all latent proclivities except for doubt (*vicikitsā*) that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it; all other latent proclivities of the desire realm drive it.

The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any latent tendency (*anuśaya*).

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the subsequent cognition (*anvayajñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all latent tendencies of the desire realm.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-field (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any knowledge (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any underlying tendency (*anuśaya*).

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-field, and one aggregate; it is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and is cognized by one consciousness; it is driven by all underlying tendencies.

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-field (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any knowledge (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any latent tendency (*anuśaya*).

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is subsumed under one element, one sense-field, and one aggregate. It is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); it is cognized by one consciousness; and it is driven by all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatragānuśaya*) of the three realms, as well as by the latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*).

That is, the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the sense-bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by knowledge (jñāna), not cognized by consciousness (vijñāna), and not driven by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
As it is with the faculty of faith, so it is with the faculties of energy (vīryendriya), mindfulness (smṛtīndriya), concentration (samādhīndriya), and wisdom (prajñendriya).

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate; it is known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), as well as the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is cognized by one consciousness. It is driven by all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of the desire realm, as well as by those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is not subsumed under any element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); it is not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any underlying tendency (*anuśaya*).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is subsumed under three elements, two sense-bases, and three aggregates; it is known by seven cognitions—excluding the cognitions of suffering, origin, and cessation—and is cognized by one consciousness; it is not driven by any underlying tendency.

That is to say, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is not subsumed under the elements (dhātu), the sense-bases (āyatana), or the aggregates (skandha); it is not known by knowledge, not cognized by consciousness, and not driven by the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," so it is with the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).

The proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are comprised within one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). They are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*); they are cognized by one consciousness (*vijñāna*). These proclivities bind all other proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

The proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are not subsumed under any realm (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); they are not known by any cognition (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any proclivity.

The proclivities associated with the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) are subsumed under one realm, one sense-base, and one aggregate. They are known by seven cognitions—excluding the subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the cognitions of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all proclivities abandoned through the vision of origin, as well as by all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are not comprised within any element (*dhātu*), sense-base (*āyatana*), or aggregate (*skandha*); they are not known by any knowledge (*jñāna*), not cognized by any consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by any proclivity.

The proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) belonging to the desire realm are comprised within one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate. They are known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*)—and are cognized by one consciousness. With the exception of the unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) that takes as its object the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [truth] and is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation belonging to the desire realm, all other proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of cessation belonging to the desire realm act as proclivities, as do all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

That is to say, the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] that are bound to the desire realm are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by the knowledges (*jñāna*), not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by proclivities.
As it is for those abandoned through the vision of cessation, so it is for those abandoned through the vision of the path.

The proclivities (anuśaya) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation are subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). They are known by seven knowledges—excluding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledges of cessation and the path—and are cognized by one consciousness. They are driven by all proclivities of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as by all pervasive proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya).

These are the proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). They are not subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), the bases (*āyatana*), or the aggregates (*skandha*); they are not known by [the six] knowledges (*jñāna*), not cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not driven by proclivities.

As it is for those associated with the desire realm, so it is for those associated with the form realm and the formless realm. The difference is as follows: the proclivities associated with the form and formless realms that are abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and through cultivation, are known by six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of cessation and the path. The rest is as previously stated.
Homage to the Most Perfectly Awakened One, the Unconditioned, the Supreme Honored One;
homage to the Most Utterly Quiescent, as well as the Sublime Path of the Three Vehicles;
homage to the Most Tranquil Mind, the Sangha of Pure Precepts and Cool Serenity.
Now, taking refuge in the Triple Gem, I wish to communicate a slight understanding;
may you deign to bestow your majestic spiritual power so that it may surely flow forth without obstruction.
Regarding the wondrous and most profound meaning, the venerable sages of antiquity—
Ultimately free from obstruction, he compiled them into various scriptures;
